name: Codex Musica — browse index (Tier-1 data for the lazy-loaded app)

items.name: Honky-tonk
items.lineage: Post-WWII Texas-and-Tennessee honky-tonk country tradition that dominated commercial country from 1945-1955 — codified through Ernest Tubb (Walking the Floor Over You 1941, the founding honky-tonk recording), Hank Williams (the honky-tonk figure, Lovesick Blues 1949, Im So Lonesome I Could Cry 1949, his 1953 death at 29 closed the founding era), Lefty Frizzell (the most-imitated honky-tonk vocalist), Webb Pierce, Faron Young, Ray Price; characterized by amplified-band dance-hall instrumentation (pedal steel guitar, fiddle, electric guitar, upright bass, drums) and lyrical content of working-class drinking, cheating, and barroom-romantic-loss
items.description: Post-WWII Texas-and-Oklahoma honky-tonk country tradition (1945-1965), forged in working-class oil-and-cattle dance halls between Dallas and Bakersfield. Standard ensemble: pedal steel (lead voice), Telecaster or hollow-body electric guitar, fiddle, upright bass moving to electric bass by mid-1950s, drum kit with brush-and-stick shuffle. Tight I-IV-V chord vocabulary in major keys; characteristic 4/4 shuffle (boom-chick) or two-step rhythmic feel. Vocal-forward storytelling about cheating, drinking, and lost love. Distinguished from Nashville Sound by absence of strings-and-choir and by direct unfiltered emotional register; distinguished from later Bakersfield Sound by less rock-and-roll backbeat. Hank Williams, Lefty Frizzell, Webb Pierce, Faron Young codified the form.
exemplars: Ernest Tubb — Walking the Floor Over You
Lefty Frizzell — If You’ve Got the Money

items.name: Bakersfield country
items.lineage: California Central Valley honky-tonk-derived country tradition that emerged in 1950s-60s Bakersfield as a West Coast reaction against the smoother Nashville Sound — codified through Buck Owens (Capitol Records Bakersfield voice from 1959 onward, Together Again 1964) and Merle Haggard (post-Owens Bakersfield extension, Mama Tried 1968, Okie from Muskogee 1969), played by the Buckaroos (Owens band led by Don Rich) and the Strangers (Haggards band); built on Telecaster-and-pedal-steel-foreground arrangement, faster shuffle tempos than typical Nashville fare, and Dust-Bowl-migration cultural lineage
items.description: California-Bakersfield country tradition (1955-1975), developed by Okie-migrant musicians displaced by Dust Bowl into San Joaquin Valley honky-tonks. Buck Owens and Merle Haggard codified the sound: Telecaster lead with characteristic biting twang (no compression), aggressive 2-and-4 backbeat (rock-and-roll-influenced), pedal steel less central than honky-tonk, drum kit driving the front. Distinguished from Nashville Sound by deliberate rejection of orchestrated strings-and-choir; distinguished from Texas-honky-tonk by faster tempo and rock-derived rhythmic foundation. Capitol Records’ Ken Nelson productions captured the aesthetic. Influenced country-rock and later alt-country.

items.name: Outlaw country
items.lineage: Early-to-mid 1970s reaction against the slick Nashville Sound establishment — codified through Waylon Jennings (Honky Tonk Heroes 1973, Dreaming My Dreams 1975), Willie Nelson (his return to Texas after the early-1970s Nashville disillusionment, Shotgun Willie 1973, Red Headed Stranger 1975, the Phases and Stages 1974), Kris Kristofferson, Johnny Cash (whose career outlaw turn aligned with the movement), David Allan Coe, Townes Van Zandt, the broader Austin Texas scene (Jerry Jeff Walker, Guy Clark) where outlaw country found its sympathetic recording-and-touring infrastructure outside the Nashville Music Row system
items.description: Outlaw country tradition (1972-1985) emerging from Austin-Texas musicians rejecting Nashville session-musician system. Willie Nelson, Waylon Jennings, Kris Kristofferson, Tompall Glaser established the form: songwriter-driven repertoire, road bands instead of session musicians, gritty unfiltered vocal production, rock-rhythm-section foundation, pedal steel still present but less polished than countrypolitan. Distinguished from Nashville Sound by deliberate-anti-polish posture and from honky-tonk by post-1972 timeline and rock-rhythm-section integration. Wanted! The Outlaws (1976 RCA compilation) was the commercial codification.
exemplars: Waylon Jennings — Lonesome On’ry and Mean

items.name: Bluegrass
items.lineage: Kentucky-and-Appalachian string-band genre codified by Bill Monroe (the founding figure, his Blue Grass Boys band of 1939-onward giving the genre its name, with the 1945-1948 lineup of Earl Scruggs banjo, Lester Flatt guitar, Chubby Wise fiddle, Cedric Rainwater bass marking the genre birth) — extended through Lester Flatt and Earl Scruggs (their post-Monroe Foggy Mountain Boys, 1948 onward), the Stanley Brothers, Jim and Jesse, the Osborne Brothers, the second-wave New Grass Revival (Sam Bush, Bela Fleck) and the modern Alison Krauss and Union Station era
items.description: Bluegrass tradition (1945-present), invented by Bill Monroe & His Blue Grass Boys (Earl Scruggs three-finger banjo joining 1945). Standard five-piece ensemble: 5-string banjo (Scruggs-style three-finger roll), mandolin, fiddle, dreadnought acoustic guitar (G-run rhythm), upright bass; no drums. Solo breaks rotate between instruments at fast tempos (140-200 BPM); three-part vocal harmony with characteristic high-lonesome lead. Repertoire: traditional ballads, gospel quartet material, instrumental tunes derived from old-time fiddle. Distinguished from old-time by Scruggs banjo (versus clawhammer), faster tempo, and codified solo-rotation form. Stanley Brothers, Flatt & Scruggs, Jimmy Martin extended the canon.
exemplars: Bill Monroe — Blue Moon of Kentucky

items.name: Old-time Appalachian
items.lineage: Pre-WWII Appalachian and southern American string-band tradition — fiddle, banjo, guitar (sometimes mandolin and bass) playing dance tunes and ballads in regional repertoires including Round Peak (Galax-Mt-Airy NC), Hammons Family (West Virginia), Skillet Lickers (Georgia), and the broader tradition documented through 1920s commercial Bristol sessions and the Library of Congress field-recording campaign
items.description: Old-time Appalachian string-band tradition (pre-1945 origins, ongoing revival post-1960s), the pre-bluegrass form of Southern-mountain music. Standard ensemble: fiddle (lead voice with characteristic cross-tunings AEAE/ADAE), clawhammer banjo (frailing-style downstroke, distinct from Scruggs three-finger), guitar (boom-chuck rhythm), sometimes upright bass or harmonica. Repertoire: square-dance tunes, Child ballads, gospel-revival hymns, breakdowns. Distinguished from bluegrass by clawhammer-not-Scruggs banjo, more relaxed tempo, vocal-with-banjo-and-fiddle (no instrumental solo rotation), modal-not-bluegrass-tonal harmony. Tommy Jarrell, Roscoe Holcomb, New Lost City Ramblers codified the modern revival.

items.name: Texas conjunto
items.lineage: Texas-Mexican (tejano) accordion-and-bajo-sexto dance-band tradition of South Texas and the Texas-Mexico borderlands, developed in the late-nineteenth-century from German-Czech accordion-polka traditions imported into Texas through Central European migration — codified through Narciso Martínez (Texas conjunto founding figure, recording 1936 onward), Santiago Jiménez Sr, Valerio Longoria, Tony de la Rosa, Flaco Jiménez
items.description: Texas conjunto / norteño tradition (1920s-present), polka-and-waltz-derived dance music from Texas-Mexican borderlands. Standard ensemble: button accordion (lead, three-row diatonic), bajo sexto (12-string rhythm-and-bass guitar), upright or electric bass (tololoche), drum kit. Repertoire: polkas, waltzes, redovas (Czech-Bohemian forms transmitted via 19th-century Central-European migration to Texas), corridos (narrative ballads), rancheras. Distinguished from Mexican mariachi by accordion-led-not-violin-led ensemble; distinguished from Tejano (Selena-era pop-conjunto) by absence of synthesizers and rock backbeat. Narciso Martínez, Santiago Jiménez Sr, Flaco Jiménez, Ramón Ayala established the canon.

items.name: Mariachi
items.lineage: Mexican son tradition centered on Jalisco-Nayarit highlands and codified through the early-20th-century studio era (1930s-1950s commercial recording boom) into the standardized mariachi-orquesta of two trumpets, three-to-six violins, vihuela rhythm-chord, guitarrón six-string acoustic-bass, and Spanish guitar. Derived from rural son jalisciense and son alteño fiddle-and-vihuela ensembles, transformed by 1907-onward Cocula-and-Tecalitlán municipal contests, professionalized via the 1925-onward Mexico City cantina circuit, and globalized through 1930s-onward Mexican golden-age cinema. The bolero-ranchera-and-son repertoire alternates 6/8-against-3/4 hemiola with vocally projected open-throat ranchera belting over instrumental triadic-and-harmonic-third doublings.
items.description: Mariachi ensemble tradition (Jalisco origin, 19th-century ranchera roots; trumpet incorporated 1930s, professional codification 1940s-1960s). Standard ensemble: 4-8 violins playing in unison-and-thirds, 2 trumpets, guitarrón (large six-string acoustic bass), vihuela (small five-string rhythm guitar), 1-2 acoustic guitars, occasional harp. Vocal lead with full-ensemble harmony backgrounds. Repertoire: rancheras (3/4 or 4/4 ballads), sones (regional dance forms), boleros, huapangos. Distinguished from norteño (different ensemble — accordion-led) and Spanish flamenco (Andalusian, not Mexican). Standardized aesthetic codified by Mariachi Vargas de Tecalitlán (1898 founded, modern recordings from 1944).
exemplars: Vicente Fernández — Por tu maldito amor
Linda Ronstadt — Canciones de Mi Padre

items.name: Ranchera
items.lineage: Mexican rural-pastoral nostalgic-song-form codified 1920s-1940s in the Mexican-revolutionary-era-and-cinema-golden-age, performed by mariachi-conjunto ensemble (typically violin-section, trumpet-pair, guitar, vihuela, guitarrón) with prominent solo-vocalist. The canonical ranchera structure: simple three-or-four-chord harmonic-progression (I-IV-V or I-vi-IV-V), 3/4 or 4/4 meter, sentimental lyrics about rural-homeland, lost-love, drinking-and-sorrow, mother-figure. The 1936-onward Mexican-golden-age-cinema established ranchera as the national-cinematic-musical-export, recorded by ranchera-cantante singers (typically male-tenor or female-mezzo) with characteristic grito-mexicano high-falsetto-cry interjection. The genre influenced Tejano, mariachi-revival, and modern norteño popular-styles.
items.description: Ranchera (codified 1930s-onward through Mexican cinema and radio establishment of mariachi-orchestra-and-solo-singer performance practice; foundations in 19th-century rural-rancho folk song-tradition with rural-and-pastoral lyric content; golden era 1940s-1960s through Pedro Infante, Jorge Negrete, José Alfredo Jiménez, Lola Beltrán, Lucha Reyes establishing the ranchera-singer-with-mariachi-ensemble idiom; tradition extends through Chavela Vargas's spare-and-emotionally-raw 1990s revival recordings and through Vicente Fernández's late-20th-century continuation; remains foundational to Mexican popular-music identity), the Mexican folk-popular song-form from rural-ranch (rancho) tradition. Defined by emotional-expressive vocal-delivery foreground (the ranchera-singer affect of full-chest-belt and grito-shout cathartic expression, distinguishing ranchera from contemporaneous bolero's smoother vocal-delivery and from mariachi-instrumental tradition), waltz-3/4 or bolero-2/4 meters, mariachi-ensemble accompaniment (the standard 4-8 violins + 2 trumpets + guitarrón + vihuela + classical-guitars ensemble, distinguishing ranchera from norteño-accordion-foreground and corrido-narrative-form), lyric content centered on lost-love-and-homeland-and-loneliness themes (ranchera subjects: el amor perdido, la querencia rancho, la nostalgia, la macho-emotional-expression tradition), and strophic verse-with-refrain song-form structure typically 3-4 minutes long. Distinguished from mariachi proper by song-form-and-vocal foreground (ranchera is the SONG; mariachi is the INSTRUMENTATION that accompanies ranchera, son, bolero, etc.); distinguished from corrido by emotional-content vs narrative-content lyric register and bolero-or-waltz meter vs corrido-6/8 meter; distinguished from bolero by emotional-cathartic-belt vocal-foreground vs bolero-romantic-smooth delivery.

items.name: Corrido
items.lineage: Mexican narrative-ballad song-form documented mid-19th-century onward, descended from Spanish-romance medieval narrative-poetic-tradition and re-rooted in the Mexican-revolutionary-era (1910-1920) as the canonical journalistic-historical-record song-form of Mexican rural-popular consciousness. The canonical corrido structure: 4-line octosyllabic-rhyming verses, typically 8-15 verses long, narrating a single historical-event (battles, bandit-exploits, assassinations, romantic-tragedies, social-injustice). Performed solo (guitar-and-voice) or with mariachi-conjunto, the corrido emphasizes textual-narrative-clarity over musical-elaboration (simple I-IV-V harmonic-progression, often unchanged across all verses). The modern narco-corrido subgenre 1970s-onward chronicles drug-trafficking-figures, replacing the revolutionary-era revolutionary-hero subject-matter with contemporary cartel-leadership.
items.description: Corrido (codified mid-19th-century Mexican-and-Texas-border narrative-ballad tradition documenting historical events, folk-heroes, revolutionary battles, and border-life narrative content; flowering through the Mexican Revolution era 1910-1920 with corridos documenting Pancho Villa, Emiliano Zapata, and revolutionary-hero subject matter — Corrido de Gregorio Cortez 1901, Corrido de Pancho Villa, Adelita as examples; mid-20th-century continuation through commercial-recording-era corridistas Antonio Aguilar, Los Alegres de Terán, Los Tigres del Norte; modern narcocorrido sub-tradition emerging 1970s-onward through Los Tigres del Norte, Chalino Sánchez, Los Tucanes de Tijuana documenting drug-trade-and-border-violence narrative content, with parallel movimiento alterado regional-Mexican subgenre extension; tradition remains continuously productive into 2020s through Peso Pluma, Natanael Cano corridos tumbados revival), the Mexican narrative-ballad song-form documenting historical events, folk-heroes, and border-life narrative content. Defined by narrative-foreground lyric content (the corrido lyric structure: opening saludo greeting, narrative-of-events stating the protagonist-and-setting-and-conflict, dramatic-climax recounting the central action, despedida farewell-verse — distinguishing corrido from ranchera's emotional-cathartic content and from bolero's romantic-content), 6/8 or 4/4 meter (the corrido-vals 3/4 meter or corrido-norteño 2/4 polka-derived meter), eight-line stanza-form with assonant rhyme structure inherited from Spanish romance-ballad tradition, accordion-and-bajo-sexto-and-guitar small-ensemble accompaniment (the norteño ensemble of accordion + bajo sexto + bass + drums, distinguishing corrido from mariachi-orchestra-accompanied ranchera), folk-hero-and-historical-event-and-revolutionary-content subject matter (Pancho Villa, Emiliano Zapata, El Mariachi Mayor, Gregorio Cortez, contemporary narcocorrido subjects), and oral-and-recorded transmission continuity (the corrido tradition is fundamentally oral-narrative even when recorded). Distinguished from ranchera by narrative-foreground vs emotional-foreground lyric register and norteño-ensemble accompaniment vs mariachi-orchestra accompaniment; distinguished from son by narrative-ballad function vs dance-music function; distinguished from huapango by polka-2/4 norteño-rhythm vs syncopated-6/8 huapango-rhythm.

items.name: Singer-songwriter folk
items.lineage: Post-folk-revival American songwriter tradition combining Greenwich Village 60s confessional vocabulary with Laurel Canyon 70s intimate production aesthetic — voice and acoustic guitar at minimum, often expanded with piano and modest band
items.description: Singer-songwriter tradition (1965-present), codified post-Greenwich-Village folk revival when Bob Dylan, Joni Mitchell, James Taylor, and Carole King moved from third-person folk-ballad to first-person confessional. Standard format: one voice plus one acoustic instrument (acoustic guitar or piano), lyric-forward intimate close-mic recording, sparse-or-no rhythm-section backing. Distinguished from earlier folk-revival by first-person confessional content (versus traditional ballad repertoire); distinguished from anglo-singer-song narrative-folk by autobiographical-not-narrative lyrical posture. Joni Mitchell’s Blue (1971) is a exemplar; Tapestry, Pink Moon, Five Leaves Left mark the form’s high points.
exemplars: Bob Dylan — Bringing It All Back Home

items.name: Polish village fiddle
items.lineage: Eastern European folk-music tradition of rural Poland — characterized by single-fiddle or fiddle-and-drum (bęben obręczowy) lead with characteristic regional repertoires including the Tatra Górale (highlanders), Kurpie (northeastern), Beskid, Podlasie, and Mazowsze styles — preserved continuously through village-based wedding and ceremonial-occasion performance and documented through the twentieth-century ethnomusicological field-recording campaign
items.description: Polish-village fiddle tradition (rural Mazowsze, Małopolska, Wielkopolska regions; pre-modern through 20th-century revival). Solo or small-ensemble fiddle plus drone-string accompaniment (basy, bass-drone-fiddle), sometimes plus baraban (frame drum). Repertoire: oberek (3/8 fast spinning dance), kujawiak (3/4 slow dance), mazurka (3/4 medium-tempo). Modal melodies in scordatura tunings (often AEAE or AEDE) producing characteristic open-string drones. Distinguished from Polish urban-academy-codified Chopin-mazurka tradition by oral-village transmission and pre-equal-temperament intonation. Jan Krzyżaniak, Stanisław Klejnas, Maria Siwiec preserved the canon; folkmusic revival from 1970s onward.

items.name: Delta blues
items.lineage: Country-blues tradition of the Mississippi Delta region — slide-guitar-and-vocal solo and small-ensemble repertoire developed in the early twentieth century through the lineage of Charley Patton (the 1929 Paramount recordings), Son House, Robert Johnson (the 1936-37 San Antonio and Dallas sessions), Skip James, Bukka White, and continuing through the post-WWII Chicago-blues electrification by Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf, and others
items.description: Delta blues tradition (Mississippi cotton-belt, 1900-1940), the rural-acoustic precursor to electric Chicago blues. Solo male vocal-with-acoustic-guitar form: steel-bodied resonator or wooden flat-top, often played with bottleneck slide (glass or metal), sometimes alternating-bass thumb pattern. Free-meter vocals (12-bar blues frame loosely observed), characteristic minor-third-and-flatted-seventh blue-notes, single-chord modal vamps as foundation. Repertoire: Robert Johnson 1936-1937 recordings, Charley Patton, Son House, Skip James, Bukka White. Distinguished from Piedmont blues by single-chord-modal-not-ragtime-fingerpicking foundation; distinguished from later electric blues by acoustic-non-amplified form.

items.name: Piedmont blues
items.lineage: Country-blues tradition of the southern Atlantic seaboard (North Carolina, South Carolina, Virginia, Georgia) — characterized by alternating-thumb fingerpicking guitar accompaniment (the so-called Piedmont style), ragtime-influenced harmonic vocabulary, and a less mournful register than Delta blues — codified through Blind Boy Fuller, Reverend Gary Davis, Blind Blake, Sonny Terry and Brownie McGhee, with continuing transmission through the folk-revival pedagogical inheritance
items.description: Piedmont blues tradition (Atlantic Coast region from Virginia to Florida, 1920s-1940s peak). Solo acoustic-guitar fingerpicking style: alternating-bass thumb pattern (ragtime-derived) under treble-string melodic figures, all-fingers-not-flat-pick technique. Repertoire: 12-bar blues plus ragtime-derived dance tunes, gospel-influenced material. Distinguished from Delta blues by ragtime-fingerpicking-foundation (versus Delta single-chord-modal vamps), more melodic-and-tonal harmonic vocabulary, less melismatic vocal practice. Blind Boy Fuller, Reverend Gary Davis, Etta Baker, Cephas & Wiggins exemplify the canon. Smithsonian Folkways and Document Records preserved field-recording archives.

items.name: Chicago blues
items.lineage: Post-WWII Chicago electric blues tradition codified through the Great Migration of Black Mississippi Delta musicians to Chicago in the 1940s-50s, with the Chess Records recording infrastructure anchoring the canon — Muddy Waters (the Chicago blues voice, Mannish Boy 1955), Howlin Wolf, Little Walter (Chicago amplified-harmonica), Willie Dixon (Chess songwriter-and-bassist), Otis Spann piano, the broader Chess house-band assembled around them
items.description: Chicago electric-blues tradition (1948-1970), urban transformation of Mississippi-Delta blues following the Great Migration. Standard ensemble: electric guitar (often slide-played), amplified harmonica (cross-harp, played through guitar amp), upright-or-electric bass walking pattern, drum kit shuffle, occasionally piano or organ. Chess Records (2120 South Michigan) was the recording center; Phil Chess engineered with characteristic mid-range-heavy small-room ambience and slap-back tape echo. Repertoire: 12-bar blues, rhumba-blues (Latin-influenced), shuffle blues. Muddy Waters, Howlin’ Wolf, Little Walter, Sonny Boy Williamson II established the Chicago canon.

items.name: Jump blues
items.lineage: Post-WWII African-American small-combo shuffle blues with tenor-saxophone foreground, codified by Louis Jordan and his Tympany Five (1939-1950), Big Joe Turner, Wynonie Harris, Roy Brown, and the late-1940s Atlantic Records small-combo catalog
items.description: Jump blues tradition (1944-1955), urban-combo swing-derived dance music bridging swing-era big-bands and rhythm-and-blues. Standard ensemble: 5-7 piece small group with saxophone (tenor often featured), trumpet, piano, guitar, upright bass walking pattern, drum kit shuffle. Vocal-forward novelty-leaning lyrics with characteristic 12-bar-blues form taken at uptempo dance pace. Repertoire: Louis Jordan & His Tympany Five (1944-1953), Wynonie Harris, Big Joe Turner, Roy Brown. Distinguished from Chicago electric-blues by small-combo-with-horns-not-harmonica ensemble and uptempo-dance-not-slow-groove rhythmic foundation. The bridge from swing to early rock-and-roll.

items.name: Black Pentecostal gospel
items.lineage: Black Pentecostal / COGIC (Church of God in Christ) liturgical music tradition characterized by Hammond B3 organ, piano, drums, electric bass, congregational call-and-response with melismatic lead vocal — codified through James Cleveland, Mahalia Jackson, the Caravans, Edwin Hawkins, Andrae Crouch, Aretha Franklins Amazing Grace (1972, New Temple Missionary Baptist Church LA)
items.description: Black Pentecostal gospel tradition (Church of God in Christ founded 1907, William Seymour’s Azusa Street Revival 1906 origin). Worship-music context distinguished from concert-gospel by congregation-active liturgical form. Standard ensemble: Hammond B3 tonewheel organ with Leslie cabinet, gospel piano (right-hand cluster runs over walking left-hand bass), drum kit, electric bass, full congregation choir plus lead-and-response soloist. Vocal practice: melismatic shouted lead with full-band-stop antiphonal congregation response, ecstatic register transitions chest-to-falsetto. Distinguished from southern-gospel quartet by congregation-not-quartet format and Black-not-white denomination context. James Cleveland, Mattie Moss Clark, Walter Hawkins canonized the Pentecostal-style modern recording.

items.name: Southern gospel piano-bass
items.lineage: White Southern Protestant sacred-music piano-and-bass-accompanied solo and small-ensemble tradition descended from the same Stamps-Baxter and Vaughan shape-note songbook lineage as Southern gospel quartet, but in a smaller-ensemble piano-led format suitable for revival meetings, country church services, and gospel-radio broadcast contexts; figures include Mosie Lister, Albert E. Brumley (the songwriter, his Ill Fly Away and Turn Your Radio On 1937 written for the Hartford Music Company)
items.description: Southern gospel tradition (1900s-onward, Stamps-Baxter Music Company shape-note convention origin, modern quartet form codified 1940s). Male-quartet vocal foundation (first-tenor, second-tenor, baritone, bass), accompanied by gospel-piano (right-hand cluster runs, left-hand stride or walking bass), sometimes electric bass and drums by 1970s onward. Repertoire: 19th-century-and-newer-composed Christian hymns, convention-songbook material, original-composition gospel-quartet pieces. Distinguished from Black-Pentecostal-gospel by quartet-not-congregation format, country-music-adjacent harmonic vocabulary, white Southern Baptist denomination context. Statesmen Quartet, Blackwood Brothers, Cathedral Quartet, Gaither Vocal Band are.

items.name: Sacred steel
items.lineage: Black Pentecostal pedal-and-lap-steel-guitar gospel tradition developed in the House of God and Church of the Living God Pentecostal denominations from the 1930s onward — the pedal steel guitar functions as the foreground praise-and-worship instrument substituting for the tonewheel organ standard in most Black Pentecostal churches; codified through Aubrey Ghent, Sonny Treadway, Calvin Cooke, the modern Robert Randolph and the Family Band post-2000s extension
items.description: Sacred steel (codified 1930s onward in the African-American Pentecostal House of God Keith Dominion church communities, particularly Florida and Mid-Atlantic congregations, with continuous tradition through to present and gospel-blues crossover from 1990s onward), the House of God Pentecostal pedal-steel-led sacred music tradition. Defined by pedal-steel guitar as the lead voice carrying gospel-melodic line in vocal-mimicking style (the steel guitarist's bar-and-pedal technique imitating the melismatic-vocal phrasing of gospel singing), electric bass and drums providing rhythm-section foundation, optional Hammond organ and electric guitar, congregational vocal participation with call-and-response between pastor-or-soloist and congregation, and worship-service performance context (the steel guitar plays during congregational singing, sermon, and altar-call sections of Pentecostal Holy Convocation). Distinguished from country pedal-steel by African-American-Pentecostal-religious context and vocal-mimicking lead-voice role; distinguished from Hawaiian steel guitar by pedal-steel construction and gospel-blues lineage; distinguished from black-gospel mainstream by pedal-steel-foreground rather than choir-and-organ centrality.

items.name: New Orleans jazz
items.lineage: New Orleans turn-of-the-20th-century African-American Creole funeral / parade / Storyville-district ensemble tradition that fused brass-band, blues, and ragtime into the foundational jazz vocabulary
items.description: New Orleans jazz jazz (codified ca. 1900-1925 in New Orleans Storyville red-light district and broader African-American-and-Creole musical communities, with the post-1917-Storyville-closure Chicago migration and 1923-onward recording-era documentation establishing the genre), the polyphonic-combo jazz tradition with collective improvisation. Defined by trumpet-clarinet-trombone front-line ensemble each playing complementary improvised-melodic counterpoint simultaneously (the polyphonic-collective-improvisation feature that distinguishes Dixieland from later jazz where soloists trade), banjo-and-tuba-and-drums rhythm-section foundation (later piano replacing tuba and string-bass replacing tuba in some second-line ensembles), repertoire of Storyville-era ragtime-derived compositions, blues-derived twelve-bar structures, and church-and-march-band material, and dance-functional 2/4-and-march-tempo metric foundation. Distinguished from later Chicago Dixieland by New-Orleans-specific polyphonic-collective-improvisation foreground; distinguished from later swing by absence of section-arrangement and big-band ensemble size; distinguished from ragtime by improvisation foreground.

items.name: Ragtime
items.lineage: 1890s-1910s composed syncopated piano dance form developed in African-American midwestern saloon and brothel piano tradition — codified through Scott Joplin (Maple Leaf Rag 1899 and The Entertainer 1902) plus Tom Turpin, James Scott and Joseph Lamb, with the form serving as the principal pre-jazz American popular dance music until eclipsed by stride and early jazz around 1920
items.description: Ragtime (codified 1890s-1910s peak with Tom Turpin's Harlem Rag of 1897 — the first ragtime composition published by an African-American composer — and Scott Joplin's Maple Leaf Rag of 1899 establishing the idiom; tradition extends through the 1920s as foundational influence on stride-piano and early-jazz lineage, fading from popular foreground after Joplin's 1917 death and the post-WWI shift toward jazz proper), the composed-piano syncopated dance music tradition that developed from itinerant African-American pianist culture in post-Civil-War Midwestern saloons, brothels, and traveling show contexts. Defined by syncopated-right-hand melody over a steady oompah-or-march left-hand bass (the rag-versus-march rhythmic friction that gives the form its name and sound), multi-strain AABBACCDD compositional structure inherited from John Philip Sousa marches, harmonic vocabulary mixing European classical chord-progression frameworks with African-American blue-note inflection and call-and-response phrase patterning, and a primarily-piano-solo instrumentation form (the most recorded format), with brass-band ragtime arrangements (James Reese Europe and the Clef Club Orchestra establishing the militarized society-band format) and fingerstyle-guitar ragtime arrangements (Blind Blake, Blind Boy Fuller, Reverend Gary Davis carrying the tradition into the 1930s as country-blues-adjacent material) operating as parallel idiomatic strains. Cultural origin from cakewalk dance music plus minstrel-show repertoire plus march tradition; distribution primarily via published sheet music (Stark Music in St. Louis, John Stillwell Stark publishing the Joplin catalog) rather than recording, with piano-roll documentation (Joplin himself cut piano rolls in 1916) and early-1900s acoustic-horn 78rpm recordings as secondary distribution paths. Distinguished from early jazz by composed-not-improvised performance practice (improvisation on rags came later, in the stride-piano tradition); distinguished from Tin Pan Alley by piano-instrumental-foreground over vocal-songbook foreground; distinguished from march music by syncopated-right-hand-melodic-friction over straight-march-2/4 rhythmic-uniformity. Lineage forward feeds stride piano (James P. Johnson, Eubie Blake, Fats Waller — the Harlem-1920s extension that retained the form while introducing improvisation), boogie-woogie piano, and through them the broader pre-bebop jazz piano vocabulary.

items.name: Stride piano
items.lineage: 1920s-1940s Harlem virtuoso solo-piano tradition extending ragtime through dramatic ten-finger leaps in the left hand alternating bass-note and chord — codified through James P. Johnson (Carolina Shout 1921), Willie The Lion Smith, Fats Waller (Ain't Misbehavin' 1929) and Art Tatum, with later inheritors including Erroll Garner and Thelonious Monk drawing directly on the stride harmonic language
items.description: Stride piano (codified 1920s-1940s across Harlem rent-party-and-cabaret-circuit performance contexts; James P. Johnson Carolina Shout 1921 establishing the idiom; flowering through Willie The Lion Smith, Fats Waller, Luckey Roberts, and the post-1925 Harlem rent-party-circuit cutting-contest culture; tradition extends through 1940s as foundation for swing-era piano vocabulary), the African-American virtuoso solo-piano tradition that bridges ragtime and jazz piano. Defined by ragtime-derived left-hand stride pattern (the alternating bass-note-on-strong-beats-and-chord-on-weak-beats with characteristic tenths-and-octave-leaps that gives the genre its name — the left hand striding between low bass-note and mid-register chord across an octave-or-tenth interval per bar), improvised right-hand melodic-and-chord-melody work over the steady stride foundation (distinguishing stride from composed-ragtime by introducing improvisation), virtuoso-display performance practice with rapid-tempo cutting-contest culture (the Harlem rent-party-circuit Saturday-night gatherings where pianists competed publicly), repertoire mixing original stride compositions with arranged Tin Pan Alley songs and ragtime translations, and overwhelmingly solo-piano performance format (some duos and trios but the tradition centers on the single virtuoso pianist). Distinguished from preceding ragtime by improvisation foreground and rapid-tempo virtuosity; distinguished from later bebop and post-bop piano by retention of regular stride left-hand foundation vs comping-and-walking-bass left-hand approach; distinguished from boogie-woogie by tenth-and-octave-leap stride pattern vs ostinato-eight-to-the-bar bass figure. Lineage forward feeds swing-era jazz piano (Earl Hines, Teddy Wilson, Art Tatum extending stride into swing-era polish), bebop piano (Bud Powell drawing on stride foundation), and through them the broader pre-modal jazz piano vocabulary.

items.name: Boogie-woogie
items.lineage: 1920s through 1940s African-American piano-blues idiom built on left-hand ostinato bass figures (walking-eighths or rolling-octaves) under right-hand blues melody — codified through Pinetop Smith’s "Pinetop’s Boogie Woogie" (1928), the Carnegie Hall From Spirituals to Swing concert (1938) bringing Albert Ammons, Meade Lux Lewis, and Pete Johnson to white audiences, and the wartime crossover into jump blues
items.description: Boogie-woogie (codified 1920s African-American piano-blues idiom from Texas-and-Louisiana barrelhouse-and-juke-joint performance contexts and the Chicago-South-Side rent-party scene; established commercially through Pinetop Smith's Pine Top's Boogie Woogie 1928 recording introducing the genre name and eight-to-the-bar foundation; flowering 1938-1944 through Albert Ammons, Meade Lux Lewis, and Pete Johnson trio performances and Carnegie Hall From Spirituals to Swing concert appearances; tradition extends as foundational influence on early-R&B piano and rock-and-roll), the African-American piano-blues idiom defined by ostinato left-hand bass figures and twelve-bar-blues frame. Defined by eight-to-the-bar left-hand bass figure (the rolling-octave-pattern, walking-bass-pattern, or broken-octave-pattern playing eight beats per bar in the bass register — the foundation that gives the genre its name and propulsive forward-motion), twelve-bar-blues frame harmonic structure (distinguishing boogie-woogie from ragtime's multi-strain march-form architecture), improvised right-hand work over the steady left-hand bass (typically blues-pentatonic-and-blue-note melodic vocabulary with parallel-thirds and tremolo-octaves as figurations), tempo range mid-fast (boogie-woogie typically faster than slow blues, around 130-180 BPM), and primarily solo-piano performance format. Distinguished from ragtime by twelve-bar-blues frame vs march-form architecture and ostinato-bass vs stride-bass; distinguished from stride piano by ostinato-eight-to-the-bar bass vs tenth-and-octave-leap stride bass and twelve-bar-blues vs Tin-Pan-Alley repertoire; distinguished from later jump-blues and rhythm-and-blues piano by solo-piano-foreground over band-with-piano format. Lineage forward feeds jump-blues (Louis Jordan band format absorbs boogie-woogie piano into ensemble), early R&B (Amos Milburn, Charles Brown), and through them the rock-and-roll piano of Jerry Lee Lewis and Little Richard.

items.name: Latin jazz
items.lineage: NYC-centered fusion of Afro-Cuban rhythmic spine (clave, montuno, tumbao) with bebop / post-bop harmonic language, codified through Machito-Bauzá Cubop (1940s), Cal Tjader-Mongo Santamaría West Coast Latin jazz (1950s-60s), and Eddie Palmieri / Tito Puente / Chucho Valdés modern Latin jazz canon
items.description: Latin jazz (codified mid-1940s onward through Dizzy Gillespie's Afro-Cuban collaborations with Chano Pozo and the 1947 Manteca and Cubana Be / Cubana Bop recordings establishing the Cubop synthesis; parallel development through Machito and his Afro-Cubans and Mario Bauzá arrangements through the 1940s-1950s mambo-jazz era; expansion into samba-jazz with Antônio Carlos Jobim and Stan Getz Getz/Gilberto 1964 establishing bossa-nova jazz; broader pan-Latin-American expansion through Eddie Palmieri, Tito Puente, Mongo Santamaría, Chucho Valdés, Irakere, and the 1990s Buena Vista Social Club revival), the jazz subgenre that integrates Afro-Cuban-and-Brazilian rhythmic foundation with bebop and post-bop jazz harmonic and melodic vocabulary. Defined by Afro-Cuban-derived clave-and-tumbao rhythmic foundation (the 3-2 or 2-3 son-clave figure organizing the entire ensemble rhythmic structure) or Brazilian samba-and-bossa-rhythmic foundation (depending on the sub-tradition: cubop and mambo-jazz lean Cuban, samba-jazz and bossa-jazz lean Brazilian), expanded percussion section augmenting standard drum-kit with congas-bongos-timbales-cowbell-shekere (the conjunto-percussion-section that distinguishes the genre from straight-jazz), bebop-and-post-bop horn vocabulary (saxophone, trumpet, trombone front-line) over the Latin rhythmic foundation, jazz harmonic frame (II-V-I and modal-vamp structures) over Latin rhythmic frame (clave-organized rather than swing-eighth-organized), and tempo range typically 110-180 BPM for cubop and mambo-jazz, slower for samba-jazz and bossa-jazz. Distinguished from straight bebop by Afro-Cuban-or-Brazilian rhythmic foundation vs swing-eighth feel and expanded conjunto-percussion vs drum-kit-only rhythm section; distinguished from non-jazz Cuban genres (son cubano, mambo, salsa) by jazz harmonic-and-melodic vocabulary and improvisational foreground over song-form-and-arrangement foreground; distinguished from samba and bossa-nova proper by jazz-improvisational-frame vs popular-song frame.

items.name: Progressive rock
items.lineage: Late-1960s through 1970s UK classical-and-jazz-influenced rock genre featuring extended composition, complex meter, virtuosic instrumental performance — codified through King Crimson (In the Court of the Crimson King 1969, the prog founding album), Yes (Fragile 1971, Close to the Edge 1972), Genesis (Selling England by the Pound 1973, the Peter Gabriel era), Pink Floyd (the post-Syd-Barrett expansion through Dark Side of the Moon 1973 and Wish You Were Here 1975), Emerson Lake and Palmer, Jethro Tull, Gentle Giant
items.description: Progressive rock (codified late-1968 through 1969 with Procol Harum's A Whiter Shade of Pale 1967 and the parallel emergence of Pink Floyd, Genesis, Yes, King Crimson, Jethro Tull, and Emerson Lake & Palmer establishing the UK lineage; golden era 1970-1976 marked by Yes Close to the Edge 1972, Genesis Selling England by the Pound 1973, King Crimson Larks' Tongues in Aspic 1973, Pink Floyd Dark Side of the Moon 1973, and Rush 2112 1976; tradition extends through later 1970s before punk-and-new-wave reaction and 1980s-onward neo-prog revival), the late-1960s through 1970s rock subgenre incorporating classical-and-jazz harmonic vocabulary and extended composition. Defined by extended-composition song-form (suite-form multi-movement compositions running 10-25 minutes typical, side-long single-piece compositions like Yes Close to the Edge or Genesis Supper's Ready, concept-album integration where individual songs serve a larger narrative-and-thematic frame), expanded harmonic vocabulary borrowed from classical-and-jazz traditions (modal interchange, chromatic mediants, polychords, extended chord-voicings beyond rock's I-IV-V foundation), virtuosic instrumental performance practice (the demand for technical mastery distinguishing prog from contemporaneous garage-rock-and-pop-rock), expanded instrumental palette (Mellotron tape-replay tape-strip strings-and-flutes-and-choir samples, Hammond B3 organ, Moog Modular and ARP synthesizers, double-neck guitars, occasional acoustic-orchestral overdubs and choir vocals), odd-meter rhythmic foundation (5/8, 7/8, 9/8, alternating-time-signature passages, polyrhythm — all uncommon in mainstream rock), and elaborate concept-album-and-stage-show theatrical presentation. Distinguished from contemporaneous hard rock by extended-composition vs verse-chorus song-form and classical-and-jazz harmonic vocabulary vs blues-rock vocabulary; distinguished from psychedelic rock by virtuosic-instrumental ambition vs experimental-trip-induction orientation; distinguished from later art-rock by instrumental-virtuosity foreground vs textural-and-aesthetic foreground. Lineage forward feeds 1980s-onward neo-prog revival (Marillion, IQ, Pendragon), prog-metal (Dream Theater, Tool, Opeth incorporating prog architecture into metal frame), and through them the broader extended-composition rock continuum.

items.name: Art rock
items.lineage: Late-1960s through 1980s art-school avant-garde-influenced rock genre — codified through David Bowie (the Hunky Dory through Scary Monsters arc 1971-1980, with the Berlin Trilogy Low / Heroes / Lodger 1977-79 as the Brian-Eno-collaboration period), Roxy Music (Roxy Music 1972, For Your Pleasure 1973), Brian Eno (the post-Roxy solo canon Another Green World 1975, Music for Airports 1978), Talking Heads (the Eno-produced trilogy More Songs About Buildings and Food 1978, Fear of Music 1979, Remain in Light 1980), Peter Gabriel (his post-Genesis Eno-influenced canon)
items.description: Art rock (codified late-1960s through 1970s art-school-and-avant-garde-influenced rock subgenre with foundations in Velvet Underground 1967-1970 art-noise lineage and the parallel emergence of Roxy Music and David Bowie 1971-1980 establishing the idiom; flowering through Brian Eno solo-era ambient-and-experimental work, Talking Heads Remain in Light 1980 and broader post-punk extension, Peter Gabriel solo era and Kate Bush 1978-onward female-art-rock lineage; tradition extends through 1980s art-pop crossover and 2000s revival), the late-1960s through 1980s art-school-and-avant-garde-influenced rock subgenre prioritizing aesthetic-conceptual-experimentation over virtuosic-instrumental-performance. Defined by aesthetic-foreground orientation (the deliberate adoption of conceptual-art and avant-garde-music aesthetic-frameworks: Roxy Music's Brian Eno-and-Bryan Ferry conceptual-glamour, Bowie's persona-cycling theatrical-conceptual practice, Talking Heads' downtown-NYC-art-school sensibility, Peter Gabriel's theatrical-narrative arrangement work, Kate Bush's art-school dance-and-narrative integration), expanded textural-and-arrangement vocabulary (treated guitars, synthesizer textures, found-sound and tape-manipulation, non-Western percussion, vocal-treatment experimentation), willingness to break verse-chorus pop song-form (extended ambient passages, spoken-word interludes, deliberate-tempo-modulation, abandoned hooks), production-foreground orientation (the studio-as-instrument approach pioneered by Eno-and-Ferry that distinguishes art-rock from contemporaneous prog-rock's instrumental-virtuosity orientation), and lyric content drawing on literary-modernist-and-postmodernist references rather than rock-romantic or political-protest themes. Distinguished from progressive-rock by aesthetic-conceptual-foreground vs instrumental-virtuosity-foreground and short-pop-song-form vs extended-suite-form; distinguished from contemporaneous post-punk by glamour-and-aesthetic-conceptualism vs political-realism orientation; distinguished from later art-pop by male-and-female-balance and rock-instrumentation foundation vs art-pop's electronic-pop-leaning instrumentation. Lineage forward feeds art-pop (Björk, Kate Bush late-era, FKA twigs), avant-pop (Frank Ocean Blonde-era, Solange A Seat at the Table), and through them the contemporary aesthetic-conceptual-pop continuum.

items.name: Glam rock
items.lineage: Early-mid-1970s UK androgynous-theatrical riff-rock — codified through T. Rex (Marc Bolans Electric Warrior 1971, Slider 1972), David Bowie (the Ziggy Stardust 1972 and Aladdin Sane 1973 glam-era persona before his Berlin Trilogy art-rock turn), Roxy Music (early glam-art-rock fusion), Slade (the British Black Country working-class glam rock canon), Sweet, Mott the Hoople, Suzi Quatro, Gary Glitter — followed by the proto-punk American extensions New York Dolls and Iggy and the Stooges glam-period albums
items.description: Glam rock (codified 1971-1976 across UK-and-US glitter-rock scenes through Marc Bolan / T.Rex Electric Warrior 1971 and David Bowie The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust 1972 establishing the idiom; parallel UK development through Slade, Sweet, Mott the Hoople, Roxy Music early-glam-era, Gary Glitter, Suzi Quatro; US development through New York Dolls, Alice Cooper, KISS Destroyer 1976; tradition fades by mid-1976 as punk-and-disco displace it, with Bowie and Roxy Music transitioning into art-rock proper), the early-mid-1970s rock subgenre defined by androgynous-theatrical performance aesthetic and anthemic-mid-tempo-riff-rock musical foundation. Defined by androgynous-theatrical performance practice (the glitter-platform-stage-costuming, makeup, and gender-fluid performance presentation that gave the genre its identifying surface; Bowie Ziggy era and T.Rex established the visual lexicon), anthemic mid-tempo riff-rock foundation (the four-on-the-floor or shuffle-feel mid-tempo grooves with simple-but-effective guitar-riff hooks distinguishing glam from contemporaneous progressive-rock's extended-virtuosity), pop-foregrounded songwriting (verse-chorus-chorus-bridge structures with strong melodic hooks, distinguishing glam from prog), production tendencies including hand-clap percussion, layered-vocal-harmony backing, occasional saxophone-or-piano features (Roy Bittan / Mike Garson piano work on Bowie tracks), and lyric content centered on theatrical-pose-and-myth-construction (Bowie's persona-cycling, Bolan's mystical-cosmic narrative, Slade's working-class-yob-anthem tradition). Distinguished from later 1980s hair-metal by pop-songwriting-foreground vs hard-rock-virtuosity-foreground and theatrical-art-school sensibility vs LA-Sunset-Strip commercial-hedonism; distinguished from contemporaneous progressive-rock by short-anthem song-form vs extended-suite composition; distinguished from punk (its near-contemporary successor) by virtuosic-musicianship and theatrical-glamour vs amateur-and-anti-virtuoso aesthetic. Lineage forward feeds glam-metal/hair-metal (the 1980s commercial-derivative that retains the visual aesthetic without the art-school sensibility), Britpop 1990s revival (Suede, Pulp drawing on glam-rock songwriting and aesthetic), and through them the broader theatrical-rock continuum.

items.name: Gothic rock
items.lineage: Late-1970s through 1980s post-punk-derived dark atmospheric rock — codified through Bauhaus (Bela Lugosi’s Dead 1979), Siouxsie and the Banshees, The Cure (Pornography 1982, Disintegration 1989), Joy Division’s Closer (1980), and the Birthday Party / Nick Cave lineage; characterized by chorused-and-flanged guitar atmospherics, theatrical-baritone vocals, and gothic-literary lyrical subject matter
items.description: Gothic rock (codified 1979-1985 emerging from late-post-punk and proto-goth scenes through Bauhaus Bela Lugosi's Dead 1979 establishing the sonic vocabulary, Joy Division parallel post-punk-to-proto-goth lineage, and the early-1980s flowering through Siouxsie and the Banshees, The Cure Pornography 1982, Sisters of Mercy First and Last and Always 1985, The Cult Dreamtime 1984; second wave 1985-1992 with The Mission, Fields of the Nephilim, Christian Death establishing US-and-UK divisions; 1990s-onward continuation through gothic-metal hybrid traditions and dark-cabaret revival), the post-punk-derived rock subgenre defined by atmospheric clean-or-chorused-guitar texture, prominent bass-guitar foreground, deep-baritone vocal delivery, and dark theatrical aesthetic. Defined by atmospheric guitar texture (chorus-and-flanger pedal effects on clean-or-lightly-overdriven single-coil guitar, repeating-figure-and-arpeggio melodic vocabulary rather than chord-strum-or-power-chord rock language, the spacious-reverberant tone characteristic of UK post-punk-era guitar production), prominent foregrounded electric bass (often with chorus or flanger effects, melodic-bass-line counterpoint to guitar arpeggios, distinctly higher in mix than typical rock practice — Peter Hook influence), deep-baritone vocal delivery (Andrew Eldritch, Peter Murphy, Ian Astbury vocal-archetype with chest-resonance-low-mid timbral signature), drum-machine-or-live-drums with prominent reverb-treated snare backbeat, melancholic-and-occult-and-apocalyptic lyric content (death, decay, romance-of-darkness, neo-Romantic and Victorian gothic literary references), and slow-to-mid-tempo (typically 80-130 BPM), minor-key-modal harmonic foundation. Distinguished from preceding post-punk by atmospheric-and-occult lyric content and dark-theatrical aesthetic vs post-punk's political-and-realist content; distinguished from contemporaneous new-wave by minor-key-modal harmonic foundation and slow-tempo dread vs new-wave's pop-major-key brightness; distinguished from later industrial by guitar-foreground vs synth-foreground orientation. Lineage forward feeds gothic-metal (Type O Negative, Paradise Lost, Cathedral incorporating gothic-rock atmosphere into metal frame), darkwave (the synth-electronic continuation), industrial-gothic crossover (Bauhaus alumni Love and Rockets, Peter Murphy solo era), and through them the broader dark-rock-aesthetic continuum.

items.name: Southern rock
items.lineage: Late-1960s through 1970s American Southern blues-rock genre — codified through the Allman Brothers Band (Live at Fillmore East 1971), Lynyrd Skynyrd (Pronounced Leh-Nerd Skin-Nerd 1973, Sweet Home Alabama 1974), the Marshall Tucker Band, Wet Willie, the Charlie Daniels Band, ZZ Top (the Texas extension), Molly Hatchet; twin-lead-guitar harmony foreground, blues-rock harmonic foundation extended with country and gospel-influenced songwriting
items.description: Southern rock (codified late-1968 through 1977 across American Southern blues-rock scenes with the Allman Brothers Band's 1969 debut establishing the idiom and twin-lead-guitar arrangement; flowering 1971-1977 through Allman Brothers At Fillmore East 1971, Lynyrd Skynyrd Pronounced Lynyrd Skynyrd 1973, ZZ Top Tres Hombres 1973, The Marshall Tucker Band, The Charlie Daniels Band, Molly Hatchet, Wet Willie; tradition crests with the 1977 Skynyrd plane crash and continues through 1980s as nostalgia-based touring tradition; revived through 1990s southern-rock and 2000s alt-country lineage), the late-1960s through 1970s American Southern blues-rock subgenre featuring twin-or-triple-lead-guitar arrangements, pedal-steel cross-pollination from country, blues-rock harmonic-melodic foundation, and Southern-Appalachian regional cultural identity. Defined by twin-or-triple-lead-guitar arrangement (the signature southern-rock textural-and-melodic frame: Allman Brothers Duane Allman + Dickey Betts harmonized-lead lines, Skynyrd Allen Collins + Gary Rossington + Steve Gaines triple-lead arrangement), blues-rock harmonic-and-melodic foundation (twelve-bar blues, modal-vamp jam-section frames, blues-pentatonic and modal-mixolydian melodic vocabulary), pedal-steel and tonewheel-organ cross-pollination from country and gospel traditions, extended-jam song-form with extended improvisational solo sections (especially the Allman Brothers extended live-jam tradition), Southern-vernacular vocal delivery (Gregg Allman, Ronnie Van Zant, Billy Gibbons regional-accent vocal-foreground), and lyric content centered on Southern-regional themes (rural-life, Confederate-flag iconography, cosmic-and-spiritual content in the Allman Brothers Mountain Jam tradition). Distinguished from contemporaneous British hard rock by Southern-vernacular vocal-foreground and twin-lead-guitar arrangement vs Marshall-stack power-chord vocabulary; distinguished from country-rock (its closest lineage neighbor) by blues-rock-foreground and Southern-rock-electric-amplification vs country-rock's acoustic-guitar-and-pedal-steel foreground; distinguished from later boogie-rock and outlaw-country by extended-jam-improvisation tradition vs verse-chorus-song-form orientation.

items.name: Country rock
items.lineage: Late-1960s through 1970s LA-centered amplified country-and-rock fusion codified by The Byrds Sweetheart of the Rodeo (1968), The Flying Burrito Brothers, Poco, the Eagles Take It Easy era, Linda Ronstadt, Emmylou Harris
items.description: Country rock (codified late-1968 through 1976 across American amplified-country scenes through Gram Parsons's pioneering work with The Byrds Sweetheart of the Rodeo 1968 and The Flying Burrito Brothers Gilded Palace of Sin 1969 establishing the amplified-country idiom; flowering 1972-1976 through Eagles Eagles 1972 / Hotel California 1976, Linda Ronstadt Heart Like a Wheel 1974, Poco Crazy Eyes 1973, Pure Prairie League Bustin' Out 1972, and the broader Laurel-Canyon LA country-rock scene; tradition extends through 1980s into adult-contemporary country and 1990s alt-country revival; influence on subsequent Americana lineage), the late-1960s through 1970s amplified-country and rock fusion subgenre. Defined by amplified-country instrumentation foundation (acoustic-and-electric guitar layering, pedal-steel as foreground melodic voice, electric bass and drum kit providing rock-rhythm-section foundation, distinguishing country-rock from purely-acoustic Nashville-traditional and from Stateside-Bluegrass), close-harmony-vocal arrangement (the Eagles three-and-four-part stacked-harmony refrains, Burrito Brothers brother-duet-and-Gram-Parsons high-harmony tradition), country-songwriting-sensibility applied to rock-album format (verse-chorus song-form with rock-album sequencing rather than singles-orientation; literary-poetic lyric register inherited from Gram Parsons cosmic-American-music vision), tempo range typically 90-130 BPM, and Laurel-Canyon LA studio-rock production aesthetic (the Bill Halverson / Glyn Johns recording approach with warm-acoustic-and-pedal-steel-foreground arrangement). Distinguished from preceding country by amplified rock-rhythm-section foundation vs country-string-band format; distinguished from preceding folk-rock (its closest lineage predecessor) by pedal-steel-foreground and country-twang-vocal-tradition vs folk-rock's 12-string-electric-guitar and folk-vocal-tradition; distinguished from contemporaneous southern-rock by acoustic-and-pedal-steel foreground vs blues-rock electric-amplification foreground.
exemplars: The Byrds (Sweetheart of the Rodeo era)
New Riders of the Purple Sage

items.name: Noise rock
items.lineage: Late-1970s through 1990s experimental dissonance-foregrounded rock — codified through Sonic Youth (Daydream Nation 1988), The Jesus Lizard, Big Black (Songs About Fucking 1987), Swans, Glenn Branca’s symphonies, and the broader Touch and Go / SST label ecosystem; characterized by detuned guitars, feedback as compositional material, and aggressive-confrontational performance aesthetic
items.description: Noise rock (codified late-1970s through 1990s American-and-international experimental-rock scenes with foundations in Sonic Youth's late-1981-onward work and the parallel emergence of Swans, Big Black, Butthole Surfers, and Glenn Branca's avant-guitar-orchestra projects establishing the idiom; flowering 1986-1992 through Sonic Youth Daydream Nation 1988, Swans Cop 1984, Big Black Atomizer 1986, The Jesus Lizard Goat 1991, Helmet Strap It On 1990; tradition extends through 1990s post-rock and 2000s avant-rock continuum), the late-1970s through 1990s experimental-rock subgenre foregrounding dissonance, feedback, prepared-guitar techniques, and noise-as-melodic-element. Defined by dissonance-and-feedback foreground (the deliberate cultivation of high-noise-floor textures as a melodic-and-textural-element rather than a defect to be eliminated; Sonic Youth's prepared-guitar techniques with screwdrivers and drumsticks under the strings; Big Black's industrial-grade distortion-and-amplification practice), alternate-and-prepared-guitar-tunings (Sonic Youth practice of using different guitar tunings on every song with extensive alternate-tuning-architecture, including dropped-tunings, retuning-mid-song, and strings-tied-with-foreign-objects), aggressive rhythmic foundation (often featuring drum-machine programming for industrial-noise-rock subset, or live-drums with prominent floor-tom and snare-roll work), confrontational-and-difficult lyric content (often anti-narrative, lyric-as-noise-element rather than lyric-as-meaning), and song-forms ranging from short-and-aggressive (Big Black) to extended-and-textural (Sonic Youth's Daydream Nation extended pieces). Distinguished from contemporaneous post-punk by noise-foregrounding and avant-garde experimentation vs post-punk's political-realism orientation; distinguished from later math-rock by fewer-prog-rhythmic-complexity and more-noise-textural orientation; distinguished from drone metal by guitar-rock-instrumentation foundation vs amplifier-and-feedback-instrumentation foundation.

items.name: Pop-punk
items.lineage: Mid-1970s onward pop-melody punk hybrid genre fusing punk's tempo, distortion, and DIY ethos with pop's harmonic and melodic vocabulary — codified through the Ramones (Ramones 1976), Buzzcocks (Singles Going Steady 1979), and the 1990s commercial breakthrough with Green Day (Dookie 1994), The Offspring (Smash 1994), Blink-182 (Enema of the State 1999), continuing through 2000s emo-adjacent revivals
items.description: Pop-punk (codified mid-1976 onward across UK-and-American punk scenes with The Ramones Ramones 1976 establishing the pop-punk idiom of two-and-a-half-minute three-chord-pop-songs played at fast-tempo with amateur-aesthetic; parallel UK development through Buzzcocks Spiral Scratch 1977 and broader UK-punk-pop crossover; 1980s-1990s revival flowering through Descendents Milo Goes to College 1982, Bad Religion Suffer 1988, Green Day Dookie 1994, The Offspring Smash 1994, Blink-182 Cheshire Cat 1995 establishing the mainstream-radio-crossover canon; 2000s-onward continuing through Fall Out Boy, Paramore, My Chemical Romance pop-punk-emo hybrid lineage; contemporary 2020s revival through Olivia Rodrigo, Machine Gun Kelly tradition); the punk subgenre fusing punk's amateur-aesthetic-and-fast-tempo with pop-melody-and-verse-chorus song-form. Defined by punk-tempo-and-amateur-aesthetic foundation (fast 150-200 BPM tempos, three-or-four-chord progressions, deliberately-amateur instrumental performance distinguishing pop-punk from later hardcore subgenres' technical proficiency emphasis), pop-melody-and-verse-chorus song-form (the 3-minute single architecture with strong melodic hooks, distinguishing pop-punk from contemporaneous hardcore-and-experimental-punk's anti-pop-orientation), distorted-power-chord guitar-foreground arrangement (overdriven humbucker-electric-guitar with prominent power-chord rhythm and brief lead-melodic figures), three-or-four-piece band format (vocal-guitar-bass-drums standard rock-band lineup), and lyric content centered on adolescent-themes (alienation, romance-and-heartbreak, suburban-dissatisfaction). Distinguished from preceding punk by pop-songwriting-craft and verse-chorus song-form vs punk's anti-pop-orientation; distinguished from contemporaneous hardcore by slower-tempo and pop-melodic-foreground vs hardcore's faster-tempo and anti-melodic-orientation; distinguished from later emo by less-introspective-confessional lyric content and brighter-major-key-melodic foundation.

items.name: Gangsta rap
items.lineage: Mid-1980s onward American hip-hop street-narrative subgenre codified through Schoolly D ("PSK What Does It Mean?" 1985), Ice-T (Rhyme Pays 1987), and the N.W.A. Straight Outta Compton (1988) breakthrough — characterized by first-person street-life narratives, hardened drum-machine production, sample-based foundations, and explicit anti-establishment lyrical content driving the late-80s/early-90s West Coast scene
items.description: Gangsta rap (codified 1986-1989 through Schoolly D's P.S.K. — What Does It Mean? 1985 and Ice-T's 6 'n the Mornin' 1986 establishing the proto-gangsta street-narrative idiom; breakthrough through NWA Straight Outta Compton 1988 establishing the LA-Compton-South-Central reference frame; flowering 1990-1996 through Ice Cube AmeriKKKa's Most Wanted 1990, Dr. Dre The Chronic 1992, Snoop Dogg Doggystyle 1993, Tupac Me Against the World 1995, Mobb Deep The Infamous 1995; East-Coast strand through Mobb Deep, Onyx, Capone-N-Noreaga; tradition extends through 2000s Southern-trap and contemporary drill-rap descendants), the mid-1980s through 1990s American hip-hop subgenre foregrounding street-narrative, drug-and-crime lyric content, and confrontational-and-political performance stance. Defined by street-narrative lyric foreground (first-person narrative-perspective accounts of inner-city Black-and-brown American experience, drug-trade depiction, violence-and-confrontation content, distinguishing gangsta from preceding party-rap and Afrocentric-conscious-rap traditions), confrontational-and-political performance stance (NWA's Fuck tha Police, Ice-T's Cop Killer, Public-Enemy-influenced political-content delivery — though Public Enemy is more conscious-rap proper), funk-and-soul-sample-based production (Dr. Dre's G-funk era developed sub-style with foregrounded P-funk samples and Moog-and-synth-bass arrangements; East-Coast Mobb Deep / Wu-Tang affiliated production using darker jazz-and-soul samples), boom-bap drum-programming foundation (the SP-1200 / MPC-60 sample-based drum-programming with hard-kick-and-snare-sample-foreground), aggressive-confrontational vocal-delivery style (chest-resonance forward vocal-delivery with aggressive-rapid-flow technique), and lyric structure typically 16-bar verses with 8-bar choruses and bridge sections. Distinguished from preceding old-school hip-hop by street-narrative-content-foreground and confrontational-stance vs party-rap orientation; distinguished from contemporaneous conscious-hip-hop by content-orientation toward street-experience-narrative vs political-philosophical-and-Afrocentric content; distinguished from later trap-rap by 1980s-1990s production-aesthetics and East/West-Coast geographic-specificity vs trap's Southern-and-online-distributed character.

items.name: Conscious hip-hop
items.lineage: Late-1980s onward American politically-engaged hip-hop with jazz-and-soul-sample foundation — codified through Public Enemy (It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back 1988), A Tribe Called Quest, De La Soul, KRS-One / Boogie Down Productions, and the Native Tongues collective; characterized by Afrocentric/Black-liberationist lyrical content, jazz-and-Stax sample beds, and didactic emcee tradition
items.description: Conscious hip-hop (codified 1987-1991 through Boogie Down Productions Criminal Minded 1987, Public Enemy It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back 1988, A Tribe Called Quest People's Instinctive Travels 1990, De La Soul 3 Feet High and Rising 1989, Jungle Brothers Done by the Forces of Nature 1989 establishing the Native-Tongues-and-Daisy-Age-and-political-rap synthesis; flowering 1991-1996 through ATCQ The Low End Theory 1991, Gang Starr Daily Operation 1992, Common One Day It'll All Make Sense 1997, The Roots Things Fall Apart 1999, Black Star Mos Def & Talib Kweli Are Black Star 1998; tradition extends through 2000s neo-soul-hip-hop crossover and 2010s through Kendrick Lamar To Pimp a Butterfly 2015, Kanye West My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy 2010 conscious-hip-hop revival continuum), the late-1980s through present-day American hip-hop subgenre foregrounding politically-and-socially-engaged lyric content. Defined by politically-and-socially-engaged lyric content (Afrocentric-and-Black-Liberation themes, anti-establishment-and-anti-racist political-content, philosophical-and-spiritual-and-historical content, distinguishing conscious-rap from gangsta-rap's street-narrative orientation and party-rap's celebration orientation), jazz-and-soul-sample-based production foundation (the jazz-loop-and-Rhodes-electric-piano sampling tradition pioneered by ATCQ and the Native Tongues collective, creating the conscious-rap sonic-signature; subsequent extension through Pete Rock, DJ Premier, J Dilla, 9th Wonder, and the broader jazz-rap continuation), intricate-rhyme-craft performance practice (multisyllabic-internal-rhyme schemes, complex-rhythmic flow technique, vocabulary-and-literary-reference foregrounding distinguishing conscious-rap MCs as wordplay-craft virtuosos), live-instrumentation incorporation (The Roots establishing the live-band hip-hop reference; jazz-instrumental-overdub-and-replay tradition), and lyric structure built on detailed-narrative-and-philosophical content with frequent 16-bar verses and call-and-response hook construction. Distinguished from contemporaneous gangsta-rap by political-philosophical-and-Afrocentric content vs street-narrative-content; distinguished from preceding party-rap and old-school-hip-hop by content-foregrounding-over-party-celebration; distinguished from later mumble-rap and trap-rap by content-foregrounding-and-rhyme-craft virtuosity vs streamed-distribution melodic-mood-pieces.

items.name: Synthpop
items.lineage: Late-1970s through 1980s synthesizer-foreground electronic pop — codified through Kraftwerk’s Trans-Europe Express (1977) and Computer World (1981) European roots, then Gary Numan ("Are Friends Electric?" 1979), Depeche Mode (Speak and Spell 1981), the Human League (Dare 1981), Soft Cell, Yazoo, and the broader British New Romantic scene — characterized by monophonic-synth lead lines, drum-machine programming, and detached-pop vocal performance
items.description: Synthpop (codified 1979-1985 through UK-and-Continental-European synth-pop scenes with The Human League Don't You Want Me 1981, Depeche Mode Speak and Spell 1981, Soft Cell Tainted Love 1981, OMD Dazzle Ships 1983 establishing the idiom; foundations in late-1970s Kraftwerk Computer World 1981 and Gary Numan The Pleasure Principle 1979 establishing the synthesizer-and-drum-machine-foreground arrangement frame; flowering 1982-1986 through Pet Shop Boys Please 1986, Erasure Wonderland 1986, Yazoo, Eurythmics, Bronski Beat, Tears for Fears Songs from the Big Chair 1985; tradition continues through 1990s revival and 2000s electroclash subsidiary), the late-1970s through 1980s electronic-pop subgenre defined by foreground-synthesizer instrumentation and drum-machine percussion. Defined by synthesizer-foreground arrangement (analog-polysynth lead-and-pad work — Roland Jupiter-8, Sequential Prophet-5, Yamaha DX7 establishing the timbres of different sub-eras), drum-machine percussion (Roland TR-808, LinnDrum LM-1, drum-machine substituting for live drum kit as the rhythm-section foundation), vocoder-and-electronic-vocal treatment (the electronic-treated-vocal sub-tradition: Kraftwerk, Daft Punk-precursor era), verse-chorus pop song-form (distinguishing synthpop from contemporaneous synth-experimental-electronic), prominent harmonic-bass synth-line (sequenced bass under the song that gives synthpop its propulsive forward-motion), and lyric content typically modern-romance-and-alienation themes calibrated for mainstream radio crossover. Distinguished from contemporaneous new-wave by synthesizer-foreground vs guitar-foreground arrangement; distinguished from earlier electronic music (Kraftwerk, Tangerine Dream) by pop-song-form vs experimental-instrumental orientation; distinguished from later 1990s synth-electronic by 1980s-era apparatus and pop-foregrounding vs 1990s rave-and-dance orientation. Lineage forward feeds 1990s electroclash and synthwave revivals, contemporary indie-electronic pop (CHVRCHES, M83), and through them the broader synthesizer-and-drum-machine pop continuum.

items.name: New wave
items.lineage: Late-1970s through mid-1980s post-punk-derived pop-rock — codified through Blondie, Talking Heads (Remain in Light 1980), Devo (Q: Are We Not Men? A: We Are Devo! 1978), The Cars (The Cars 1978), Elvis Costello (My Aim Is True 1977), and the broader Stiff Records / Sire Records ecosystem; characterized by angular-rhythm-section, ironic-detached vocals, and pop-song-form embrace distinguishing it from punk
items.description: New wave (codified 1977-1985 across UK-and-American post-punk-derived pop-rock scenes with foundations in Talking Heads Talking Heads 77 and Blondie Plastic Letters 1977 establishing the idiom; flowering through Elvis Costello My Aim Is True 1977, The Cars The Cars 1978, Devo Q: Are We Not Men? A: We Are Devo! 1978, The Police Outlandos d'Amour 1978, Squeeze Cool for Cats 1979, XTC Drums and Wires 1979, The B-52's 1979, and the broader Power Pop, Two-Tone Ska, and Post-Punk-Pop subsidiary genres; tradition extends through mid-1980s before alt-rock-and-college-radio absorbs the lineage), the late-1970s through mid-1980s post-punk-derived pop subgenre defined by angular guitar texture and synthesizer accents over verse-chorus pop song-form. Defined by angular-guitar texture (the chorus-and-flanger-treated-clean-guitar with melodic-figure-and-arpeggio voicing rather than power-chord-rock language; Andy Summers in The Police, Adrian Belew in Talking Heads, Joe Walsh-influenced angular work), synthesizer accents (analog-monosynth and string-machine pad-and-stab work supplementing the guitar-foreground arrangement, distinguishing new-wave from synthpop's synthesizer-foreground orientation), verse-chorus pop song-form (short 3-minute single architectures distinguishing new-wave from extended-prog-or-jam-rock), prominent reggae-and-ska-and-Latin rhythmic influence (The Police's reggae-rock, Talking Heads' Afrobeat-fusion, the Two-Tone-Ska revival), and lyric content alternating new-wave-modern-alienation themes (Talking Heads' Psycho Killer, Devo's satirical-modernity) with straight pop-romance content. Distinguished from contemporaneous synthpop by guitar-foreground vs synthesizer-foreground arrangement; distinguished from preceding punk by pop-songwriting-craft and instrumental-musicianship vs amateur-aesthetic orientation; distinguished from later alternative-rock and college-rock (the lineage successors) by 1980s-pop-radio-crossover orientation vs 1990s alternative-rock's independent-radio orientation. Lineage forward feeds 1980s alt-rock and college-rock (R.E.M., The Replacements, Pixies drawing on new-wave songwriting), 1990s power-pop revival (Weezer, Fountains of Wayne), and through them the broader pop-rock continuum.

items.name: Folk rock
items.lineage: Mid-1960s through 1970s amplified folk-rock fusion codified by The Byrds Mr. Tambourine Man (1965), Buffalo Springfield, Crosby Stills Nash and Young, Simon and Garfunkel late-60s catalog
items.description: Folk rock (codified mid-1965 through 1972 across UK-and-American amplified-folk scenes with The Byrds Mr. Tambourine Man cover 1965 establishing the electrified-folk idiom and Bob Dylan's electric Newport-1965 controversy crystallizing the genre boundary; foundations in earlier Greenwich-Village folk-revival lineage and Bob Dylan acoustic-protest era; flowering 1965-1972 through The Byrds Sweetheart of the Rodeo 1968, Simon and Garfunkel Bridge Over Troubled Water 1970, Crosby Stills Nash and Young Déjà Vu 1970, Joni Mitchell Blue 1971, James Taylor Sweet Baby James 1970, and parallel UK Fairport Convention Liege and Lief 1969 and Pentangle electric-folk-revival; tradition extends through 1970s singer-songwriter era), the mid-1960s through 1970s amplified-folk subgenre fusing acoustic-folk songwriting tradition with electric-rock instrumentation. Defined by amplified-folk arrangement frame (acoustic guitar plus electric-guitar-and-bass-and-drums backing, distinguishing folk-rock from purely-acoustic folk-revival material), narrative-and-poetic lyric foreground (the lyric-driven craft tradition inherited from Greenwich-Village folk-revival lineage with literary-poetic ambition distinguishing folk-rock from rock-romantic standard fare), close-harmony backing-vocal arrangement (Crosby Stills Nash high-stacked harmony, the Byrds chiming-12-string-and-three-part-harmony signature), 12-string Rickenbacker electric-guitar timbre (Roger McGuinn's chiming arpeggiated voicings as the genre's sonic identifier), tambourine-and-light-percussion arrangement frame, and tempo range typically 80-120 BPM. Distinguished from preceding folk-revival by amplified-electric-instrumentation foundation; distinguished from contemporaneous rock by lyric-and-songwriting-craft foreground over rhythm-and-riff foreground; distinguished from later country-rock (its close lineage successor) by absence of pedal-steel and country-twang-vocal-tradition foreground. Lineage forward feeds country-rock (Eagles, Gram Parsons, Burrito Brothers absorbing folk-rock arrangement into country-instrumentation frame), singer-songwriter tradition (James Taylor, Carole King, Joni Mitchell carrying forward the folk-rock songwriting tradition into solo-pop format), and through them the broader Americana-and-roots-rock continuum.

items.name: Skiffle
items.lineage: UK 1953-1958 working-class amateur DIY folk-jazz hybrid genre — codified through Lonnie Donegan’s "Rock Island Line" (1954, his Chris Barber Jazz Band session) and subsequent solo records, with the Chas McDevitt and Nancy Whiskey "Freight Train" (1957) reaching the US Top 40; characterized by amateur-acoustic instrumentation (washboard, tea-chest bass, acoustic guitar, banjo) and American-folk repertoire adapted for UK youth
items.description: Skiffle (codified 1953-1958 in UK trad-jazz-scene-and-coffee-bar working-class amateur DIY-folk-jazz hybrid; Chris Barber Jazz Band's skiffle-segment with Lonnie Donegan vocal-and-guitar performances of Lead Belly and Woody Guthrie material establishing the idiom 1954-1956; Donegan's Rock Island Line 1955 hit single launching mainstream-UK skiffle boom; flowering 1956-1958 through The Vipers, Wally Whyton, Chas McDevitt, with several thousand amateur skiffle groups emerging across UK working-class neighborhoods including the Quarrymen formed 1956 by John Lennon and Paul McCartney before becoming The Beatles, plus the same trajectory for The Hollies, The Searchers, and most British 1960s beat bands; tradition fades by 1958 as rock-and-roll absorbs the lineage), the UK 1950s working-class amateur DIY-folk-jazz hybrid genre that served as the seed-bed for British Invasion rock. Defined by DIY-amateur instrumentation foundation (acoustic guitar plus tea-chest bass — a homemade bass-instrument constructed from a tea-shipping crate, broomstick, and single rope-or-string — washboard percussion, harmonica, kazoo, and optional banjo; the deliberately-amateur instrumentation distinguishing skiffle from contemporaneous professional UK trad-jazz and from American folk-revival), American-folk-and-blues repertoire (Lead Belly, Woody Guthrie, and pre-war Mississippi-and-Carolina blues material adopted as UK skiffle source material), shouted-and-projected vocal delivery, fast-tempo and rhythmic-drive emphasis (the propulsive forward-motion that distinguished skiffle from slower American-folk-revival), and short 2-3-minute song-form architecture. Distinguished from contemporaneous UK trad-jazz by amateur-DIY-instrumentation vs professional brass-and-reed instrumentation; distinguished from American folk-revival by faster-tempo and rhythm-drive emphasis; distinguished from later British Invasion rock by acoustic-and-DIY instrumentation vs electric-amplified instrumentation. Lineage forward feeds the entire British Invasion (essentially every major British 1960s beat band started as a skiffle group), the UK folk revival (Bert Jansch, John Renbourn drawing on skiffle-era American-folk repertoire), and through them the broader UK rock-and-folk lineage.

items.name: Jug band
items.lineage: 1920s and 1930s African-American Memphis-and-Cincinnati DIY blues string-band tradition — codified through the Memphis Jug Band (recorded 1927-1934), Cannon’s Jug Stompers (Gus Cannon with Noah Lewis), and the Dixieland Jug Blowers — characterized by amateur-improvised instrumentation (clay jug as bass, kazoo, washboard, harmonica, banjo, guitar) and country-blues repertoire performed for working-class audiences
items.description: Jug band (codified 1924-1934 across African-American Memphis-and-Cincinnati-and-Louisville performance-and-recording circuits; Memphis Jug Band led by Will Shade emerging 1926-onward through Victor recording sessions; Cannon's Jug Stompers led by Gus Cannon emerging 1927-1930 through Victor sessions including the Walk Right In 1929; parallel development through Cincinnati Jug Band, Whistler and his Jug Band, Tub Jug Washboard Band, Earl McDonald's Original Louisville Jug Band; tradition fades by mid-1930s as electric-blues displaces it; revival 1960s through Even Dozen Jug Band, Jim Kweskin Jug Band, and Lovin' Spoonful precursor lineage), the 1920s-1930s African-American Memphis-and-Cincinnati-area DIY blues-and-popular-song string-band tradition. Defined by DIY-instrumentation foundation (the jug-band-instrument signature: ceramic-or-glass jug blown across the opening for low-register bass-substitute notes — the genre-defining instrument that gives the tradition its name — washboard for percussion, harmonica, kazoo, plus acoustic guitar, banjo, fiddle, and mandolin for harmonic-and-melodic foundation), blues-and-popular-song repertoire (mixing twelve-bar-blues with vaudeville-and-popular-song material, distinguishing jug-band from purely-blues delta and piedmont traditions), call-and-response group-vocal arrangement, mid-tempo dance-rhythm foundation (the propulsive forward-motion that distinguished jug-band from slower-tempo blues), and entertainment-and-busking performance context (street-corner-and-medicine-show performance practice rather than juke-joint-and-dance-hall). Distinguished from hokum-blues vaudeville (its closest cousin) by Memphis-and-Cincinnati lineage vs Chicago-and-NYC vaudeville-circuit and folk-narrative lyrical content vs double-entendre humor content; distinguished from delta-blues by group-band format vs solo-with-guitar format; distinguished from piedmont fingerpicking by jug-and-percussion ensemble foundation. Lineage forward feeds 1960s jug-band revival, country-blues string-band revival, and through them the broader American-string-band continuum.

items.name: Yacht rock
items.lineage: Late-1970s through mid-1980s smooth West-Coast AOR pop-rock codified by Steely Dan Aja and Gaucho, the Doobie Brothers post-Michael McDonald era, Toto, Christopher Cross, Kenny Loggins, the Eagles Hotel California aesthetic
