Ended abruptly with the 1949 Communist takeover that classified shidaiqu as yellow music / huang se yinyue and banned the genre in Mainland China; the tradition continued in British Hong Kong through Pathé Hong Kong (Yao Lee and Pan Wan-ching late careers) and seeded the 1970s-onward Mandopop and Cantopop traditions. Distinguished from later Mandopop by pre-revolutionary Shanghai origin and acoustic-jazz-band orchestration rather than Taiwan-Mainland-Hong-Kong 70s-onward production; distinguished from contemporaneous Shanghai jazz instrumentals by Mandarin-language vocal-foreground; distinguished from Western jazz of the same era by Chinese melodic-vocabulary and Mandarin lyric content.
exemplars: Zhou Xuan — When Will You Return
Yao Lee — Rose Rose I Love You

items.name: Jīngjù (Beijing opera)
items.lineage: Late-18th-century onward Chinese capital-region operatic synthesis emerging in Beijing from the Anhui-Hui troupes 1790 and the Hubei kunqu-pihuang merger 1820s onward, codified by the four great male role-types (sheng, jing chou-and-dan painted-face roles) and the four schools of female dan voice. Built on jinghu-erhu fiddle accompaniment with bangu-and-paigu percussion section setting the jianzipu rhythmic patterns. Court patronage in the Qing late-imperial period gave way to commercial troupe-theaters of late-Qing and Republican-era Shanghai-and-Beijing. The vocal stylization layers melismatic-modal pihuang (xipi-and-erhuang aria modes) with declamatory speech-tone alignment, where Mandarin tones constrain melodic contour.
items.description: Jingju / Beijing opera (codified 1790 onward, with the Anhui troupes' 1790 arrival in Beijing as the foundation event and Mei Lanfang's 1920s-1940s reform period as crystallizing era), the Chinese codified-classical theater tradition. Defined by codified role-types (sheng — male, dan — female, jing — painted-face, chou — clown), each with distinctive vocal-style conventions and movement-vocabulary, melodic system organized around two main musical modes (xipi — bright and lively, erhuang — somber and lyrical), instrumental ensemble led by jinghu high-pitched fiddle (bamboo-bodied two-string spike fiddle giving the genre its signature timbre) with yueqin moon-lute, sanxian three-string lute, and high-and-low percussion (gongs, cymbals, ban wood-clapper), elaborate stylized-acting and operatic-singing-and-movement integration, and repertoire drawn from historical-and-legendary narrative material. Distinguished from kunqu (the older Chinese classical opera) by faster pace and military-and-acrobatic emphasis; distinguished from regional Chinese operas by Beijing-court codification and pan-Chinese standardization status.

items.name: Gǔqín
items.lineage: Chinese seven-string scholar-zither solo tradition with documented written scores (jianzipu tablature-notation) dating from the Han-dynasty (206 BCE-220 CE) onward, making it the oldest continuously-notated musical tradition. Constructed of paulownia-tung-wood top and zi-wood bottom with thirteen mother-of-pearl hui position-markers and silk or steel-nylon strings. The repertoire layers Wei-Jin-and-Tang dynasty meditative-philosophical pieces with Song-Yuan-and-Ming court-and-scholar-amateur literati compositions, performed solo in studio-and-garden settings as a wenrenhua scholar-painting-music-poetry integrated-art-form practice. Microtonal sliding (yin-and-rou portamento), harmonics (fan-yin), and silent-finger gestures comprise the canonical performance vocabulary.
items.description: Guqin (continuous tradition pre-Han onward across Chinese literati culture, with extant repertoire of approximately 3000 pieces preserved through Ming-Qing-era handbook codifications and continuous master-disciple transmission to present), the seven-string Chinese zither solo tradition of literati culture. Defined by the qin instrument itself (a 4-foot horizontal long-zither with seven silk-or-modern-nylon strings, no movable bridges — the strings rest on a fixed nut and are stopped by the player's left hand on the unmarked but indicated playing surface), meditative-sparse performance aesthetic (the guqin tradition explicitly opposes virtuosic-display-foregrounded performance, instead prizing contemplative-restrained gesture and silent-pause-as-musical-element), microtonal sliding ornamentation (the guqin specialty of slow-glissando left-hand techniques producing extensive pitch-bend decoration), tablature notation specific to the guqin (distinct from Chinese ensemble notation, indicating finger-position and technique rather than pitch directly), and solo-or-small-chamber performance contexts in literati gardens, scholar's studios, and contemporary concert settings. Distinguished from guzheng (Chinese larger zither, 21-25 strings, popular tradition) by literati-not-popular framing and seven-string-not-multi-string configuration; distinguished from Japanese koto (its descendant) by Chinese pre-Han-onward source and absence of movable bridges.

items.name: Wenrenyue
items.lineage: Chinese scholar-amateur literati chamber music tradition with guqin (seven-string zither) and xiao (vertical bamboo flute) at its core — codified through the Tang dynasty (618-907 CE) scholar-official aesthetic, continued through Song-Yuan-Ming-Qing dynasties, formalized in the seven major guqin schools (Wu, Yu, Shu, Jiu Yi, Mei An, Zha’an, and Guangling), and preserved through the 20th-century rescue work of Zha Fuxi and the Beiping Guqin Research Society
items.description: Chinese scholar-amateur music tradition (文人乐, "literati music") centered on the seven-string guqin. Pre-modern transmission via private teaching among Confucian-Daoist scholar-officials; meditative-philosophical performance context (private contemplation, small gatherings of like-minded scholars, ritual self-cultivation). Repertoire codified in qin-pu tablature manuals across Ming and Qing dynasties (c. 1425-1911 commercial publication). Distinct from court-music (yayue) and theatrical traditions in its private-amateur-aesthetic and metaphysical-literary conceptual framework. The guqin-silk-string sound — soft, microtonal, with extensive left-hand vibrato (yin) and slide ornamentation — is to the tradition; modern steel-string substitutions are considered inauthentic.

items.name: Shakuhachi honkyoku
items.lineage: Japanese Fuke-Zen shakuhachi five-hole bamboo-flute solo tradition with the 36-piece honkyoku canonical-repertoire codified by the Komuso mendicant-monk lineage of the Edo-period (1603-1868). Originated from Tang-dynasty Chinese chi imported via 8th-century Buddhist transmission, transformed through medieval Japanese ascetic-monastic practice into a meditative suizen blowing-as-zen contemplative discipline. Each honkyoku piece is ametrical-rhythmically-free (no fixed pulse), built around the wabi-sabi aesthetic of single-tone meri-kari microtonal bending, atari-and-mura-iki breath-attack and breath-noise as expressive elements, and silence as compositional structure. The Meiji-era 1871 suppression of the Fuke sect transitioned the repertoire from religious to concert context.
items.description: Shakuhachi honkyoku (codified 17th century onward in Japan through Fuke-shu Zen Buddhist komuso ('priests of nothingness') practice, with continuous tradition through Edo-period Fuke transmission and post-Meiji-Restoration secularization to present), the Japanese Zen Buddhist solo bamboo-flute repertoire. Defined by the shakuhachi instrument (a 1.8-foot end-blown bamboo flute with five finger-holes, played as a meditative-spiritual practice tool), breath-as-meditation aesthetic (the shakuhachi-practice use of long-sustained-tones and breath-control as Zen-meditation discipline), free-meter rhythmic organization (no fixed pulse — phrase-pace follows breath-cycle), broad timbral-effect palette (deliberate-uneven-tone, breath-sound prominence, characteristic muraiki overblown-attack and koro-koro chamber-shake fingering ornaments), repertoire of approximately 36 traditional honkyoku pieces preserved across regional schools (Kinko-ryu and Myoan-ryu the lineages), within solo-meditation-practice performance contexts (the broader shakuhachi tradition also encompasses sankyoku-trio chamber-ensemble with koto and string-lute, separate from honkyoku scope). Distinguished from broader Japanese chamber-music by Zen-Buddhist-meditation framing and free-meter foundation; distinguished from Chinese xiao despite related instrument by Japanese-Zen-tradition; distinguished from later Japanese flute-and-shakuhachi popular tradition by traditional-honkyoku repertoire.

items.name: Koto
items.lineage: Japanese koto thirteen-string movable-bridge zither tradition with the sankyoku chamber-trio canonical-ensemble configuration (koto-shakuhachi-shamisen). Imported from Tang-dynasty Chinese guzheng via 8th-century Japanese-court transmission, refined through Edo-period (1603-1868) school-lineage codification by the Ikuta and Yamada schools, and modernized 20th-century-onward through Miyagi-school-and-Sawai-school neoclassical compositional expansion (including the seventeen-string bass-koto innovation). Repertoire layers honkyoku solo-canonical pieces, jiuta-sankyoku chamber-trio works with shamisen-derived song-lyrics, and 20th-century-onward shin-nihon-ongaku modern-Japanese-music compositions.
items.description: Koto (codified 17th century Japan through Yatsuhashi Kengyō's establishment of the modern sōkyoku solo and chamber repertoire, with continuous tradition through Edo-period pleasure-quarter and family-instruction lineage to present-day conservatory and amateur practice), the Japanese thirteen-string zither tradition. Defined by the koto instrument (a 6-foot horizontal long-zither with 13 silk-or-nylon strings tuned by movable bridges placed under each string), played with three picks worn on right-hand thumb-and-index-and-middle, repertoire of sōkyoku solo and chamber compositions in the danmono variation-form and other genres, kumiuta vocal-with-koto accompaniment forms, and chamber-ensemble pieces with shamisen and shakuhachi (the sankyoku trio). Performance contexts: traditional concert hall, family-disciple instruction, and conservatory pedagogy. Distinguished from Chinese zheng (its predecessor) by Japanese tuning-system and movable-bridge configuration; distinguished from later Japanese koto-pop fusion by classical-tradition framing.

items.name: Pansori
items.lineage: Korean epic-narrative solo-vocal tradition with single sorikkun (singer-storyteller) accompanied by single buk barrel-drum gosu (drummer) and aniri spoken-narration interludes between sung passages. Codified late-17th-and-18th-century onward in Cholla-province (southwestern Korean peninsula) from earlier shamanic kut-ritual narrative-chant, evolved through 19th-century master-disciple-school lineages into a 3-to-8-hour concert form covering twelve canonical madang epic-narratives (now five surviving: Chunhyangga, Simcheongga, Heungbuga, Sugungga, Jeokbyeokga). The vocal technique stresses sangchung-cheong middle-register, jjokbal-hoek tonal-coloration, and gyeongdrumeokpan throat-tearing rough-vocal-quality (deliberately broken via years of practice), with strict jangdan rhythmic-cycle alternation from slowest 18/8 jinyangjo to fastest 4/4 hwimori.
items.description: Pansori (codified 17th-19th century Korea, with the Five Surviving Pansori — Chunhyangga, Simcheongga, Heungbuga, Sugungga, Jeokbyeokga — as the repertoire and 19th-century master singers establishing the regional schools), the Korean epic-narrative singing tradition. Defined by single vocalist (sorikkun) accompanied only by buk hourglass-shaped drum played by gosu drummer, performance of hours-long historical-or-legendary narrative pieces (a full Chunhyangga performance can extend past five hours), three-element vocal performance combining sori (sung-melodic passages), aniri (spoken-narrative passages), and ballim (gestural-dramatic acting), characteristic vocal aesthetic prizing tonal-husky raspy-textured voice (the pansori-chwang voice produced through years of training in the deep-voice waterfall practice), and audience response patterns where audience interjects chuimsae encouraging-shouts during performance. Distinguished from Korean folk songs (minyo) by epic-narrative scale and trained-vocalist specialty; distinguished from Korean court music by folk-narrative origin and emergence from itinerant gwangdae performers; distinguished from changgeuk (later Korean operatic adaptation of pansori material) by solo-not-ensemble performance.

items.name: Samul nori
items.lineage: 1978-onward Korean four-instrument concert-percussion ensemble codified by the Kim Duk-soo founding troupe, derived from rural pungmul village-ritual-and-harvest-procession percussion of the late-Joseon era. The four instruments — kkwaenggwari small-gong-leader, jing large-gong-pulse, janggu hourglass-drum, buk barrel-drum — interlock through five canonical jangdan rhythmic-pattern movements (Bibari, Samdo-Sori, Yeongnam, Honam-udo, Jwadodulgi) that compress regional pungmul styles into a 60-90 minute staged concert form. The genre catalyzed the 1980s-onward Korean traditional-music revival and is widely taught in Korean elementary curricula.
items.description: Samul nori (codified 1978 in Seoul as concert-stage formalization of pungmul village-festival drumming, with the founding ensemble SamulNori — Kim Duk-soo, Kim Yong-bae, Lee Kwang-soo, Choi Tae-hyun — establishing the four-instrument quartet format and the modern repertoire that crystallized agricultural-ceremonial drumming into virtuosic concert presentation; the name samul-nori meaning literally "four-instrument-play" describes the quartet structure), the Korean four-instrument percussion tradition that translates rural pungmul agricultural-festival music into concert-virtuoso format. Defined by the four-instrument quartet (kkwaenggwari small flat brass gong as lead-and-time-keeper played by sangsoe leader; jing large hanging brass gong providing phrase-marker low-fundamental tones; janggu hourglass drum as primary rhythmic-melodic voice with two distinct heads producing high-and-low contrasting timbres; buk barrel drum providing steady-pulse foundation), interlocking polyrhythmic structure where each instrument plays a distinct rhythmic-and-timbral role that combines into composite groove, repertoire of named traditional rhythms (Yeongnam-nori, Uddari-nori, Samdo-sang-mo-gi) drawn from regional pungmul traditions and reformatted for concert presentation, performer-virtuosity foreground (samul nori specifically emphasizes rapid-tempo and rhythmic-complexity virtuosity that distinguishes it from village-pungmul antecedent), and continuous-pulse 4/4-or-12/8 rhythmic foundation organized around shifting tempo gradations through extended pieces. Distinguished from preceding pungmul village-festival drumming by concert-stage-not-festival-procession context, four-quartet-fixed-instrument-format vs flexible-village-ensemble, and virtuosic-tempo emphasis; distinguished from contemporary Korean kumi-daiko-influenced taiko drumming by Korean-not-Japanese instrumentation and melodic-not-purely-percussive emphasis (kkwaenggwari and jing carry pitch-content); distinguished from janggu-solo-virtuoso traditions by ensemble-rather-than-solo orientation. Lineage: 1978 founding of SamulNori-the-ensemble crystallized the genre; subsequent decades produced multiple major samul nori ensembles internationally and integrated samul nori into Korean concert-stage modern-traditional music infrastructure.
exemplars: SamulNori (Kim Duk-soo, Kim Yong-bae, Lee Kwang-soo, Choi Tae-hyun)

items.name: Mongolian long-song (urtyn duu)
items.lineage: Mongolian urtyn-duu ceremonial-long-song tradition with sustained-melismatic vocal-line over morin-khuur horse-head-fiddle drone-accompaniment, the canonical singing style of the inner-Asian steppe nomadic-pastoralist horse-and-herder culture. intangible-cultural-heritage $1-onward, with three regional variants (Eastern Khalkha aristocratic-court style, Western Oirat folk-rural style, Southern Inner-Mongolia diasporic style). Long-songs unfold over 5-20 minute durations through ornamental-throat-glottal techniques (kazargai, shuranhai), strict-textual three-line couplets typically about horses, mountains, ancestors, and steppe-landscape, and free-rhythm ametrical pulse anchored only by breath-phrase boundaries.
items.description: Mongolian long song / urtyn duu (continuous tradition pre-Mongol-Empire onward across Mongolia and Inner-Mongolian-Chinese steppe pastoralist communities, with Buryat, Khalkha, and Oirat regional sub-traditions), the pastoralist solo vocal form. Defined by extremely extended phrases (single melodic lines stretching across 30-60 seconds without breath-pause, the genre name urtyn meaning long), elaborate melismatic ornamentation including specific Mongolian-vocal techniques (shurankhai falsetto-yodel-jumps, niin-bekhtir vibrato, and other regional-style decoration), often-unaccompanied solo performance or accompanied by morin khuur horsehead-fiddle (the Mongolian fiddle with two horsehair strings), lyric content addressing pastoral-life subjects (horse imagery, nomadic-landscape, family-and-clan, philosophical reflection), and ceremonial-and-festival performance contexts at naadam festivals and family gatherings. Distinguished from Mongolian throat-singing (khoomei) by melodic-rather-than-overtone vocal foundation; distinguished from short-song (bogino duu) by extended-phrase-length and melismatic-decoration foreground; distinguished from Tuvan long-song by Mongolian-Khalkha specificity.

items.name: Javanese gamelan
items.lineage: Javanese bronze-percussion court-and-village tradition tuned in slendro five-tone-and-pelog seven-tone systems, with two parallel lineages: the kraton-court refined-style of Yogyakarta and Surakarta (16th-century onward, Mataram successor sultanates) and the village kemasan rural-ensemble style. The full court gamelan comprises 30-to-40 instruments organized into balungan core-melody bonang-saron, panerusan elaborating-melody gender-rebab-suling, and gong-kempul colotomic-structural-time-markers, performed cyclically through gendhing pieces of nested 8-16-32-64-128 beat irama tempo-density levels. The wayang shadow-puppet performance is the canonical embedding context, where gamelan accompanies dalang puppeteer-narration through pathet modal sections aligned to night-narrative time.
items.description: Javanese gamelan (codified continuously from at least 9th century Javanese court contexts through to present, with central-Javanese karaton (court) gamelan of Yogyakarta and Surakarta as the codifying-classical lineage), the Javanese bronze-metallophone ensemble tradition. Defined by sléndro (5-tone) and pélog (7-tone) tuning systems each with distinct emotional-and-occasion association, cyclical colotomic structure where punctuating gongs of various sizes mark the cycle's metric divisions (gong ageng marking the longest cycle, kenong-kempul-kethuk subdividing within), interlocking instrumental textures with multiple metallophones playing complementary phrases at different rhythmic densities, dance-and-shadow-puppet wayang-kulit performance contexts, and sindhen female solo vocal and gérong male chorus singing on top of the instrumental texture. Distinguished from Balinese gamelan by slower tempos, absence of paired-tuning shimmer, and tuning-flexibility within a single performance; distinguished from Sundanese gamelan by central-Javanese lineage and karaton classical context.

items.name: Balinese gamelan
items.lineage: Balinese Hindu-syncretic bronze-percussion ensemble tradition descended from the same Javanese gamelan lineage but diverged sharply 14th-century onward into a faster-tempo brighter-tuned (panca-nada five-tone but at higher pitch register) more virtuosic-rhythmic ensemble idiom. The major sub-traditions: gamelan-gong-kebyar 1915-onward 20th-century innovation with explosive-tutti starts-and-stops, gamelan-semar-pegulingan slower-court-elegant-style, gamelan-gambuh oldest-court-dance-accompaniment, gamelan-angklung four-tone-bamboo-rattle ensemble for cremation-ceremonies, and gamelan-jegog deep-bass bamboo-xylophone West-Bali variant. The interlocking kotekan two-instrument-paired hocket-figuration creates the characteristic Balinese rhythmic-texture impossible in solo execution.
items.description: Balinese gamelan gong kebyar (codified ca. 1915 in northern Bali following social transformation that moved gamelan from courts to village sekehe associations), and earlier ceremonial styles (gambuh, gambang, semar pegulingan), the Balinese tuned-percussion ensemble tradition. Defined by paired-tuning systems where male-female (pengumbang-pengisep) instrument pairs differ by 5-8 cents to produce the shimmering acoustic-beats characteristic of Balinese sound, kotekan interlocking-melodic-pattern technique where two players alternate fast notes to create a single composite line at twice the speed, hammered bronze keyed instruments (gangsa, jegogan, jublag) and gong-chimes (reong, trompong), kendang drum direction, and gong-cycle metric organization. Distinguished from Javanese gamelan by faster tempos, paired-tuning shimmer, and absence of pelog-and-slendro mode-flexibility within a single piece (Balinese ensembles are tuning-fixed); distinguished from Sundanese gamelan by Balinese island-Hindu ceremonial framing.

items.name: Kulintang
items.lineage: Maguindanao and Maranao (Mindanao, Philippines) horizontally-laid bossed-gong-set ensemble tradition predating Spanish contact
items.description: Kulintang (codified pre-Islamic onward across southern Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei across Maranao, Maguindanao, T'boli, and Tausug ethnic groups in Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago), the Philippine-and-Bornean Mindanao gong-row tradition. Defined by the kulintang instrument itself (a row of 8 graduated knobbed-bossed bronze gongs laid horizontally on a wooden frame, with the smallest-and-highest-pitched at the right and largest-and-lowest at the left), played as the melodic-lead voice over an ensemble of agung large suspended gongs, gandingan large pair-of-gongs, and dabakan goblet-drum providing rhythmic foundation, repertoire of binalig and other regional-style traditional pieces, and ceremonial-and-festival performance contexts. Distinguished from Javanese and Balinese gamelan by gong-row-not-keyed-metallophone construction and Mindanao-not-Indonesian regional lineage; distinguished from other Philippine lowland Christian musical traditions by Muslim-Mindanao cultural framing.

items.name: Dangdut
items.lineage: Indonesian working-class popular-music genre that emerged in late-1960s Jakarta — fusion of Indian filmi rhythmic foundation (the dang-dut onomatopoeic name describes the Indian-tabla-derived rhythmic pattern), Malay popular song melodic vocabulary, and rock-instrumental electric-band foundation; codified through Rhoma Irama (the king of dangdut, his Soneta Group from 1973 onward), Elvy Sukaesih, the modern Via Vallen and Nella Kharisma koplo-dangdut Javanese-flavored extension
items.description: Dangdut (codified 1968-1975 in Jakarta through Rhoma Irama's Soneta Group recordings, with deeper roots in 1950s-60s Indonesian Orkes Melayu and earlier Hindi-film-influenced cinema soundtrack), the Indonesian popular song form synthesizing Hindustani filmi, Arab, and Malay influences. Defined by the gendang two-headed drum playing tabla-imitating patterns (the dang and dut sound names give the genre its name), melismatic vocal delivery with maqam-influenced ornamentation, electric guitar lead over bass-and-drums-and-electronic-keyboard back-line, song-form alternating verse-chorus with extended dance breaks, lyrical content addressing working-class concerns and romantic-melodrama subjects, and tempos around 110-130 BPM with a characteristic offbeat-emphasis groove. Distinguished from Hindustani filmi by Indonesian-language vocals and gendang-not-tabla rhythm; distinguished from Arab tarab by pop-form-rather-than-classical structure; distinguished from later koplo (a faster Javanese subgenre) by tempo and rural-vs-urban dance-floor framing.

items.name: Mor lam
items.lineage: Isan (Northeast Thailand) and Lao traditional and popular vocal-and-khaen tradition — mor lam literally means expert singer in Lao; the Isan/Lao genre built on the khaen (bamboo mouth-organ with 16 pipes in two rows) and the lead-vocal improvising long-form Lao-language sung-poetry over the khaen drone-and-melody foundation; figures Banyen Rakkaen, Pornsak Songsang, Chaweewan Damnern, and the modern Jintara Poonlarp
items.description: Mor lam (continuous tradition centuries-onward in Lao Buddhist and Northeast-Thai Isan ethnic-Lao communities, with codified-modernized regional sub-styles — mor lam klon traditional unaccompanied verse-form, mor lam ploen modernized small-band arrangement, mor lam sing electric-band high-tempo dance form), the Lao and Northeast-Thai sung-poetry tradition. Defined by improvised lam (sung-poetry verses) over khaen mouth-organ drone-and-melody accompaniment (the bamboo-pipes free-reed instrument that is the Lao mor lam instrument), call-and-response between male-and-female lam-singer pairs in courtship-and-philosophical-debate exchanges, repertoire spanning religious-Buddhist material, romantic-courtship, social-commentary, and historical-narrative subjects, and electric-band modernization (mor lam sing) extending the format into Thai-pop-club territory while retaining the khaen and lam-singing centrality. Distinguished from Thai luk thung by Lao-Isan-not-central-Thai linguistic-and-musical lineage; distinguished from Cambodian phleng kar by Lao-not-Khmer lineage; distinguished from Lao classical court music by folk-and-popular-not-courtly framing.

items.name: Powwow song
items.lineage: Plains-Northern intertribal Native American powwow drum-circle song tradition — the pan-tribal Native American performance format that emerged in the late-19th-century post-reservation period from older tribal-specific song traditions (Plains Lakota / Dakota / Crow, Great Lakes Ojibwe, Northern Plains Cree) and codified through the 20th century into an intertribal cultural-renewal celebration network; performed on the powwow drum (a single large frame drum shared by 6-10 drummers in a circle) with unison falsetto-high vocable lyrics — drum groups: Black Lodge Singers (Blackfeet), Northern Cree Singers, Whitefish Bay Singers (Ojibwe)
items.description: Powwow / inter-tribal pan-Indian song (codified 1880s onward, descending from Northern Plains Lakota and Southern Plains Kiowa traditional warrior-society song repertoire, with modernized inter-tribal powwow circuit established through the 20th century and continuous tradition through to present), the Northern and Southern Plains intertribal singing tradition. Defined by all-male vocal group seated around a single large frame drum (the powwow-drum, a 3-4-foot-diameter rawhide-headed double-headed drum) playing a steady-pulse foundation, multi-part call-and-response vocal performance with high-falsetto lead alternating with chorus response, repertoire of intertribal honor-songs, dance-songs (men's traditional, men's grass, men's fancy, women's traditional, women's jingle, women's fancy), and ceremonial-songs, vocables (non-lexical syllabic vocal sounds — heya-heya-yo) carrying much of the melodic content alongside language verses, and Northern-style higher-tessitura and Southern-style lower-tessitura regional vocal aesthetics. Distinguished from any single-tribe traditional song by inter-tribal pan-Indian framing; distinguished from later Native American flute and contemporary pop by traditional-ceremonial framing.

items.name: Huayno
items.lineage: Quechua-and-Aymara Andean dance-song tradition with anhemitonic-pentatonic five-tone (no half-step) melodic-vocabulary and characteristic short-short-long iambic-dance pattern (Q-Q-half rhythm) over moderate-fast 2/4 metric pulse. Pre-Columbian-origin (likely Inca-Imperial 1438-1533 onward, though oral-tradition extends earlier) with post-colonial mestizaje fusion (Spanish-criollo) integration of guitar, harp, charango ten-string-small-armadillo-back-guitar, and bandurria. Regional variants span Cuzco huayno-cusqueño (slower-court-elevated), Ayacucho huayno-ayacuchano (faster-rural), Junín huayno-orquestino (brass-band-and-saxophone modernized), and Aymara huayño-altiplánico (Bolivian-highland variant). The canonical instrumental ensemble includes quena vertical-notch-flute and zampoña panpipes.
items.description: Huayno (pre-Columbian Quechua and Aymara origin, codified for performance/recording from 1920s onward across Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, northern Argentina, and northern Chile), the Andean dance-song form in syncopated 2/4 with characteristic dotted-eighth-sixteenth phrase rhythm. Defined by the charango (small armadillo-back lute now usually wood), quena and zampoña (notched-end and pan-pipe flutes), bombo legüero or bombo andino frame drum, and Quechua-or-Aymara-language vocal lines often delivered as plaintive female solo or call-and-response community singing. Performance contexts span chicha-bar dance hall, festival procession, and family ceremony. Distinguished from cumbia colombiana by Andean-not-coastal-Caribbean lineage and indigenous-Andean instrumentation; distinguished from chicha (later urban Lima electric variant) by acoustic instrumentation and traditional rural framing.

items.name: Bambuco
items.lineage: Colombian national rhythm and song-form in characteristic 6/8 meter with three-against-two syncopation — codified through the late-19th-century Andean Colombian school (Pedro Morales Pino, the bandola virtuoso who systematized the trio andino instrumentation), 20th-century anchors Garzón y Collazos (the post-WWII bambuco-trio voice, El Camino de la Vida 1951), Silva y Villalba, the modern Gustavo Adolfo Renjifo and Carranguero-tradition Jorge Velosa extensions; performed by the trio andino of tiple, bandola andina, and classical guitar with vocal duet or trio
items.description: Colombian Andean string-trio song tradition with characteristic compound-duple rhythmic foundation (6/8 over implied 3/4 hemiola). Tiple-bandola-guitar instrumental architecture is, though many recordings reduce to tiple-and-guitar duo or feature voice with both. Mestizo cultural origin in the eastern Andean highlands of Colombia (Cundinamarca, Boyacá, Tolima); 19th-century pasillo-and-bambuco repertoire codified in early-20th-century commercial recordings. Lyrical content centers on pastoral subjects, romantic longing, and regional pride. Distinct from coastal Colombian cumbia (Caribbean accordion-and-percussion idiom) and llanero joropo (eastern-plains harp-and-cuatro idiom) by Andean string-trio architecture and European-derived harmonic vocabulary.
exemplars: Trío Morales Pino — Colombian Andean catalog

items.name: Son jarocho
items.lineage: Mexican Veracruz-Gulf-Coast Afro-Mestizo-Indigenous son tradition with characteristic jarana five-double-course strum-guitar, requinto-jarocho four-string lead-melody-guitar, harp, quijada-de-burro donkey-jawbone scraper, and zapateado wooden-platform dance-percussion. Originated late-17th-century in the Sotavento lowlands south of Veracruz-Port out of Afro-Cuban habanera, Spanish-baroque fandango, and Indigenous-Totonac musical-fusion. The canonical La Bamba is the most internationally recognized son jarocho son, but the tradition spans 80+ son sones with characteristic 6/8-against-2/4 sesquialteral hemiola, call-and-response sung verses (often improvised, decimas Spanish-poetic-form), and circular fandango community-dance-and-music-making fiesta-context. The 1970s-1980s son-jarocho-revival reconnected urban Mexico City to rural Sotavento source-communities.
items.description: Son jarocho (codified 18th century onward in Veracruz Mexico, with Afro-Mestizo synthesis of Spanish, indigenous-Mesoamerican, and African elements, and 20th-century revival through La Bamba commercial success and the Movimiento-Jaranero traditional-revival from 1979 onward), the Afro-Mestizo Veracruz son tradition. Defined by jarana-jarocha (small eight-string Veracruz guitar in five-courses) strumming foundation, requinto-jarocho (smaller four-string lead instrument played with horn-pick) carrying melodic line, harp (arpa jarocha) supplying additional melodic and bass material in expanded ensembles, improvised décima and copla verse traditions (10-line and 4-line poetic stanza forms with elaborate rhyme scheme), syncopated 6/8-and-3/4 hemiola metric organization, foot-percussion zapateado from dancers on a wooden tarima platform providing additional rhythmic foundation, and son repertoire addressing romantic, festive, and traditional subjects. Distinguished from son cubano by Mexican-Veracruz-not-Cuban lineage and jarana-foundation; distinguished from Mexican mariachi by Veracruz-not-Jalisco regional origin and jarana-not-violin-and-trumpet centrality; distinguished from Colombian Caribbean coastal traditions by Veracruz Afro-Mestizo specificity.

items.name: Mento
items.lineage: Jamaican rural folk-and-dance music tradition that preceded ska as the dominant Jamaican popular music genre — codified through the post-WWII commercial recordings of Lord Flea, Count Lasher, the Jolly Boys, Stanley Beckford, Harold Richardson; built on a fusion of West African rhythmic foundations, European-derived quadrille dance forms, and Caribbean Spanish-influenced song structures
items.description: Mento (codified 1900s onward in rural Jamaica, with golden era 1950s-early-1960s before ska and reggae overtook it as Jamaica's dominant pop genre), the Jamaican rural folk music ancestral to ska and reggae. Defined by banjo as melodic and rhythmic lead (the mento-instrument inherited from Jamaican-and-broader-Caribbean string-band tradition), acoustic guitar providing harmonic accompaniment, rhumba box (a Cuban-derived large bass-thumb-piano with metal lamellae played as the bass-line foundation), hand-percussion (maracas, scraper, hand drums) providing additional rhythmic layer, vocal performance often in Jamaican Patois with humorous-and-bawdy lyric content, and tempos around 100-130 BPM with characteristic offbeat-emphasis groove that fed forward into ska's chop-strum upbeat. Distinguished from later ska by acoustic-not-electric instrumentation and pre-1960 timestamp; distinguished from Trinidadian calypso by Jamaican-not-Trinidadian lineage and rhumba-box-not-iron-percussion bass; distinguished from country-blues by Caribbean-not-American-South origin.

items.name: Calypso
items.lineage: Trinidadian narrative-and-topical song tradition emerging from post-1834 Emancipation kalinda stick-fighting chant, codified through the post-WWII commercial recording era — Mighty Sparrow (Slinger Francisco), Lord Kitchener (Aldwyn Roberts), Lord Invader, the Roaring Lion, Lord Melody, Calypso Rose; performed during the Trinidad and Tobago Carnival season (October-February preparation, with Carnival Monday-Tuesday peak) in calypso tent venues and competition contexts
items.description: Calypso (early-19th century Trinidad onward, codified during 1930s-1950s through Port-of-Spain Carnival competition and US-export commercial era 1944-1956), the Trinidadian narrative-satirical song form descended from West African praise-and-shame song traditions transmitted through French-creole kaiso. Defined by lyric content of sharp social commentary, political satire, romantic boast, and topical wordplay (the calypsonian's verbal-virtuosity premium); horn-led syncopated brass-and-rhythm-section arrangements; emcee-style vocal delivery alternating composed verses with extempore-style improvisation; performance contexts spanning Carnival calypso tents, road-march street parade, and 1950s US folk-revival concert; and characteristic up-tempo two-bar percussive feel that prefigured ska. Distinguished from later soca by tempo and lyric foreground over rhythmic foreground; distinguished from Jamaican mento by Trinidadian-not-Jamaican lineage and brass-not-banjo backline; distinguished from steelpan music by vocal-foreground form (though calypsonians frequently performed with steelpan ensembles).

items.name: Soca
items.lineage: Trinidadian dance-music genre codified by Lord Shorty (Garfield Blackman) in 1973 as soul-of-calypso — a faster-tempo party-anthem derivation of calypso that became the dominant Carnival-season dance-floor format; extended through Machel Montano (the modern soca voice), Superblue (Austin Lyons), Bunji Garlin, Kes the Band, and the broader Caribbean Carnival circuit
items.description: Soca (codified 1973-1978 onward through Lord Shorty's pioneering recordings establishing the genre as the soul-of-calypso descendant, with continuous tradition through to present and golden eras 1980s and 2000s-onward), the Trinidadian dance-music genre descended from calypso. Defined by faster tempo than calypso (130-160 BPM compared to calypso's 90-110), electronic production foundation (programmed kick-and-snare, synth-bass and synth-pad textures, sampled or programmed brass-section punctuation rather than live brass-section foundation), festival road-march functional context (the soca-specific Carnival-procession function where the music drives the road-march dance-floor), Trinidadian-English vocal performance with characteristic rhyme-and-rhythm-flow MC-style delivery, and lyrical content addressing Carnival-celebration, romantic-and-social-commentary, and Trinidadian-political subjects. Distinguished from straight calypso by tempo and electronic-production foreground; distinguished from later chutney-soca (Indo-Trinidadian variant) by Afro-Trinidadian centrality; distinguished from later dancehall by Trinidadian-not-Jamaican lineage and Carnival-road-march functional context.

items.name: Kompa
items.lineage: Haitian dance-music genre invented in 1955 by Nemours Jean-Baptiste (kompa-direkt, the founder) and developing in parallel with Webert Sicots cadence-rampa lineage — the dominant secular popular-music genre of Haiti and the broader Haitian diaspora (Miami, New York, Montreal, Paris); extended through Tabou Combo (the second-generation kompa band, formed 1968), Skah Shah, Coupé Cloué, Magnum Band, Sweet Micky
items.description: Kompa / compas direct (codified 1955 onward through Nemours Jean-Baptiste's Conjunto International establishing the genre, with parallel Webert Sicot tradition and continuous Haitian dance-music presence through to present), the Haitian dance music genre. Defined by methodical mid-tempo groove around 90-110 BPM, electric-or-acoustic guitar lead lines providing melodic foreground, accordion or synth supplying additional melodic texture (the kompa-traditional accordion lineage from Cuban conjunto influence, replaced or supplemented by synth in modern kompa), conjunto-like horn-and-percussion arrangement extending the basic guitar-and-vocal core, French-and-Haitian-Creole vocal lyrics addressing romantic and social-life subjects, and characteristic offbeat-emphasis groove organized around the kata percussion pattern. Distinguished from kompa direct by sub-style nuance; distinguished from Dominican merengue by Haitian-not-Dominican lineage and slower tempo; distinguished from Trinidadian calypso by French-Haitian-Creole language and conjunto-derived ensemble.

items.name: Kizomba
items.lineage: Angolan-Lusophone slow-tempo partner-dance tradition codified circa 1980 — evolution from semba (its faster ancestor), characterized by 24/16 polyrhythmic foundation, Portuguese-Creole vocals, and intimate dance-hold close-position partner couples; Eduardo Paim and Bonga as the canonical early-80s codifiers, with the genre spreading across the Lusophone Atlantic
items.description: Kizomba (codified 1980s onward Angola, descending from semba dance and zouk influence, with international diffusion from 2000s onward through Portuguese and Cape Verdean diaspora), the slow sensual Angolan dance music genre. Defined by Portuguese-language vocal performance with smooth romantic-tenor delivery, programmed slow-zouk-derived back-line at 60-80 BPM with characteristic three-step-pattern percussion, electric-bass and synth-pad accompaniment supplying melodic foundation, optional acoustic-or-electric guitar lead voice, and lyric content addressing romantic-yearning subjects suited to close-partnered slow-dance choreography. Distinguished from semba (its parent) by slower tempo and absence of vigorous-leaping dance-form; distinguished from straight zouk by Angolan-Portuguese-language lineage and slower tempo; distinguished from later kuduro (faster Angolan electronic genre) by sensual-slow rather than aggressive-fast register.

items.name: Kuduro
items.lineage: Angolan high-tempo electronic dance genre codified in late-1980s Luanda — characterized by 140-150 BPM hectic kick patterns, Portuguese-Kimbundu vocals, batida rhythmic foundation; Tony Amado, Buraka Som Sistema (Portuguese-Angolan diaspora), and DJ Marfox extending the canon through the 2000s into international electronic music
items.description: Kuduro (codified 1989 onward in Luanda Angola, descending from semba and zouk lineages and crystallizing through Tony Amado's pioneering recordings, with international visibility from 2000s onward through Buraka Som Sistema), the Angolan high-tempo dance music genre. Defined by rapid programmed batidas around 140-160 BPM (the kuduro batida pattern of stuttered kick-and-percussion programming providing the genre's signature angular rhythmic feel), shouted hooks in Portuguese and Kimbundu, MC-style vocal verses delivered over the beat with high-energy projection, electronic synth-pad and bass programming, optional sample-and-vocal-chop production effects, and dance-form choreography of athletic-and-acrobatic floor-and-leap movements (the dance gives the genre its name — kuduro is Portuguese for hard-bottom referencing the dance's grounded-stomping aesthetic). Distinguished from kizomba by tempo and aggressive-not-sensual register; distinguished from semba by post-1989 timestamp and electronic-not-acoustic instrumentation; distinguished from later baile funk (Brazilian parallel) by Angolan-Portuguese-language and Luanda-not-Rio lineage.

items.name: Reggaeton
items.lineage: Puerto Rican dembow-based dance subgenre codified through Vico C (the foundational late-1980s figure), DJ Playero’s underground compilations (1991 onward), Daddy Yankee’s breakthrough Barrio Fino (2004), Don Omar, Tego Calderón — characterized by 90-100 BPM dembow rhythm (from the Shabba Ranks "Dem Bow" sample), Spanish-language reggaeton-flow vocals
items.description: Reggaeton (codified 1995-2004 onward in Puerto Rico through DJ Playero, DJ Negro, and the underground perreo-club scene, with international breakout through 2004 onward via Daddy Yankee's Gasolina), the Puerto Rican-Panamanian dembow-rooted urbano genre. Defined by the dembow rhythm (a programmed boom-ch-boom-chick percussion pattern derived from Shabba Ranks's 1990 Dem Bow riddim, with kick on 1 and 3 and offbeat snare-and-clap producing the genre's signature feel), sung-rapped vocal performance often alternating melodic-pop-chorus with rapped-MC verses, Spanish-language lyric content addressing romantic-and-explicit themes (perreo dance-and-courtship, social-flex, Puerto-Rican-urban specificity), tempos around 90-100 BPM with prominent halved-tempo perception, and synth-pad-and-bass programming with optional acoustic-or-electric-guitar lead. Distinguished from Latin trap by dembow-rhythm foundation rather than 808-foundation; distinguished from earlier Spanish reggae by post-1995 timestamp and dembow-codification; distinguished from cumbia by Caribbean-not-South-American lineage.

items.name: Latin trap
items.lineage: Puerto Rican-Dominican Latin-trap subgenre codified through Bad Bunny (X 100PRE 2018), Anuel AA, Ozuna, Bryant Myers — characterized by 70-80 BPM trap-808 programming with reggaeton-dembow accents, autotuned-Spanish-language vocals, and the Hear This Music label catalog driving its mainstream crossover
items.description: Latin trap (codified 2014 onward, with Bad Bunny, Anuel AA, Bryant Myers, and the Puerto Rican-and-Atlanta scene crystallizing the genre), the Atlanta-trap-pivoted-into-Spanish-urbano subgenre. Defined by 808 sub-bass foundation (the trap-genre signature deep-and-pitched bass note carrying the harmonic foundation), hi-hat triplets and double-time hi-hat-rolls programmed over halved-tempo perception, melismatic auto-tuned Spanish-language vocal performance often pitched-and-processed for melodic flow, lyric content addressing romantic-and-explicit themes, drug-references, and Latin-urban specificity, tempos around 130-150 BPM but read at half-speed by the listener due to 808-drop placement, and production aesthetic borrowing directly from Atlanta trap. Distinguished from reggaeton by absence of dembow rhythm and trap-based-rather-than-Caribbean-percussion programming; distinguished from cloud-rap by retention of trap-808 foundation; distinguished from English-language trap by Spanish-language vocal foreground and Latin-urbano industry framing.

items.name: Sludge metal
items.lineage: Southern US doom-and-hardcore fusion genre that emerged in late-1980s New Orleans — codified through Eyehategod (the NOLA sludge band, In the Name of Suffering 1990, Take As Needed for Pain 1993), Crowbar (Kirk Windsteins band, Crowbar 1993), Acid Bath (When the Kite String Pops 1994), Down (Phil Anselmos NOLA supergroup); fuses doom metal slow-tempo and Sabbath chord vocabulary with hardcore punk vocal aggression and Southern blues-rock harmonic foundations
items.description: Sludge metal (codified 1989 onward through Eyehategod, Crowbar, and Acid Bath establishing the New Orleans sludge lineage, with parallel and successor work through Iron Monkey, Electric Wizard, and the broader 1990s sludge-and-doom scene), the slow-downtuned-dense-distortion subgenre. Defined by slow tempo around 60-80 BPM, downtuned guitars (often dropped-D, drop-C, or further detunings) producing thick low-end heaviness, dense-distortion-and-fuzz guitar tone with extended sustain, hardcore-derived screamed-and-shouted vocal delivery, doom-metal harmonic foundation (Sabbath-derived heavy-blues riff vocabulary applied at slower tempo), and song-content addressing addiction, mental-illness, urban-decay, and Southern-gothic subject matter. Distinguished from straight doom by hardcore-derived screamed-vocal foreground over clean-melodic vocal; distinguished from straight hardcore by tempo and downtuned-heavy guitar foundation; distinguished from later post-metal by absence of post-rock dynamic-arc structure.

items.name: Stoner metal
items.lineage: Southern California desert-rock-derived heavy-blues-revival genre that emerged in early-1990s Palm Desert and Los Angeles — codified through Kyuss (the founding band from Palm Desert, Welcome to Sky Valley 1994), Queens of the Stone Age (Josh Hommes post-Kyuss continuation, Songs for the Deaf 2002), Sleep (the Bay Area parallel canon, Sleeps Holy Mountain 1992 and the legendary 60-minute single-track Dopesmoker 2003), Fu Manchu, Monster Magnet; built on Sabbath chord vocabulary plus blues-rock pentatonic vocabulary plus down-tuned heavy-fuzz amplifier worship
items.description: Stoner metal / stoner rock (codified 1990s onward through Kyuss, Sleep, and Fu Manchu establishing the California-desert sound, with continuous tradition through to present and parallel doom-stoner-and-stoner-rock subgenres), the early-1970s English heavy-blues-rock-derived psychedelic riff music subgenre. Defined by downtuned guitars (drop-C, drop-B, or further detunings) producing thick low-end heaviness, bluesy modal-pentatonic riff vocabulary drawn from Sabbath-and-early-70s heavy-blues-rock heritage, fuzz-and-wah pedal-effected guitar tone with extended sustain, vocal performance often clean-melodic with light-distortion or psychedelic-effected processing, song-form built on extended riff-progression with extended jam-improvisation sections (the Kyuss desert-jam-aesthetic), tempos around 90-120 BPM, and lyric and visual themes addressing cannabis-culture, desert-and-southwest landscape, and psychedelic-mystical experience. Distinguished from straight doom by faster tempo and retention of clean-melodic vocal; distinguished from drone-doom by song-form structure; distinguished from psychedelic-rock by post-1990 timestamp and metal-derived guitar-tone weight.

items.name: Post-metal
items.lineage: US and European long-form instrumental-foregrounded metal-and-post-rock fusion that emerged from late-1990s onward — codified through Isis (the Boston-area post-metal band, Oceanic 2002, Panopticon 2004), Pelican (the Chicago instrumental-only canon, The Fire in Our Throats Will Beckon the Thaw 2005), Cult of Luna (Swedish), Russian Circles (Chicago instrumental-only), Neurosis (the founding pre-post-metal Oakland band, Through Silver in Blood 1996); built on extended-composition song structures (10-20 minute pieces), ambient-textural sections alternating with heavy crescendo peaks
items.description: Post-metal (codified 2002 onward through ISIS's Oceanic and Cult of Luna's first-album establishing the post-rock-extended-into-metal aesthetic, with parallel tradition through Pelican, Russian Circles, and Neurosis), the metal subgenre extending post-rock dynamic arc and atmospheric layering across heavy-and-quiet sections. Defined by long-form song-structures (regularly extending past 8-12 minutes) built on extended dynamic arcs (the post-rock crescendo-form translated into metal context), atmospheric layering combining clean-guitar texture sections with full-distortion heavy sections, retention of metal-derived guitar-tone and percussion in heavy sections (downtuned guitars, slow-and-heavy riffs, double-kick drumming), instrumental-foreground with vocals appearing as textural-shouts or post-rock-style absent vocal sections, and through-composed song-forms abandoning verse-chorus structure. Distinguished from straight post-rock by retention of metal-aggression in heavy sections; distinguished from sludge metal by post-rock dynamic-arc structure; distinguished from atmospheric black metal by retention of song-form-not-blast-beat foundation.

items.name: Deathcore
items.lineage: Mid-2000s onward American extreme metal subgenre fusing death-metal's growl-vocal-and-blast-beat vocabulary with metalcore's breakdown-section conventions and pig-squeal / inhale-scream vocal techniques — codified through Suicide Silence (The Cleansing 2007), Whitechapel (This Is Exile 2008), Job for a Cowboy (Doom EP 2005), Carnifex, Despised Icon (The Healing Process 2005), Thy Art Is Murder
items.description: Deathcore (codified 2005-2010 through California and Florida scenes, fusing 1990s death metal with 2000s metalcore breakdown structure), the hybrid metal subgenre. Defined by death-metal architecture (downtuned 7- and 8-string guitars, blast-beat percussion, growled vocals) grafted onto metalcore breakdown structure (heavy syncopated chugged-guitar low-tempo breakdowns mid-song designed for moshpit response), alternation between blast-beat sections and breakdown-chug sections rather than continuous metal aggression, vocal delivery alternating death-growl with hardcore-punk pig-squeal and clean-singing chorus sections, and a mid-2000s Hot-Topic-era youth audience and live-show centrality. Distinguished from metalcore by death-metal-not-thrash riff vocabulary and growled-not-shouted vocal; distinguished from death metal by breakdown-structure foreground and clean-vocal chorus; distinguished from slam death metal by hardcore-breakdown rather than groove-metal lineage.

items.name: Mathcore
items.lineage: Late-1990s through 2000s US extreme-metal-and-hardcore fusion genre incorporating math rock complex meter and rapid time-signature changes — codified through Converge (Jane Doe 2001), Dillinger Escape Plan (Calculating Infinity 1999, Miss Machine 2004), Botch, Coalesce, the modern continuation through Cult Leader and Frontierer
items.description: Mathcore (codified late-1990s onward, with The Dillinger Escape Plan's Calculating Infinity as crystallizing record, descending from hardcore-punk-and-grindcore lineage), the metalcore-and-grindcore-derived subgenre. Defined by hardcore-punk-and-metalcore aggression foundation augmented with irregular-meter changes, dissonant chord voicings (atonal or polychord harmonic vocabulary), aggressive metric-and-tempo accelerations within songs, blast-beat percussion alternated with breakdown sections, screamed-and-shouted vocal delivery, and song-form built on through-composed sectional structure rather than verse-chorus. Distinguished from straight metalcore by irregular-meter and dissonant-harmony foregrounding; distinguished from grindcore by retention of metalcore song-length and hardcore-derived structural conventions; distinguished from progressive metal by hardcore-punk lineage rather than 70s-prog-rock heritage; distinguished from math rock by metal-aggression and screamed-vocal delivery.

items.name: Grindcore
items.lineage: UK and US extreme-metal-and-hardcore fusion that emerged in the mid-late 1980s — codified through Napalm Death (Birmingham UK, Scum 1987 the foundational album with You Suffer the 28-second-song sonic-economy gesture), Carcass (Liverpool UK gore-grindcore, Reek of Putrefaction 1988), Repulsion (Michigan US founding band, Horrified 1989), the modern continuation through Pig Destroyer, Magrudergrind; hardcore-punks compressed-song-format extended to its logical conclusion
items.description: Grindcore (1985-1989 UK Birmingham, codified through Napalm Death's Scum and From Enslavement to Obliteration albums establishing the genre's extreme-short-form fusion of hardcore punk and death metal), the extreme-short-form metal subgenre. Defined by song lengths often under 60 seconds (Napalm Death's You Suffer at 1.3 seconds remains the genre-extreme example), blast-beat percussion at extreme tempo (snare-and-kick alternating at 240+ BPM), tremolo-picked thrash-and-punk-derived riffs, indecipherable shouted-and-growled vocal delivery (often alternating high-shriek and low-grunt within the same song), political-and-anarchist-and-medical-grotesque lyric content, and DIY-anarcho-punk-aesthetic production and distribution. Distinguished from death metal by shorter song-lengths and hardcore-punk lineage; distinguished from hardcore punk by metal-derived guitar tone and growl-vocal; distinguished from powerviolence (a related subgenre) by metal rather than hardcore primary lineage.

items.name: Atmospheric black metal
items.lineage: European atmospheric-foregrounded subgenre of black metal that emerged from the Norwegian and Scandinavian second-wave black metal scene in the mid-1990s — codified through Emperor (In the Nightside Eclipse 1994, the symphonic-atmospheric breakthrough), Burzum (Hvis lyset tar oss 1994), Ulver (Bergtatt 1995), early Enslaved, Wolves in the Throne Room (the US Cascadian black metal extension from 2006 onward, Two Hunters 2007); characterized by long-form composition (often 8-15 minute pieces), tremolo-picked melodic-guitar foregrounded over blast-beat percussion, ambient-keyboard-or-synth pads, and false-fold ventricular shriek vocals
items.description: Atmospheric black metal (1994 onward, descending from Norwegian second-wave black metal but extending toward ambient and post-rock), the long-form black metal sub-style that subordinates riff-aggression to immersive textural sustain. Defined by tremolo-picked tonal-modal guitar washes processed through heavy reverb so individual notes blur into harmonic clouds, blast-beat drumming pushed to or beyond the threshold of pulse-perception, shrieked or distantly-mixed vocals that read as another textural layer rather than foreground voice, song lengths regularly past ten minutes structured around long crescendos rather than verse-chorus, and lyrical/visual themes of nature mysticism, isolation, cosmic contemplation. Distinguished from Norwegian second-wave black metal by softened production and post-rock structural debt; distinguished from drone-doom by retention of black-metal blast-beat percussion and shriek vocal; distinguished from post-metal by black-metal lineage and rejection of clean-singing.

items.name: Melodic death metal
items.lineage: Gothenburg Swedish melodic death metal canon that emerged in the early 1990s — codified at Studio Fredman (Fredrik Nordström producer-engineer) through In Flames (The Jester Race 1996, Whoracle 1997), Dark Tranquillity (The Gallery 1995), At the Gates (Slaughter of the Soul 1995, the post-Heartwork melodic death recording), Soilwork; characterized by twin-guitar harmony NWOBHM-influenced melodic leads over death metal rhythm-section foundation, growled vocals retained from death metal but with cleaner production aesthetic
items.description: Melodic death metal / Gothenburg melodic death (codified 1993-1997 in Gothenburg Sweden through At the Gates, In Flames, and Dark Tranquillity establishing the sound), the death metal subgenre fusing death-metal aggression with NWOBHM-derived melodic dual-guitar harmonies. Defined by death-metal foundation (tremolo-picked riffs, blast-beat percussion, growled-vocal delivery) overlaid with twin-guitar harmonized lead-lines drawing on Iron Maiden and Thin Lizzy NWOBHM melodic-harmony vocabulary, midtempo song-form built on extended verse-chorus with melodic-bridge sections rather than death-metal's pure-aggression continuous riff-juxtaposition, alternation between growled-verse and clean-sung-or-shouted-chorus sections (subgenre-dependent), and a more-melodic-than-death-metal harmonic-and-melodic vocabulary using Aeolian and Dorian modal voicings rather than pure-dissonance. Distinguished from straight death metal by melodic-twin-guitar-foreground and NWOBHM lineage; distinguished from later metalcore by Gothenburg-not-American origin and retention of death-metal-foundation rather than hardcore-foundation; distinguished from power metal by death-growl vocal and lower-register guitar foundation.

items.name: Footwork
items.lineage: Chicago footwork dance-music genre evolved from juke and ghetto-house through the late-2000s — characterized by 160 bpm syncopated triplet-based programming, chopped-and-pitched sampled vocals, sparse arrangement designed for the underground dance-battle-circuit footwork dance — codified through DJ Rashad (Double Cup 2013, the genre's breakthrough album), DJ Spinn, Traxman, RP Boo, and the Teklife crew
items.description: Footwork (codified 2005 onward in Chicago South Side and West Side dance battle scenes, with international visibility through RP Boo, DJ Rashad, and Hyperdub label releases 2012 onward), the Chicago dance music genre paired to the footwork dance battle. Defined by 160 BPM tempo with a half-time perceptual feel that accommodates the foot-pattern-as-percussion of dancers, chopped-and-stuttered vocal samples (often single-syllable repetitions of source-record vocals manipulated rhythmically), syncopated kick-drum patterns that push and pull against the grid rather than locking to four-on-floor, sparse melodic content (single bass notes or simple two-note patterns), and song-form built on rapid-cut sectional transitions designed for dance-battle response. Distinguished from Chicago house by tempo and battle-format origin; distinguished from juke (the parent genre) by post-2005 timestamp and more-stutter-heavy production; distinguished from drum-and-bass by genre lineage and absence of breakbeat-and-amen-break heritage.

items.name: Jersey club
items.lineage: Newark New Jersey dance-music genre evolved from Baltimore club through the late-2000s — characterized by 130 bpm syncopated kick-drum patterns, chopped vocal-sample hooks (including the signature Triton bed-squeak sound), bouncing 5-beat rhythmic foundation, and an explicit local-dance-scene context — codified through DJ Tameil, DJ Lilman, DJ Sliink, UNIIQU3, Trippy Turtle
items.description: Jersey club (codified 2000s onward Newark New Jersey, descending from Baltimore club lineage via DJ Tameil's Brick Bandits crew), the Newark-Philadelphia-area club music subgenre. Defined by chopped sample triplets at ~135 BPM (the Jersey-club signature where vocal samples and other source materials are chopped into triplet rhythmic patterns over the kick), signature kick-pattern of stuttered-kick and the bed-squeak sample (a high-pitched looped vocal sample that became the genre's identifying sound), repurposed 90s-and-2000s R&B vocal samples chopped-and-rearranged, and dance-floor association with regional Jersey-club dance battles. Distinguished from Baltimore club (its parent) by post-2000 timestamp and bed-squeak-and-triplet-chop signature; distinguished from Philly club by Newark-not-Philadelphia centrality (though closely related); distinguished from juke and footwork by genre lineage and tempo difference.

items.name: Microhouse
items.lineage: Berlin-and-Cologne minimal-techno genre extending Chicago-house's rhythmic foundation through clicks-and-cuts micro-detail textural aesthetic and Kompakt-label-associated restrained-palette arrangement — codified through Akufen (My Way 2002), Matthew Herbert, Ricardo Villalobos (Alcachofa 2003, Fizheuer Zieheuer 2006), Luciano, Magda, with the genre serving as the early-2000s Cologne-Berlin minimal-aesthetic mainstream
items.description: Microhouse / minimal house (codified 2002-2005 through Cologne's Kompakt label and Berlin's Perlon label scenes, descending from minimal-techno and Cologne's earlier dub-techno lineage), the minimal-techno-influenced house subgenre. Defined by sparse arrangement built on clicks-and-cuts foley-and-percussive-fragment textures (the genre's signature aesthetic of using small environmental sound samples as percussion), repurposed micro-sample foundations rather than traditional house drum-machine-and-synth palette, four-on-floor kick foundation with sparse hi-hats and percussion programmed at quiet dynamic levels, atmospheric-pad textures filling the harmonic space, and tempo around 122-126 BPM. Album-format release lineage (Pole, Akufen, Matthew Dear early productions) over single-track-DJ-format. Distinguished from straight house by minimal arrangement and micro-sample foreground; distinguished from minimal techno by retention of house tempo and mid-tempo groove; distinguished from dub techno (its ancestor) by absence of long-decay chord-pad foreground.

items.name: Hardstyle
items.lineage: Late-1990s onward Dutch hard-electronic-dance genre evolved from hardcore-techno and gabber through tempo deceleration to 150 bpm and the addition of reverse-bass kick-drum compositional convention — codified through Showtek, Headhunterz, Brennan Heart, Wildstylez, and the Q-dance festival-and-event-promotion network, with the form serving as the Dutch hard-dance commercial mainstream
items.description: Hardstyle (codified 2002 onward in Netherlands and Belgium, descending from gabber and trance lineages and crystallizing through Q-dance promoter and the Defqon.1 festival circuit), the Dutch hard-dance subgenre. Defined by a reverse-bassline pattern where the bass note plays after the kick (rather than before/with it like four-on-floor house), distorted kick on every beat with extended kick-tail decay (the hardstyle-kick is the genre signifier — a heavily-processed kick with sustained pitch-falling tail), midtempo around 145-155 BPM (slower than gabber's 180+), euphoric synth-lead melody and breakdown sections with build-up-and-drop arrangement, and big-room festival-stage performance context. Distinguished from gabber by midtempo and melodic-uplift over relentless-aggression; distinguished from trance by harder-and-distorted percussion-foreground; distinguished from happy hardcore by darker-mood and slower tempo.

items.name: Gabber
items.lineage: Mid-1990s Rotterdam hard-electronic-dance subgenre characterized by 180-200 bpm distorted-kick-drum dominance, aggressive sub-bass, and explicit working-class-Rotterdam subcultural identity — codified through DJ Paul Elstak, Rob Gee, Neophyte, the Rotterdam Records label, and the genre's explicit anti-Amsterdam-house cultural posture
items.description: Gabber (1990-1996 Rotterdam, codified through Paul Elstak's Rotterdam Records and the Thunderdome festival/compilation series), the Rotterdam hardcore-techno offshoot. Defined by tempos pushed past 180 BPM (often 200-230 BPM in genre-extreme work), distorted-clipped kicks (the gabber-kick — a heavily-distorted Roland TR-909 kick pushed into clipping where the distortion product becomes the kick's identifying sound), shouted-and-screamed MC vocal delivery (the hakkûh-energy aesthetic of stomping-and-shouting), industrial-and-rave sampling (sirens, vocal stabs, Acapella-and-orchestral hits), and dance-floor association with the hakken stomping dance and skinhead-adjacent youth subculture. Production lineage emerging from Belgian new-beat and acid-house intensification. Distinguished from happy hardcore by darker mood and absence of euphoric-uplift production; distinguished from speedcore (its faster offspring) by sub-200 BPM ceiling; distinguished from industrial by dance-floor function.

items.name: UK drill
items.lineage: British drill subgenre codified through London scenes (mostly Brixton and Tottenham) circa 2014-2016 — characterized by the doubled-hi-hat-and-skipping-snare drill signature carried from Chicago but slower (140 BPM with the half-time feel), JME and Skepta’s grime influence absorbed, regional-London-Patois vocal delivery
items.description: UK drill (codified 2012 onward in London Brixton-and-Lambeth-and-Tottenham scenes, with 67 collective and Headie One among foundational artists), the British drill subgenre. Defined by sliding 808 sub-bass patterns that shift on every count (the UK-drill-specific feature of bass-line moving more aggressively than Chicago drill's sliding patterns, often shifting through multiple notes per bar), doubled hi-hat triplets at high-tempo perception (faster than Chicago drill's grid), distinctive percussion-fill programming with snare-roll-and-cymbal-crash sectional transitions, MC vocal verses delivered in characteristic London accent and Multicultural London English vocabulary, lyric content addressing London gang-rivalry, postcode-specific neighborhood references, and confrontational-violent narratives, and tempos around 140-150 BPM with halved-tempo perception. Distinguished from Chicago drill (its parent) by London-not-Chicago lineage, faster sliding-808, and London-vocabulary; distinguished from grime by drill-genre 808-foundation rather than grime's 130-BPM and synth-square-wave foundation; distinguished from later Brooklyn drill by UK-specific London-accent and earlier 2012-foundational-timestamp.

items.name: French rap
items.lineage: French-language hip-hop tradition that emerged in 1989-1991 — Dee Nasty (the Paris hip-hop DJ-pioneer), MC Solaar (Qui Sème le Vent Récolte le Tempo 1991, his wordplay-driven Paris voice), IAM (the Marseille collective, Lécole du Micro dArgent 1997), Suprême NTM (Saint-Denis suburb voice, NTM 1993), Assassin, the Mafia K1 Fry collective; carrying through the modern continuation: Booba, Rohff, Diam s, La Fouine, Sexion dAssaut, PNL, Damso, Aya Nakamura, with Paris and Marseille remaining the dominant scene capitals
items.description: French rap / rap français (codified 1990 onward, with Suprême NTM and IAM as primary architects of the Marseille-and-Paris foundational scene through the early-90s, and successive waves through cloud-rap and trap-français 2010 onward), the French-language hip-hop tradition. Defined by literary-aspiration vocal-text aesthetic with extensive vocabulary, complex multisyllabic rhyme-scheme construction in French, references to French literature and cinema alongside hip-hop genre conventions, geographically-specific banlieue (suburban-housing-project) subject matter and political-immigration-and-class-struggle thematics, and production palette varying by era (early sample-based boom-bap-derived, 2010-onward trap-and-cloud-rap programmed). Distinguished from American hip-hop by French-language focus and banlieue-not-ghetto subject; distinguished from Algerian rap by France-not-Algeria production and post-immigration-second-generation rather than first-generation perspective; distinguished from Belgian-French rap by Paris-and-Marseille industry centrality.

items.name: Korean rap
items.lineage: Korean hip-hop subgenre codified through Drunken Tiger (1999-onward), Tiger JK, Outsider, and the early-2000s Korean hip-hop scene that later expanded through Epik High, Verbal Jint, Dynamic Duo — characterized by Korean-language flows over US-and-Korean-hybrid production, the Show Me the Money television format as institutional vehicle
items.description: Korean rap / K-rap (codified 1999 onward, with Drunken Tiger and Epik High as foundational crews and underground-and-streaming-era Korean hip-hop scenes 2010 onward, distinct from idol-pop K-pop), the Korean hip-hop tradition separate from idol-pop. Defined by trap-and-boom-bap production palette drawing on contemporary American hip-hop techniques, Korean-and-English code-switching vocal verses, lyric content addressing personal narrative, social commentary, and Korean-cultural specificity (Seoul neighborhood references, generational disaffection, Korean education-and-career pressure subjects), competitive freestyling-and-cypher culture (the Show Me the Money TV competition codifying public visibility), and underground-club-circuit and streaming-platform distribution. Distinguished from K-pop by absence of idol-group industrial structure and retention of MC-foregrounded hip-hop conventions; distinguished from Japanese hip-hop by Korean-language and Korean-cultural specificity; distinguished from Chinese hip-hop by Korean-not-Mandarin language.

items.name: Rebetiko
items.lineage: Greek urban underclass blues-equivalent that emerged in the Piraeus port district and Athens working-class quarters after the 1922 Asia Minor Catastrophe brought Greek refugees from Smyrna and other Anatolian cities — codified through the recordings of Markos Vamvakaris, Vassilis Tsitsanis, Yiorgos Batis, Yiannis Papaioannou, Rita Abatzi, Roza Eskenazi, and the Piraeus Quartet across the 1930s-1940s
items.description: Rebetiko (codified 1922-1955 onward in Greece, particularly Piraeus port and Athens Athens-suburban hashish-den (tekes) scenes, with the 1923 Greco-Turkish-population-exchange refugee migration from Asia Minor seeding the genre and golden-era 1934-1953 establishing the recording catalog), the Greek urban folk-song tradition of the early-20th-century refugee and underclass milieu. Defined by bouzouki and baglamas (small-portable bouzouki) lead-melodic instruments, classical-and-acoustic guitar harmonic accompaniment, vocal performance with characteristic raspy-husky aesthetic and melismatic ornamentation drawing on Asia Minor maqam-influenced melodic vocabulary, lyric content addressing refugee-displacement, urban-poverty, drug-and-criminal-underworld subjects, romantic-melancholy, and prison-experience, and tekes (hashish-den) and taverna performance contexts. Distinguished from later Greek laiko (popular) tradition by pre-1955 underclass-marginal context; distinguished from Greek folk by urban-not-rural origin; distinguished from chanson-classique despite shared cabaret-tavern intimacy by Greek-language and bouzouki-instrumentation.

items.name: Laikó
items.lineage: Post-rebetiko Greek popular song that emerged in the 1950s-1960s as rebetiko transitioned from tavern-context to commercial-nightclub-context — codified through Manolis Chiotis (who introduced the three-course-to-four-course (trichordo-to-tetrachordo) bouzouki conversion and electric amplification), Stelios Kazantzidis (the voice of laiko), Marinella, Stratos Dionysiou, Yiannis Parios, Glykeria, and the Athens Minos / Columbia Greece / Lyra label catalog
items.description: Post-WWII Greek popular-song tradition (laikó: "of the people"), succeeding rebetiko as the urban Greek mass-entertainment idiom from the late 1940s through the 1980s. Retains bouzouki as central instrument but adds full band arrangement (rhythm section, orchestra in studio recordings) and shifts from underclass-bohemian rebetiko subjects toward broad-audience love-and-loss lyrical themes. Substitutes Western functional harmony for the modal dromoi inheritance (though modal traces persist in melodic phrasing). Bouzouki playing technique evolves from rebetiko’s plectrum-driven taximi improvisation toward more ornamental virtuoso lines. Distinct from entechno (literary art-song) and skyladiko (later working-class subgenre).

items.name: Sevdalinka
items.lineage: Bosnian melancholy-romantic urban song tradition that emerged in the late-Ottoman period (post-1463 Ottoman conquest of Bosnia) and codified through the Austro-Hungarian administrative period (1878-1918) into the recording-era 20th century — 20th-century figures Himzo Polovina, Safet Isović (the 1950s-70s sevdalinka voice), Zaim Imamović, Beba Selimović, and the modern Damir Imamović and Amira Medunjanin sevdalinka revival; melismatic vocal melody with Ottoman makam-influenced modal vocabulary over saz, accordion, and violin accompaniment
items.description: Sevdalinka (codified late-Ottoman-period onward in Bosnian-Herzegovinian urban centers Sarajevo and Mostar, with continuous tradition through to present and 20th-century commercial-recording era from 1930s onward), the urban Bosnian song tradition with Ottoman Turkish musical roots. Defined by dwell-on-emotion melismas (the sevdalinka specialty of stretched-out vocal phrases lingering on a single emotional inflection), accordion-and-saz Ottoman-derived ensemble accompaniment (saz long-neck plucked-lute, accordion adopted from later European influence, with optional violin and tambura), Bosnian-language lyric content addressing sevdah (the Bosnian-specific affect of melancholic-romantic longing similar to Portuguese saudade), characteristic minor-mode melodic vocabulary with Phrygian-and-Hijaz Ottoman-maqam inflection, and intimate-cafe and family-gathering performance contexts. Distinguished from Serbian and Croatian regional folk by urban-Bosnian-Ottoman heritage; distinguished from Albanian saze by Bosnian-language and saz-and-accordion-instrumentation; distinguished from Turkish classical despite shared Ottoman heritage by Bosnian language and folk-not-classical framing.

items.name: Bulgarian women's choir
items.lineage: Bulgarian state-radio female-voice choir tradition codified by composer Philip Koutev from 1952 onward (Philip Koutev State Ensemble) and brought to international attention through Marcel Cellier (original 1975 Disques Cellier, 1987 Nonesuch Explorer) release Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares; reharmonizes Bulgarian village folk-song repertoire (Rhodope and Pirin regional traditions) for concert-stage female chorus
items.description: Bulgarian women's choir (codified 1952 onward through the Bulgarian State Female Choir Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares ensemble, with Filip Kutev's curated arrangements of Bulgarian village choral tradition establishing the sound and 1986-onward Western European exposure through 4AD label releases), the state-curated ensemble singing tradition. Defined by close-interval clusters and dissonant-harmony foreground (the Bulgarian-major-second and minor-second harmonic intervals between vocal parts producing the characteristic edgy harmonic palette), cuttingly-bright open-throat female vocal production aesthetic (the otkrit glas open-voice technique of Bulgarian-village folk vocal tradition), drone-and-melody texture organization (one or more voices sustain a drone while others carry melody), repertoire of arranged Bulgarian-village songs from regional folk traditions (Shop, Pirin, Strandzha regional sources), and concert-hall performance contexts replacing original village-context. Distinguished from Bulgarian village-original choral by curated-orchestrated arrangement and concert-stage context; distinguished from Eastern Orthodox choral by secular-folk-source repertoire; distinguished from broader Balkan polyphonic traditions by Bulgarian-specific harmonic-clusters vocabulary.
exemplars: Trio Bulgarka — The Forest is Crying

items.name: Hardanger fiddle
items.lineage: Western Norwegian Hardangerfjord regional fiddle tradition — the hardingfele with four playing strings and four-or-five sympathetic resonance strings tuned in scordatura bondetraditional (peasant-traditional) tunings, performed solo for traditional dance forms (springar, gangar, halling, pols) at weddings and seasonal celebrations
items.description: Hardanger fiddle (codified ca. 17th century onward in Norwegian western-coast valleys of Hardangerfjord, Telemark, and Setesdal, with continuous tradition through to present and a folkloric-revival from 1960 onward), the Norwegian regional fiddle tradition. Defined by the hardingfele instrument (a violin-family instrument with 4-5 sympathetic resonant strings under the bowed 4 main strings creating constant sympathetic-vibration drone), repertoire of slåtter (dance-tunes) organized by regional sub-style and dance-form (gangar — march-walking dance, springar — leaping triple-meter dance, halling — male-display dance, lydarslått — listening-piece without dance), highly-ornamented melodic decoration with characteristic regional bowing-and-grace-note conventions, solo or duo (pair-fiddle) performance, and Norwegian-rural performance contexts at weddings and festivals. Distinguished from standard Norwegian fiddle by sympathetic-strings construction and regional-repertoire specificity; distinguished from Swedish nyckelharpa by bowed-not-keyed and Norway-not-Sweden lineage; distinguished from Scottish fiddle by ornamentation conventions and slåtter-not-strathspey-and-reel repertoire.

items.name: Sámi yoik
items.lineage: Indigenous Sámi (northern Norway / Sweden / Finland / Russia) vocal tradition of singing-about rather than singing-of — a yoik does not have a subject, it IS its subject; modal vocal melismatic tradition known by region-specific names (luohti in North Sámi, juoiggus in Inari Sámi, vuolle in Lule Sámi, leu_dd in Skolt Sámi), often unaccompanied solo with occasional sálldi frame drum
items.description: Sámi yoik (continuous tradition pre-Christianization onward across Sápmi homeland — northern Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Russia's Kola Peninsula — with continuous tradition through colonial-era suppression and 1970s-onward revival), the indigenous Sámi vocal form. Defined by short repeating motivic cells that is rather than describes its subject (the philosophical-aesthetic core of yoik — a yoik does not represent a person, animal, place, or natural phenomenon, it presents that subject directly through sound), characteristic vocal-style with throat-derived production and sustained-and-glottal-stop ornamentation, mostly-vocables (non-lexical syllables) with optional minimal-text content, traditional unaccompanied solo performance with later folkloric-revival adoption of frame-drum and synthesizer accompaniment, and ceremonial-and-personal-song repertoire (named-yoiks for individuals, place-yoiks for landscape features, animal-yoiks).
