items.lineage: Cuban big-band brass-and-saxophone urban-popular-dance music codified 1939-onward in Havana from son-cubano accelerated-and-orchestrated for big-band swing-orchestra adaptation. The mambo-typical ensemble: four-trumpets, five-saxophones (two altos, two tenors, plus baritone), piano, contrabass, congas, bongos, timbales, claves, maracas, and güiro. The mambo-section open-improvisation montuno-equivalent features brass-shouts (mambos), saxophone-and-piano riffs over ostinato-vamp, and percussion-and-vocal call-and-response. The 1947-onward Mexico-City-and-NYC-Palladium mambo-craze made it the international Cuban-dance-music ambassador; the 1950s saw mambo-fused-with-jazz (Afro-Cuban jazz, Latin-jazz), with cha-cha-chá and pachanga emerging as next-generation variants.
items.description: Mambo (codified 1938-1955 through Havana-Mexico-City-New-York Cuban big-band scene, with Pérez Prado, Tito Puente, Tito Rodríguez, and Machito as primary architects and golden era 1950-1955), the Cuban-derived big-band dance music genre. Defined by large jazz-influenced ensemble (5+ trumpets, 4+ saxophones, trombone, piano, bass, congas, bongos, timbales, and vocals), Afro-Cuban rhythm-section foundation built on clave-pattern (forward and reverse 3:2), call-and-response between brass section, sax section, and rhythm section, montuno piano-vamp foundation, and tempos around 140-180 BPM with strong dance-floor-functional pulse. Distinguished from son cubano by larger ensemble and big-band-jazz instrumentation; distinguished from earlier Cuban danzón by faster tempo and absence of slow opening; distinguished from later salsa (which descends from it) by big-band ensemble size and pre-1965 timestamp.

items.name: Cha-cha-chá
items.lineage: Cuban couple-dance and music genre invented 1953-onward in Havana from danzón-de-nuevo-ritmo modernization, named after the characteristic triple-step (one-two-cha-cha-cha) percussive-foot pattern. The canonical orquesta-charanga ensemble: solo flute (typically wooden five-key flute), three-or-four violins, contrabass, piano, timbales, congas, and güiro scraper. The tempo (around 120 BPM, moderate, danceable for non-professionals) and the simplified chord-progressions (typically I-IV-V or II-V-I in major keys) made cha-cha-chá the most accessible Cuban couple-dance for non-Cubans, fueling its massive 1950s-1960s American-and-European mainstream popularity. The structure is verse-and-montuno like son cubano, with the montuno open-improvisation section often featuring extended flute-and-violin solos over coro-pregón call-and-response.
items.description: Cha-cha-chá (codified 1953-1954 in Havana through violinist-bandleader Enrique Jorrín's adaptation of mambo and danzón, named for the three-step foot-pattern's rhythmic articulation), the 1950s Cuban dance form that became the international ballroom dance phenomenon of the late 50s. Defined by the characteristic three-step (1-2-cha-cha-cha) syncopated foot-pattern carried into the rhythm-section's güiro-and-claves articulation, charanga-style flute-and-violin orchestration over piano-bass-tumbadoras (timbales-replacement-by-conga in some bands), tempos around 110-130 BPM, and song forms with vocal montuno call-and-response and instrumental break sections for dance. Performance contexts: Havana dance halls, ballroom dance studios, US Latin-jazz crossover venues. Distinguished from mambo by slower tempo and three-step foot pattern; distinguished from danzón by faster tempo and absence of slow opening section; distinguished from later salsa by charanga instrumentation rather than conjunto brass-and-percussion line.

items.name: Charanga
items.lineage: Cuban orquesta-charanga light-flute-and-violin orchestral-dance ensemble derived from danzón-orquesta-típica modernization 1920s-onward, codified into the canonical charanga-francesa instrumentation by 1930s. The ensemble: solo wooden five-key flute, two-to-four violins, piano, contrabass, timbales, congas, and güiro. Initially attached to danzón-cubano repertoire, charanga expanded into danzonete, cha-cha-chá, mambo-charanga, and pachanga (Eduardo Davidson 1959 innovation) as the genre absorbed son-cubano-and-mambo influences. The charanga-soneando style 1960s-onward incorporated trombone-and-trumpet-and-saxophone via the salsa-Nuyorican charanga-orquesta hybridization. Modern charanga revival 1990s-onward foregrounds the flute-violin texture as the canonical timba alternative-to-brass.
items.description: Cuban dance-ensemble configuration with five-key flute and violins as melodic-front, piano and bass mid, timbales and guiro percussion; played danzón, danzonete, cha-cha-chá, mambo across the 20th century.

items.name: Guaracha
items.lineage: Cuban up-tempo song-and-dance form, the satirical-comic cousin to son cubano, prominent in the Sonora Matancera repertoire and the Celia Cruz canon
items.description: Cuban up-tempo song-and-dance with sharply-syncopated melodic-vocal phrasing, satirical-narrative lyric mode, and call-and-response montuno; sibling form to son with faster tempo and looser narrative structure.

items.name: Rumba cubana
items.lineage: Afro-Cuban secular drum-and-vocal folkloric tradition (yambú / guaguancó / columbia subforms) originating in Havana and Matanzas tenement-courtyard contexts
items.description: Afro-Cuban secular drum-and-vocal tradition; conga-trio interplay (quinto soloing, tumba grounding, conga middle) over claves, lead-and-chorus call-and-response vocals; three regional styles yambú, guaguancó, columbia.

items.name: Guaguancó
items.lineage: Cuban couple-dance rumba subform with the characteristic vacunao symbolic-pursuit-and-evasion choreographic structure, codified 1880s-onward in Havana-and-Matanzas Afro-Cuban barrios out of solar-tenement-courtyard improvised drumming. Built on three-conga interlocking pattern (tumbador low-pulse, tres-dos middle-syncopation, quinto high-improvisation lead), clave 3-2 or 2-3 wood-block timekeeper, and palitos cáscara stick-on-drum-shell pattern. Vocal structure follows decimas Spanish-poetic-form opening (canto), coro-call-and-response chorus, and montuno open-improvisation section. The faster-tempo rumba-columbia and slower-tempo rumba-yambú are the sibling subforms.
items.description: Guaguancó (codified 19th century Havana and Matanzas, the most internationally-known of the three rumba sub-styles — yambú, guaguancó, columbia), the mid-tempo Afro-Cuban rumba sub-style. Defined by clave-3:2 (forward) rhythmic foundation with prominent quinto improvisational drumming (the smallest-and-highest-pitched conga drum carrying the improvisational-virtuosic line over the foundational tumbadora-and-tres-golpes pattern), couple-dance choreography of male-pursuit-and-female-vacunao-deflection (the flirtatious-pursuit narrative giving the dance its sexual-charged energy), call-and-response between lead-vocalist and chorus, claves and palitos sticks providing additional rhythmic foundation, and lyric content addressing daily-life subjects, romantic boast, and barrio-neighborhood references. Distinguished from yambú by mid-tempo rather than slow tempo and presence of vacunao dance-figure; distinguished from columbia (the third rumba sub-style) by couple-dance rather than solo-male-display format; distinguished from later salsa by acoustic-percussion-only ensemble.

items.name: Danzón
items.lineage: Cuban late-19th-century elegant-couple-dance tradition derived from European-contradanza imported through Haitian-French Saint-Domingue refugees 1791-onward, codified 1879-onward in Matanzas-and-Havana by orquesta-típica orchestral ensembles. The dance unfolds through ABACA rondo-form (introduction-and-paseo-promenade, A-section, B-section, A-return, C-trio-section, A-return), allowing partner-couples to alternate between dancing and resting during instrumental-trio-sections. The classic charanga-francesa ensemble: two flutes (one wooden, one metal), two violins, contrabass, piano, timbales (with cáscara stick-rhythm-on-shell), and güiro scraper. The danzón seeded the cha-cha-chá 1953-onward and danzonete vocal-variant 1929-onward and remains a living tradition through danzonera dance-hall events in Havana, Mérida, and Mexico-City.
items.description: Formal-court couple-dance form of the late 19th and early 20th centuries; charanga-ensemble instrumentation, sectional ABACA structure with elaborated thematic sections, ancestor of cha-cha-chá and mambo.

items.name: Cumbia colombiana
items.lineage: Colombian Caribbean-coast cortejo-procession couple-dance tradition originating mid-17th-century onward in Cartagena-and-Barranquilla Atlantic-coastal-region from Afro-Indigenous-Spanish fusion (enslaved-Africans-of-the-Bantu-Yoruba diaspora + Zenú-Wayuu Indigenous-coast + Spanish colonial Catholic-feast-day procession). The canonical conjunto-de-cumbia ensemble: gaitas Indigenous-Wayuu vertical-clay-and-cane flutes (gaita-macho lead, gaita-hembra accompaniment), tambor-mayor low-bass-drum (African-derived), llamador high-pulse-drum, alegre middle-improvisation-drum, maracas-and-guache shakers. The cumbia-clave 4-beat pattern emphasizes beats 1 and 3 (the conga-pattern echo). The 1940s-1960s commercial-mainstream cumbia adaptation by big-band-with-accordion-and-brass (cumbia-de-orquesta) spread Colombian-cumbia internationally; the 1960s-onward Peruvian-Mexican-and-Argentine cumbia-variants emerged from this diaspora.
items.description: Colombian Caribbean-coast dance music descended from indigenous-African-Spanish triple-heritage; gaita flute or accordion lead over tambora drum and bass, characteristic dotted-eighth back-line; spread continent-wide.

items.name: Cumbia peruana (chicha)
items.lineage: Peruvian Amazonian-and-coastal cumbia hybrid 1960s-onward, evolved from Colombian-cumbia-mainstream into a distinct fuzz-electric-guitar-led psychedelic-rock-fused subform centered in Lima, Iquitos, and Chiclayo. Built on Colombian-cumbia 4-beat-clave rhythmic-foundation but substituting electric-guitar (often with fuzz, wah, reverb, surf-twang) and electric-bass for the original gaitas-and-acoustic-bass. The chicha-cumbia 1965-1975-era originated in Andean-migrant Lima working-class-barrios and fused Andean huayno-pentatonic melodic-vocabulary with cumbia-rhythm and Anglo-American garage-and-psychedelic guitar-aesthetics. The 1970s-cumbia-amazonica branch (Iquitos-and-Pucallpa Amazon-basin) added more Afro-Caribbean and Brazilian-Northeastern-forró rhythmic-elements. 2000s-onward international-rediscovery via reissue-labels.
items.description: Cumbia peruana / chicha (1968 onward, originating in the Peruvian Amazon-region oil-boom towns of Pucallpa and Iquitos, codified through Lima migrant-class amateur-band cumbia in the 1970s), the urban Peruvian cumbia variant. Defined by Colombian cumbia back-line foundation (the cumbia rhythmic pattern and accordion-derived melodic phrasing) fused with Andean huayno melodic-modal vocabulary on twangy surf-derived electric guitar, lead electric-guitar lines often using Andean pentatonic phrasing rather than Colombian cumbia's diatonic vocabulary, vocal delivery in Spanish addressing migrant-class urban-Peruvian subject matter, full electric-band instrumentation (electric guitars, bass, drum kit, congas, timbales, and synthesizer keyboard), and a working-class Lima migrant audience listening at provincial-association dance halls. Distinguished from cumbia colombiana by Peruvian-Andean melodic vocabulary and electric-guitar foreground; distinguished from acoustic huayno by urban-electric-band instrumentation; distinguished from later cumbia electrónica by acoustic-band-not-DAW production.

items.name: Vallenato
items.lineage: Colombian-Caribbean accordion-led song-form codified 1940s-onward in Valledupar (Cesar-department, northeastern Colombia) from earlier 19th-century rural-troubadour traditions of the Magdalena-basin cattle-ranch lineage. The canonical ensemble: button-accordion (the diatonic Hohner-3-row accordion imported via 1880s-onward German maritime-trade with Caribbean-port-cities), caja-vallenata small two-headed drum, guacharaca grooved-bamboo scraper. The four canonical vallenato airs: paseo moderate-tempo-narrative, merengue (different from Dominican) faster-6/8, son slower-double-meter, and puya fastest-rural-virtuosic. The lyric-tradition is heavily narrative-storytelling, often improvised, and the Vallenato-Festival-de-la-Leyenda annual competition (since 1968) codifies regional standards.
items.description: Northern Colombian accordion-led narrative-song tradition organized in four traditional aires (paseo, son, merengue, puya); lead vocal narrative over accordion-led trio with caja-and-guacharaca back-line.

items.name: Joropo
items.lineage: Venezuelan-and-Colombian-Llanos plains cattle-ranch song-and-dance tradition with characteristic 3/4-against-6/8 hemiola-and-sesquialteral rhythmic-foundation. The canonical ensemble: arpa-llanera 32-string diatonic-harp (Venezuelan) or cuatro-y-bandola small-four-string-and-mandolin variant (Colombian), maracas, and either capacho large-shaker or bass. The vocal-style features high-projected open-throat cattle-driving register with improvised contrapunteo dueling-poet improvised-verse-exchange. The corrido-joropo storytelling-narrative-form, the pasaje-joropo slower-romantic-lyrical-form, and the joropo-recio fast-virtuosic-improvisational-form comprise the canonical variants. Embedded in cattle-ranch llanero rural-pastoral culture spanning the Orinoco-river-basin grasslands of Venezuela and eastern Colombia.
items.description: Joropo (codified 19th century in the Venezuelan-and-Colombian llanos plains region as cattle-ranch dance music, with continuous tradition through to present and folkloric-codification through 20th-century recorded performance), the Venezuelan-Colombian llano dance and song tradition. Defined by 3/4-with-hemiola metric organization (the joropo-specific 6/8-vs-3/4 metric ambiguity creating the signature push-pull feel), arpa llanera (Venezuelan harp — small portable diatonic harp with no pedals) and cuatro (four-string guitar-like instrument) ensemble at the core, often extended with maracas, contrabass, and occasional bandola llanera pear-shaped lute, vocal delivery in Spanish often with extended-note sustained-cry vocal style and syllabic-rapid-fire verses alternating, and dance-form choreography built on zapateado foot-stamping and partnered turning patterns. Distinguished from cumbia colombiana by inland-llanos-not-coastal-Caribbean lineage and harp-ensemble instrumentation; distinguished from Andean huayno by Venezuelan-and-Colombian-not-Andean-Quechua lineage; distinguished from Mexican son jarocho by Venezuelan-not-Mexican origin despite both featuring harp.

items.name: Merengue dominicano
items.lineage: Dominican-Republic national-couple-dance and rhythm 1850s-origin (recorded canon 1970-1995), codified into modern merengue-típico by mid-20th-century with three-instrument perico-ripiao canonical-ensemble: tambora two-headed barrel-drum, güira metallic-scraper, and accordion (originally diatonic German button-accordion imported via late-19th-century Hamburg-trade routes). The 2/4 fast-tempo merengue-clave (one-bar pattern: down-down-up-down on tambora) accelerates and accents the second eighth-note. The 1960s-1980s era added brass-section merengue-orquesta (modeled on Cuban big-band mambo) and electric-bass-and-keyboards, culminating in the international 1980s-merengue-mainstream wave. Three regional-variants: merengue-típico-cibaeño (Cibao-region accordion-led), merengue-de-orquesta (urban-Santo-Domingo big-band), and merengue-de-calle (1990s-onward street-and-urban variant).
items.description: Dominican fast-tempo dance music; characteristic two-step foot pattern, accordion-or-saxophone lead over tambora-guiro-bass back-line, jaleo call-and-response; spread continent-wide as accessible dance form.

items.name: Candombe uruguayo
items.lineage: Afro-Uruguayan drum-procession tradition traced to 18th-century African slave processions through Montevideo — performed by the cuerda de tambores ensemble of three drum sizes (chico small high-pitched lead-rhythm, repique medium-pitched conversational, piano deep bass) carried on shoulder straps and played with one hand and one stick; the annual Desfile de Llamadas during Carnival brings comparsas through Barrio Sur, Palermo, and Cordón Montevideo neighborhoods with their costumed dancers and full cuerda batteries — figures Pedro Ferreira, Romero Ferreira, the modern Hugo Fattoruso extensions
items.description: Afro-Uruguayan drum-and-procession tradition centered on three barrel-drum tessituras (chico, repique, piano) playing interlocking patterns; processional cuerda formations through Montevideo neighborhoods, llamadas-festival apex.

items.name: Forró brasileiro
items.lineage: Brazilian Northeast accordion-led couple-dance tradition with three-instrument pé-de-serra canonical-ensemble: sanfona (accordion or button-accordion), zabumba (large two-headed flat-drum), and triângulo (steel triangle). Codified mid-20th-century by Pernambuco-and-Paraíba interior-rural-migration into urban-Recife and Rio-São-Paulo migrant-communities. The three canonical rhythmic-subforms — baião moderate-tempo with characteristic eighth-note zabumba dotted-pattern, xote slow-couple-dance derived from Czech schottische, xaxado fast-syncopated rural-bandit-cangaceiro dance — comprise the forró repertoire. The pé-de-serra traditional-style coexists with forró-eletrônico 1990s-onward electronic-bass-and-drum-machine variant centered in Bahia-and-Ceará.
items.description: Northeastern-Brazilian dance music played on accordion-zabumba-triangle trio; baião, xote, arrasta-pé sub-rhythms, semi-improvised vocal narration of sertão pastoral life, festa junina season.

items.name: Marinera peruana
items.lineage: Peruvian coastal courtship dance with three regional variants (norteña, limeña, serrana) and characteristic guitarra-cajón-vocal ensemble
items.description: Marinera (codified 1893 onward through José Alvarado's renaming of zamacueca to marinera in honor of the Peruvian Navy after the War of the Pacific, with regional-stylistic differentiation continuing — marinera limeña of coastal Peru, marinera norteña of Trujillo and northern Peru), the Peruvian coastal courtship dance with elaborate handkerchief-flag choreography. Defined by guitar-and-cajón duo or small-ensemble accompaniment (guitar providing harmonic foundation with rasgueado, cajón providing rhythmic foundation), characteristic 6/8-against-3/4 hemiola metric organization, partnered courtship-dance choreography where dancers wave white handkerchiefs in elaborate flirtation patterns, and song-form alternating sung verses with instrumental dance-break sections. Limeña and norteña sub-styles differ in tempo (norteña faster, more sophisticated) and instrumentation (norteña sometimes adds accordion or wind instruments). Distinguished from Chilean cueca and Bolivian zamacueca by Peruvian-specific marinera codification post-1893; distinguished from huayno by coastal-not-Andean lineage and characteristic handkerchief choreography.

items.name: Psytrance
items.lineage: Goa-derived psychedelic trance subgenre, codified through 1990s Goa-coast Indian beach-party scene (Goa-trance as immediate predecessor) and the move toward digital-DAW production through Astrix, Infected Mushroom, Vibrasphere, and the broader Israeli-and-European psytrance label ecosystem
items.description: 140-150bpm psychedelic trance descended from late-90s Goa scene; rolling 16th-note bassline locked to four-on-the-floor kick, layered acid-saw leads and FM-bell timbres, evolving filter-and-effect arc over 8-minute peak-builds.

items.name: Goa trance
items.lineage: Mid-1990s Indian-beach electronic dance subgenre, codified through full-moon parties on Goa beaches (Anjuna, Vagator) — Goa Gil as the canonical DJ-organizer, with characteristic 130-140 BPM tempo, acid-bass-line foundation, Indian-modal melodic motifs, and analog-synth-and-303 production aesthetic
items.description: Mid-90s Indian-beach-scene trance ancestor of psytrance; phrygian-and-harmonic-minor melodic-modal vocabulary, layered analog-synth arpeggios over four-on-floor kick, sample-collage Indian-and-mystic vocal fragments.

items.name: Progressive trance
items.lineage: Late-1990s and 2000s long-arc trance subgenre characterized by 7-12-minute track lengths with extended dynamic build-and-release arcs — codified through Sasha and John Digweed’s Northern Exposure mixes (1996-1999), Hernán Cattáneo’s Buenos Aires DJ sets, and the GU (Global Underground) mix-CD series
items.description: Progressive trance (codified 1996 onward through Sasha & John Digweed's Northern Exposure mixes establishing the genre and continuing through Tiesto, Above & Beyond, and the broader trance-festival circuit), the long-arc trance subgenre. Defined by extended progressive build-and-release dynamics across 8-12 minute song-lengths, restrained melodic content (sustained-pad chord progressions and minimal lead-line phrases rather than hook-foregrounded melodic-anthem trance), deep-and-pulsing four-on-floor kick foundation around 128-134 BPM, atmospheric-pad and synth-arpeggiator textures filling the harmonic-and-melodic space, and long sectional development through filter-sweeps, gradual layer-additions, and breakdown-and-build dynamic structures. Distinguished from uplifting trance by restrained-not-anthemic melodic foreground; distinguished from psy-trance by absence of acid-303-and-Goa-mode foundations; distinguished from deep house by trance-genre faster tempo and synth-pad-foregrounded harmonic vocabulary.

items.name: Uplifting trance
items.lineage: 2000s emotional-trance subgenre characterized by major-key melodic builds, gated-pluck synth leads, and big-room cathartic drops — codified through Armin van Buuren, Above and Beyond, Paul van Dyk, and the Trance Around the World radio show as the disseminating institution
items.description: 136-140bpm emotional-melodic trance organized around expansive chord-progression breakdowns followed by anthemic four-on-floor drops; lush pad-and-supersaw textures, classical-derived major-key emotional palette.

items.name: Vocal trance
items.lineage: Pop-vocal trance subgenre fusing trance instrumentation with female-led vocal performances — codified through Tiësto featuring Kirsty Hawkshaw "Just Be" (2003), Armin van Buuren’s collaborations with Sharon den Adel, ATB and York-style productions, characterized by main-room emotional-vocal builds
items.description: Vocal trance (codified 1996 onward through Above & Beyond, Tiësto, ATB, and the broader trance-festival circuit establishing the genre's pop-song-structured commercial appeal), the pop-song-structured trance subgenre. Defined by foregrounded female-vocal melody (the vocal-trance-configuration where the lead female vocal-line sits above the trance instrumental foundation as the song's primary melodic-foreground), verse-chorus song-structure overlaid on trance instrumental foundation (rather than trance's traditional long-form sectional vamps), trance-genre rhythmic foundation (four-on-floor kick around 132-138 BPM, programmed bassline, atmospheric synth-pad and arpeggiator textures), trance-build-and-release dynamic structure with breakdown-and-build-and-drop arrangement, and lyric content addressing romantic-uplift, transcendent-experience, and emotional-positive subjects. Distinguished from straight trance by retention of pop-song-structure and vocal-foreground; distinguished from progressive trance by hook-foreground over restrained-build-arc; distinguished from straight pop by trance-instrumental foundation and dance-floor-functional tempo.

items.name: Cumbia electrónica
items.lineage: Late-2000s electronic remix-and-production genre re-engineering traditional Colombian-Mexican cumbia rhythmic foundation through digital production techniques — codified through ZZK Records (Buenos Aires-based label, Frikstailers, Chancha Via Circuito), Toy Selectah, Dengue Dengue Dengue, Bomba Estéreo (Elegancia Tropical 2012), and the broader Latin-American electronic-tropical-bass scene
items.description: Cumbia electrónica / digital cumbia (2005 onward, codified through the Argentinean ZZK Records scene in Buenos Aires and parallel Mexican Sonidero ZZK-adjacent producers), the electronic remix and production of cumbia source-material. Defined by sliced-and-pitched accordion samples lifted from classic cumbia source records (1960s-80s Colombian and Mexican cumbia recordings), classic cumbia back-line preserved underneath digital editing (the recognizable cumbia rhythmic signature stays intact), modern electronic processing (filter sweeps, time-stretched stutters, sub-bass replacement of original electric bass), tempos around 95-110 BPM, and lyric content optional or fragmentary (often spoken-word samples rather than sung verses). Distinguished from straight cumbia by digital-DAW production and sample-based construction; distinguished from cumbia colombiana by post-2005 timestamp and electronic-not-acoustic ensemble; distinguished from house and techno by cumbia rhythmic foundation and Latin-American genre lineage.

items.name: Baile funk (funk carioca)
items.lineage: Rio-favela 1985-onward block-party street-music built on the Tamborzão two-bar Brazilian-funk-percussion pattern with Miami-bass / electro-funk roots imported via 1980s American-vinyl-records trade. The genre evolved through four phases: melô-rap early-period (1985-1995, English-language samples over Volt-mix Atomic-Dog DNA), funk-melody and funk-consciente mid-period (1995-2005, Portuguese-language MC vocals layered over 808-kick patterns), proibidão hardcore underground (2000s-onward, drug-trafficking-themed-lyrics often banned from mainstream airwaves), and bregafunk-and-funk-150bpm modern-period (2010s-onward, accelerated-tempo Rio-and-Recife regional variants).
items.description: Rio favela-developed dance music built on tamborzão back-line samples derived from Miami bass; fast-tempo MC vocals in Brazilian Portuguese over chopped-up sample-based productions; block-party origin.

items.name: Tribal guarachero
items.lineage: Mexican-American electronic dance subgenre codified circa 2008-2012 in Monterrey, Mexico — characterized by 130-140 BPM accelerated cumbia rhythm with synth-flute melodies and tribal-drum patterns; DJ Erick Rincón, DJ Otto, and the 3BallMTY collective as canonical exponents
items.description: Mexican-and-Mexican-American electronic dance descended from prehispanic-flute-and-drum sample fusion with house and Cuban tribal; aggressive 130bpm tempo, pre-Columbian-flute samples, hand-percussion programming.

items.name: Perreo electrónico
items.lineage: Electronic perreo Latin-trap fusion codified through 2010s Puerto Rican reggaeton evolution — Bad Bunny’s X 100PRE (2018) and YHLQMDLG (2020) as breakthrough crossover records, Rosalía’s perreo-trap collaborations, characterized by 90-100 BPM dembow rhythm with autotuned-reggaeton vocals over electronic production
items.description: Electronic-derived perreo dance music descending from reggaeton with electronic-club production sensibilities; harder synth bass and 808 sub-bass, occasional house-music influence on tempo and structure.

items.name: Global bass
items.lineage: Pan-Latin-American electronic global-bass subgenre fusing cumbia, dembow, kuduro, and dancehall — codified through Bersa Discos, Soundway Records, and Nacional Records labels post-2010; characterized by digitally-produced tropical-rhythm samples with sub-bass and house-tempo foundations
items.description: Tropical bass (codified 2005 onward as production-school bracket for tropical-rhythms-meets-club-bass crossover work, with parallel North American, European, and Latin-American producer scenes establishing the genre as umbrella-term for cumbia, dembow, baile, Andean-electronic, and other Latin-tropical-derived club-bass productions), the tropical-rhythms-meets-club-bass crossover production-school bracket. Defined by tropical-rhythm source vocabularies (cumbia, dembow, baile funk, soca, Andean huayno-and-cumbia, kuduro, and other Latin/Caribbean/African-derived rhythmic foundations) translated into club-bass-music production aesthetics, modern electronic production techniques (DAW-based programming, sampled-vocal-chops, sub-bass replacement of original acoustic-bass, processed-and-pitched effects), tempos varying widely (90-150 BPM depending on source rhythm), DJ-set-functional song-form with extended sectional vamps, and a producer-and-DJ-circuit ecosystem distributing through Boiler Room and underground club networks. Distinguished from straight tropical genres by post-2005 timestamp and electronic-club production; distinguished from straight house and techno by tropical-rhythm foundation; distinguished from broader Latin-electronic by tropical-bass-specific umbrella-term framing.

items.name: 90s eurodance
items.lineage: 1990s pan-European mainstream dance-pop genre fusing house's four-on-the-floor with rap verses and pop choruses on a 120-130 bpm template — codified through Snap! (The Power 1990), 2 Unlimited (No Limit 1993), Ace of Base (The Sign 1993), Haddaway (What Is Love 1993), Real McCoy, Culture Beat, La Bouche, Captain Hollywood Project
items.description: Eurodance (codified 1990-1998 across central Europe with primary production centers in Italy, Germany, Sweden, and the Netherlands, with golden era 1993-1996 establishing the sound), the early-to-mid-90s European commercial dance subgenre. Defined by rapping-male-and-singing-female vocal pair (the eurodance-signature configuration where a male MC delivers verses and a female vocalist delivers the melodic chorus), four-on-floor kick foundation around 130-140 BPM, octave-jumping or saw-lead synth-bass lines, melodic synth-lead hooks designed for radio-friendly chorus material, programmed drum-machine percussion with prominent claps and synth-snare on beats 2 and 4, and English-language lyric content optimized for pan-European chart performance. Distinguished from straight house by faster tempo and rap-and-sing vocal-pair configuration; distinguished from earlier hi-NRG by post-1990 timestamp and rapping-vocal-foreground; distinguished from later trance by retention of pop-song-form structure and absence of extended trance-build-and-release dynamics.

items.name: Italo dance
items.lineage: Late-1990s through early-2000s Italian commercial-dance genre evolved from italo-disco through eurodance, characterized by accelerated 140-150 bpm tempo, melodic synth-lead lines, and earnest pop-vocal hooks — codified through Eiffel 65 (Blue 1999), Gigi D'Agostino (L'Amour Toujours 1999, La Passion 2000), DJ Lhasa, Prezioso, with the genre serving as a distinct continental commercial-dance regional scene
items.description: Italo dance (codified late-1990s through 2000s Italian-developed commercial dance-pop, descending from italo-house and eurodance lineages), the Italian commercial dance subgenre. Defined by saw-lead synth hooks (single-octave-jumping or arpeggiated melodic lead lines using sawtooth-wave synthesis as the genre signifier), female-soprano vocal performance often delivering pop-anthem chorus material in English-with-Italian-accent or Italian-with-English-chorus code-switching, four-on-floor kick foundation around 130-140 BPM, programmed bassline alternating root-octave or arpeggio patterns, and big-room production aesthetic with sidechain-compression pumping. Production lineage emerging from Italian commercial-radio dance industry. Distinguished from italo-house by faster tempo and absence of piano-stab foreground; distinguished from eurodance by Italian production lineage and saw-lead foreground; distinguished from later electro-house by retention of pop-melodic-vocal centrality.

items.name: Hi-NRG
items.lineage: early-1980s onward gay-club-derived electronic dance music characterized by 130+ bpm tempo, electronic-disco production (sequenced bass, mechanical hi-hat patterns), and intense emotionally-direct pop-vocal lead — codified through Patrick Cowley (Megatron Man 1981, the Sylvester collaborations), Bobby O, Lime, Hazell Dean, Divine (the 1980s Bobby O recordings), with the form serving as a precursor to acid-house and techno
items.description: Hi-NRG (codified late-1970s through mid-1980s, descending from disco and crystallizing through Patrick Cowley's San Francisco productions and parallel UK Stock-Aitken-Waterman work), the late-70s through 80s commercial-gay-disco descendant electronic dance subgenre. Defined by tempos pushed to 130-140 BPM (faster than mainstream disco's 110-120 BPM), octave-jumping bass-synth lines (the bass-note alternating between root and octave on consecutive sixteenths), four-on-floor kick foundation with prominent claps and synth-drum percussion, melodic high-energy synthesizer lead lines, vocal performance often by female-and-male singers delivering pop-anthem chorus material, and dancefloor association with gay-club scenes (the genre developed in San Francisco gay-bar circuits as disco's commercial mainstream moved on). Distinguished from straight disco by tempo and synthesized-bass over funk-bass; distinguished from later eurodance by 80s timestamp and Italo-disco-and-American-gay-club lineage; distinguished from electroclash by sincerity rather than ironic-revival framing.

items.name: Freestyle music
items.lineage: Mid-1980s onward Latino-and-Italian-American urban-dance genre developed in New York and Miami clubs, characterized by 808-drum-machine programming, electronic sub-bass, and emotional Latino-soul vocal lead — codified through Shannon (Let the Music Play 1983), Lisa Lisa and Cult Jam (I Wonder If I Take You Home 1984), Exposé, The Cover Girls, Stevie B, Sa-Fire
items.description: Freestyle (codified 1983-1989 New York and Miami, descending from electro-funk and crystallizing through Latin-Caribbean diaspora communities in both cities), the 80s Latin-Caribbean dance-pop genre that fused electro production with romantic-vocal-pop conventions. Defined by electro-derived programmed-drum-machine back-line patterns (often Roland TR-808 with Linn-LM1 doubling) replacing earlier disco-rhythm-section, melodic-vocal-foreground performance often by Latina female singers delivering high-emotional teenage-romance lyric content, synth-bass-and-pad accompaniment, song-form alternating verse-pre-chorus-chorus with extended dance-floor-suitable vamps, and tempos around 110-128 BPM. Lyrics typically Spanish-English bilingual or English with Spanish phrases. Distinguished from straight electro-funk by song-foreground over instrumental-foreground; distinguished from Latin freestyle by absence of pure-Spanish-language recording; distinguished from Miami bass by tempo and absence of low-end-hyper-foregrounding.

items.name: UK garage and 2-step
items.lineage: Late-1990s UK club-music genre extending US garage through the syncopated 2-step rhythm (kick on beats 1 and 3 only, snare on the off-beats) — codified through Tuff Jam, Wookie, MJ Cole (Sincere 2000), Artful Dodger (It Ain't Enough 2000), Craig David (Born to Do It 2000), So Solid Crew, and continuing through the late-2000s revival
items.description: UK garage and 2-step (codified 1995-2001 UK club scene, with first-wave speed-garage 1995-1997 and second-wave 2-step 1997-2001 establishing the sound through artists like Todd Edwards, MJ Cole, Artful Dodger, and So Solid Crew), the late-90s UK club genre. Defined by sped-up Jersey-garage tempo around 130-140 BPM, shuffled syncopated back-line where kick-and-snare placement avoids straight four-on-floor in favor of broken patterns (the 2-step pattern with kick on 1 and 3 and snare on the and-of-2 and the and-of-4 or other syncopated placements), ragga-and-R&B-derived vocal samples and live-vocal hooks, sub-bass and synth-bass programming, optional brass-section samples, and dance-floor association with UK-garage clubs and pirate-radio circuits. Distinguished from US garage-house by UK-not-NYC lineage and 2-step rhythmic foundation over four-on-floor; distinguished from later dubstep (which descended from UK garage and grime) by retention of vocal-foreground and song-form pop-craft; distinguished from grime by 130-140-BPM-not-138-BPM and dance-floor-functional structure over MC-foreground.

items.name: Liquid funk (drum & bass)
items.lineage: Early-2000s onward drum-and-bass subgenre emphasizing soulful-jazz harmonic foundation, melodic content, and accessible vocal-pop arrangement against rolling drum-and-bass percussion — codified through Calibre, High Contrast (True Colours 2002), Logistics, Netsky (Netsky 2010), London Elektricity, and the broader Hospital Records label catalog
items.description: Melodic-and-musical drum-and-bass sub-style softening the breakbeat aggression of jungle; jazz-and-soul-derived chord progressions, smooth-vocal collaborations, deeper sub-bass focus over chopped breaks.

items.name: Dubstep (140 bass-music)
items.lineage: Mid-2000s south London electronic-dance genre evolved from UK garage through tempo deceleration to 140 bpm and the introduction of the dubstep half-step rhythmic feel — codified through Skream (Skream! 2006), Benga, Burial (Burial 2006, Untrue 2007), Mala, Coki, Loefah, Plastician, and the FWD>> club and DMZ night which served as the genre's incubator
items.description: Dubstep at 140 BPM (codified 2002-2007 South London through Croydon's Big Apple Records scene with FWD>> club residency, and pre-American-2010-bro-step transformation), the mid-2000s UK club-derived bass-music. Defined by halved-tempo syncopated back-line where the kick lands on beat 1 and the snare lands on beat 3 (a half-time feel against the 140-BPM grid producing a 70-BPM perceived pulse), sub-bass wobble lead lines created through LFO-modulated synth bass, sparse syncopated percussion programming with prominent skipping hi-hats, dark moody atmospheric pads underneath, and lyric content (when present) drawing on London grime MC traditions or Jamaican-vocal-sample reggae heritage. Distinguished from later American-style brostep by sparser arrangement and absence of distortion-and-aggression foreground; distinguished from drum-and-bass by halved-tempo perception and sub-bass-foreground; distinguished from grime by 140-BPM rather than 130-BPM and instrumental-vocal balance.

items.name: Lovers' rock
items.lineage: UK Black-British soft-soul reggae subgenre that emerged from 1976 onward as the Black British response to Jamaican roots-reggae — codified through Louisa Mark (Caught You in a Lie 1975), Janet Kay (Silly Games 1979, the #2 UK chart breakthrough), Carroll Thompson, Sandra Cross, Brown Sugar, the Investigators production team (Dennis Bovell); female-vocal-led with softer mixing aesthetic and lyrical content centering on female romantic interiority
items.description: UK-developed Black-British reggae sub-style centering soul-and-pop romantic vocals over reggae one-drop back-line; smoother production, female-vocal-led, intimate-song-form rather than dancehall-dance focus.

items.name: 2-Tone ska revival
items.lineage: UK 1979-1981 multiracial ska revival movement centered on Coventry — codified through the 2 Tone Records label (founded 1979 by Jerry Dammers of The Specials) and its catalog: The Specials, The Selecter, Madness, The Beat, The Bodysnatchers, Bad Manners — translating original 1960s Jamaican ska into the post-punk era with explicit anti-racist political content and Two-Tone-checkerboard graphic identity
items.description: British 1979-81 ska revival fusing punk-intensity with original Jamaican ska back-line; mixed-race lineups, anti-racist agitational subjects, hard-edged guitar-and-horn arrangements over ska off-beat skanks.

items.name: Reggae fusion (modern)
items.lineage: Late-1990s onward Caribbean popular-music genre fusing reggae rhythmic and vocal vocabulary with hip-hop, pop, R-and-B, and electronic-dance production techniques — codified through Sean Paul (Dutty Rock 2002), Shaggy (Hot Shot 2000), Sean Kingston (Sean Kingston 2007), Magic! (Don't Kill the Magic 2014), with the form serving as the international-mainstream commercial-reggae substream
items.description: Reggae fusion modern (codified 1990s onward through Jamaican-and-international artists blending reggae with hip-hop, R&B, and pop production aesthetics, with continuous tradition through to present), the contemporary genre-crossing reggae production. Defined by reggae rhythmic foundation (one-drop or rockers-style drum patterns, off-beat skanking guitar or keyboards, deep bass) overlaid with dancehall-derived programmed elements, hip-hop-and-R&B production techniques, and pop-song-form structural conventions, vocal performance combining reggae-singer or dancehall-deejay delivery with R&B-melismatic-and-pop-melodic vocal techniques, lyric content addressing romantic-and-social-commentary subjects in English-and-Patois code-switching, and chart-oriented commercial production polish targeting cross-genre playlists. Distinguished from straight roots-reggae by post-1990 timestamp and pop-and-R&B-production blending; distinguished from straight dancehall by retention of reggae melodic-and-instrumental-tradition over digital-riddim foreground; distinguished from straight pop by retention of reggae rhythmic-signature foundation.

items.name: Dub poetry
items.lineage: Jamaican-British poetic-spoken-word performance tradition over reggae rhythm backing — codified through Linton Kwesi Johnson (UK Black-British, the figure, his 1978 Dread Beat an Blood the founding album), Mutabaruka (Jamaican), Oku Onuora (Jamaican, who coined the genre name in 1979), Mikey Smith (Jamaican), Benjamin Zephaniah (UK Black-British)
items.description: Dub poetry (codified 1970s-1980s Jamaica and London through Mutabaruka, Linton Kwesi Johnson, and Oku Onuora), the Jamaican-and-British performance form of recited poetry over reggae and dub back-lines. Defined by spoken-word recitation of original written-poetry (the poetry exists as written text first, then performed) over reggae rhythm-section and dub-style mixing-board treatment, agitational-postcolonial subject matter (police violence, immigrant rights, anti-colonial politics, racial-class struggle), Jamaican-Patois or Black-British-English vocal delivery, and a performance circuit through poetry venues, university lectures, and reggae festival appearances. The genre sits between literary tradition and music — readers and listeners both engage. Distinguished from straight reggae by spoken-word-not-sung delivery and poetry-as-primary-text; distinguished from rap by older origin and literary-tradition framing; distinguished from spoken-word with backing track by genre-specific reggae-and-dub instrumentation.

items.name: Russian bard song (avtorskaya pesnya)
items.lineage: Soviet-era guitar-and-poet song (avtorskaya pesnya, literally authorial song) tradition codified by Vladimir Vysotsky (the raspy-voice baritone), Bulat Okudzhava (the gentle-tenor Arbat-Street troubadour), Alexander Galich (the dissident émigré voice), Yuri Vizbor (the mountain-climbing-and-friendship songwriter) — circulated through magnitizdat (self-distributed-tape underground circulation) under Soviet censorship rather than official Melodiya release
items.description: Soviet-era poet-with-guitar tradition centered on literary-quality lyric authorship and intimate kitchen-and-campfire performance; samizdat-circulated tape recordings, intelligentsia-counter-culture aesthetic.

items.name: Polish poezja śpiewana
items.lineage: Polish sung-poetry tradition setting the work of Polish poets (Wojciech Mlynarski, Agnieszka Osiecka, Jeremi Przybora, Konstanty Ildefons Galczynski) to song composed and performed by singers including Marek Grechuta (the figure), Czesław Niemen, Ewa Demarczyk, Stan Borys, Magda Umer, Anna Treter — emerging from the post-1956 Polish artistic thaw and developing in dialogue with French chanson and German Liedermacher traditions
items.description: Polish "sung poetry" tradition setting literary-Polish poetry to original musical settings; piano-and-voice or guitar-and-voice intimate-cabaret-style delivery, Piwnica pod Baranami.

items.name: Czech písnička
items.lineage: Czech songwriter folk-poetic song tradition codified through Karel Kryl (the émigré protest voice of the 1968 Prague Spring), Jaromír Nohavica (the working-class storyteller), Vladimír Mišík (the rock-adjacent variant), Hutka, the Plastic People of the Universe (samizdat psychedelic-rock variant), and the broader Czech literary-poetic song tradition under and after Communist rule
items.description: Czech and Slovak folk-poetic songwriter tradition; semi-acoustic intimate format, country-and-tramping-folklore subjects intermixed with literary settings; Velvet-era counter-culture agitational-allegorical tradition.

items.name: South Slavic kantautor
items.lineage: Yugoslav-era and post-Yugoslav successor singer-poet tradition spanning Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian, Slovenian, Macedonian, and Montenegrin language traditions — codified through Đorđe Balašević (the Vojvodina Serbian kantautor, active 1978 until his death in 2021), Arsen Dedić (the Croatian voice), Bora Đorđević and Riblja Čorba (the rock-and-kantautor crossover), Vlatko Stefanovski (the Macedonian guitar-virtuoso continuation), and the post-Yugoslav diaspora extensions Branimir Štulić and Azra
items.description: South Slavic kantautor / kantautorska pesma (1968 onward, codified during late-Yugoslav-era cultural ferment through Arsen Dedić, Đorđe Balašević, and the broader Yugoslav singer-poet circuit, with successor-state continuation through Croatian, Serbian, Bosnian, Slovenian, and Macedonian lineages), the Yugoslav-era and successor-state singer-poet tradition. Defined by literary-poetic content alongside agitational-political-and-personal lyric subject matter, acoustic-guitar-foundation accompaniment occasionally extended with piano, accordion, fiddle, and small-ensemble configurations, characteristic conversational vocal delivery prioritizing literary-text clarity over operatic-projection or pop-belt, repertoire addressing romantic-melancholy, social-commentary, generational-disaffection, and post-Yugoslav-war reflection in successor-state era, and intimate-club and concert-hall performance contexts. Distinguished from Russian estrada by South-Slavic-language and singer-poet-not-state-curated framing; distinguished from later Yugoslav rock by acoustic-singer-songwriter format; distinguished from straight Yugoslav folk tradition by original-composition-not-traditional-repertoire focus.

items.name: Cantorial khazonus (chazzanut)
items.lineage: Ashkenazi Jewish synagogue cantorial tradition — the solo lead-singer (chazzan / khazn / cantor) liturgical practice of the Eastern European Yiddish-speaking world, codified through Yossele Rosenblatt (the golden-age chazzan, 1882-1933), Gershon Sirota, Mordechai Hershman, Moishe Oysher, Jan Peerce (the cantor-to-opera-tenor crossover), Moshe Koussevitzky
items.description: Ashkenazi synagogue cantorial tradition centered on virtuosic male tenor solo voice; modal-prayer recitative organized by nusach (mode-of-occasion), highly ornamented melismatic vocal phrasing, golden-age 1900-1950.

items.name: Hasidic niggun
items.lineage: Hasidic Jewish wordless-melody (niggun, plural niggunim) tradition sung at farbrengen celebratory gatherings, weddings, the Rebbes tisch (table), the third Shabbat meal (seudah shlishit), and post-prayer celebratory contexts across the major Hasidic dynastic courts — Lubavitch (Chabad), Breslov, Bobov, Modzitz (founded 1898, particularly known for its musical-niggun creativity), Vizhnitz, Ger, Satmar; sung communally with the inherited dynasty-specific niggun repertoire, often slow-contemplative accelerating to fast-ecstatic, accompanied by hand-clapping and table-thumping but without instruments on Shabbat or Yom Tov
items.description: Hasidic mystical-devotional wordless-melody tradition; congregational-male-massed vocal repetition of short modal phrases building intensity through repetition; tisch and farbrengen ceremonial context.

items.name: Yemenite Torah cantillation
items.lineage: Yemenite Jewish liturgical Torah-cantillation tradition that preserves what scholars consider one of the most archaic surviving teamim (Masoretic cantillation-sign) reading traditions, descended from the Yemenite Jewish community continuously resident in Yemen from at least the 5th century until the Operation Magic Carpet mass-emigration to Israel 1949-50; characterized by Saadia Gaon-derived liturgical Hebrew pronunciation and microtonal modal vocabulary distinct from Ashkenazi or Sephardi traditions
items.description: Yemenite Jewish liturgical recitation of the Pentateuch; centuries-old ta’amei mikra (cantillation accent) tradition, monophonic-vocal-only chant in Hebrew, considered closest extant continuation of pre-diaspora-era practice.

items.name: Sephardi bakkashot
items.lineage: Sephardi Jewish Saturday-night-into-pre-dawn-Sunday-morning supplicatory liturgical-poetry singing tradition performed during the autumn-and-winter months — built on Arab maqam-derived modal vocabulary, classical Arabic and Hebrew poetic structures (piyyutim by Yehuda Halevi, Ibn Gabirol, Israel Najara), with the Aleppo Syrian school (the dominant Eastern Sephardi tradition until the 1947 dispersal) and parallel Salonican / Western Sephardi tradition (until the 1943 Nazi destruction of Greek Jewry), continuing today in Israeli, Mexican, Argentine, and Brooklyn Syrian-Sephardi communities
items.description: Sephardi bakkashot (codified medieval-period onward in Aleppo Syria and Jerusalem Sephardi Jewish communities, with continuous tradition through to present and modernized concert-stage performance from 1950s onward), the Sephardi Jewish pre-dawn devotional song tradition. Defined by Hebrew-and-Aramaic poetic-text repertoire (medieval and early-modern Sephardi liturgical poetry with mystical-and-supplicatory subject matter), Arab-maqam-derived melodic-modal organization (Sephardi bakkashot uses the maqam system shared with Arab classical music — the same eight maqamat with regional Sephardi names), unaccompanied vocal performance in synagogue contexts (Jewish liturgical practice excludes instrumental accompaniment in synagogue, though concert-stage performance sometimes adds oud-and-qanun-and-percussion), pre-dawn-Sabbath performance schedule (the bakkashot are sung in the hours before Saturday-morning prayer service during winter months), and call-and-response between hazzan cantor and congregation. Distinguished from Ashkenazi piyyut by Sephardi-Aleppo-Jerusalem origin and maqam-melodic-system foundation; distinguished from Arab classical despite shared maqam system by Hebrew-language and Jewish-religious framing; distinguished from later modernized concert-stage performance by traditional pre-dawn-Sabbath context.

items.name: Qur'anic recitation (tajwīd)
items.lineage: Islamic scriptural recitation tradition (tajweed: "elocution") codifying pronunciation rules for the Qur’an across the 10 canonical qira’at (reading systems) — exemplified through Egyptian reciters Mahmoud Khalil Al-Hussary, Mohamed Siddiq El-Minshawi, Abdul Basit Abd us-Samad whose 1950s-70s recordings became the international auditory canon
items.description: Codified scriptural recitation tradition with strict pronunciation rules and elaborate maqam-based melodic-modal phrasing; reciters trained in seven readings (qira’at), recitation forms tartil and tajwid sub-modes.

items.name: Naʿat (Islamic devotional song)
items.lineage: Pan-Islamic devotional poetry-recitation tradition in praise of the Prophet Muhammad (Arabic naʿat literally means description / praise) — performed at Mawlid an-Nabi celebrations, milad-un-Nabi processions, private home and mosque gatherings; codified through the Urdu-language naat khwani tradition in Pakistan and India (reciters Owais Raza Qadri, Junaid Jamshed, Sami Yusuf), with parallel Arabic-and-Turkish-and-Indonesian language traditions across the broader Muslim world
items.description: Islamic devotional poetry-song-of-praise to the Prophet Muhammad; sung in Urdu, Arabic, Persian, Turkish, or other Muslim-region languages; ranges from solo-vocal to compact-ensemble formats with frame-drum and harmonium.

items.name: Athān (Islamic call to prayer)
items.lineage: Islamic ceremonial call-to-prayer (adhān) tradition broadcast five times daily from mosque minarets — codified through the seven phrases (takbīr, shahāda, hayya, etc.) in unmetered melismatic-modal singing, varying by regional tradition (Turkish, Egyptian, Maghrebi, Persian, Indo-Pakistani recitation schools)
items.description: Athan, Islamic call-to-prayer (codified ca. 622 CE Medina, performed five times daily — fajr at dawn, dhuhr at noon, asr in afternoon, maghrib at sunset, isha at night — across the Muslim world), the unaccompanied vocal proclamation that summons the faithful to salat. Defined by the fixed Arabic text (the shahada-centered formulaic seven phrases), maqam-based melodic-vocal recitation that varies by regional tradition (Hijazi, Egyptian, Turkish, Persian, Maghrebi, sub-Saharan, Indonesian — each a distinct melodic-style school), live mosque-minaret delivery (now also amplified loudspeaker broadcast across the umma), and the muezzin specialty of trained vocal art balancing pious solemnity with technical melodic skill. Distinguished from Quranic recitation by liturgical-call vs scriptural-recital function and shorter fixed text; distinguished from Sufi sama by mosque-public-call vs zikr-circle context.

items.name: Anāshīd (Islamic vocal-only devotional)
items.lineage: Islamic instrument-free devotional vocal tradition (nashīd plural anāshīd: "hymns") characterized by male-chorus a cappella or daff frame-drum accompaniment — codified through Sami Yusuf’s 2003 Al-Mu’allim record, Maher Zain, and Mesut Kurtis as canonical late-twentieth-century English-Arabic-bilingual exponents
items.description: Islamic devotional song restricted to voice and frame-drum percussion only (excluding melodic-pitched instruments per certain Islamic legal interpretations); congregational-or-soloist delivery, Arabic and other Muslim-language texts.

items.name: Candomblé ceremonial
items.lineage: Bahian Yoruba-Nagô / Bantu-Jeje liturgical drumming tradition of the orixá-honoring terreiro — codified through the early-19th-century Yoruba and Fon enslaved-people religious continuity in Salvador, formalized through the Casa Branca, Gantois, and Ilê Axé Opô Afonjá foundational terreiros; characterized by the rum-rumpi-lê three-drum ensemble, agogô bell, and chants in Yoruba-derived liturgical language
items.description: Brazilian Yoruba-Bantu-derived sacred ceremonial music for orixá worship; three atabaques (rum, rumpi, lê) interlocking with agogô bell, lead-and-chorus call-and-response in Yoruba liturgical language.

items.name: Lukumí ceremonial
items.lineage: Cuban Yoruba-derived Afro-Cuban religious-ritual song-and-drumming tradition preserved since the 17th-century-onward enslaved-Yoruba (Nigerian and Beninese) population, organized around the worship of the orichas (Yoruba deities transposed into Catholic-saint syncretism). The canonical batá-drum ensemble: three two-headed hourglass-shaped sacred-drums (iyá largest, itótele middle, okónkolo smallest) interlock through complex polyrhythmic patterns (toques) specific to each oricha. Each oricha has dedicated rezos invocational-songs, suyeres invocational-melodic-fragments, and toques rhythmic-patterns identifying-and-summoning the deity. The Lucumí ritual-vocabulary preserves substantial pre-colonial Yoruba liturgical-text untranslated. The 1959-onward Cuban revolution suppressed-and-then-tolerated santería; the 1990s-onward post-Special-Period economic-opening reopened public ritual practice.
items.description: Cuban Yoruba-derived sacred ceremonial music for orisha worship; three batá drums (iyá, itótele, okónkolo) playing toques specific to each orisha, lead-and-chorus call-and-response in Lukumí liturgical language.

items.name: Haitian vodou ceremonial
items.lineage: Haitian vodou ceremonial music tradition — three principal drum-batteries governing the spirit-pantheons they call: asoto (West African Yoruba-derived), rada (Dahomeyan-derived, calmer spirits), petwo (Kreyol-Haitian innovation, hot fierce spirits); manbo or houngan officiants lead the ceremony with songs (chante vodou) summoning the lwa to mount worshippers in trance possession
items.description: Haitian Vodou ceremonial music (codified through the 1791-1804 Haitian Revolution period synthesizing Yoruba Fon-Ewe Kongo and other West-African enslaved-people's traditions with French Catholicism in colonial Saint-Domingue, with continuous practice through to present-day Haiti and the Haitian diaspora), the Afro-Catholic-syncretic sacred ceremonial music for lwa-spirit worship. Defined by multiple drum-rite traditions (Rada from Dahomey-Yoruba lineage with three-drum manman-segon-bula ensemble; Petwo from Kongo lineage with hot-and-fast tempo; Nago from Yoruba lineage; each rite has distinct rhythms, drums, songs, and lwa-pantheon associations), call-and-response between mambo or houngan priest-singer and chorus, ason rattle and ogan iron-bell rhythmic foundation, possession-trance ceremonial function where music summons specific lwa spirits to mount serviteurs, and a year-cycle of ceremonies tied to specific lwa feast days. Distinguished from secular Haitian music (rara, kompa, racine roots-fusion) by ceremonial function and rite-specific repertoire; distinguished from Cuban Santería by Haitian-Vodou pantheon and Petwo-rite-specific hot-fast tempo.

items.name: Umbanda ceremonial
items.lineage: Rio and São Paulo 1908-onward syncretic Afro-Catholic-spiritualist liturgical tradition founded by Zélio Fernandino de Moraes (1908 first session) — fusing Catholic saints, candomblé orixás, Kardecist spiritualism, and Indigenous Brazilian ancestor cults; characterized by the gira ceremonial circle, pontos-cantados invocation songs, atabaque drum accompaniment, and the caboclo / preto-velho / criança guide-spirit roles
items.description: Early-20th-century Brazilian syncretic Afro-spiritualist tradition combining candomblé, indigenous, and Kardecist-spiritualist elements; pontos cantados (sung points) for spirit-line invocation, atabaque-drum-and-vocal architecture.
exemplars: Caboclo Sete Flechas — pontos cantados archive
Coral de Umbanda do Rio de Janeiro

items.name: Lo-fi hip hop (chillhop)
items.lineage: Mid-2010s onward online-distributed instrumental-hip-hop genre characterized by tape-saturated downtempo beat-tape production, jazz-and-soul sample foundations, and study-and-relax-targeted use context — codified through Nujabes (Modal Soul 2005, posthumously canonical), J Dilla (Donuts 2006, the lineage-bearing predecessor), and developed through ChilledCow and Lofi Girl YouTube live-streams, with countless bedroom-producer contributors
items.description: Streaming-era ambient-instrumental hip hop derived from boom-bap aesthetics processed through cassette-warble emulation; chopped jazz-and-soul samples, vinyl-static-and-tape-saturation, study-and-sleep listener context.

items.name: Vaporwave
items.lineage: 2010s online-distributed electronic micro-genre nostalgically recontextualizing 1980s-1990s corporate-mall-and-soft-rock background music through pitch-shifting, chopping, and ironic-commentary visual presentation — codified through Macintosh Plus (Floral Shoppe 2011, the founding vaporwave album), Vektroid, Saint Pepsi, Blank Banshee, and continuing through the broader online-aesthetic vaporwave subscene
items.description: Vaporwave (codified 2010-2014 internet-circulated electronic music micro-genre, with Macintosh Plus's Floral Shoppe and James Ferraro's Far Side Virtual establishing the sound and parallel Tumblr-and-A E S T H E T I C visual culture establishing the genre's visual-and-textual register), the mid-2010s internet-circulated electronic music genre. Defined by slowed-down chopped 80s-90s smooth-jazz, corporate-Muzak, and adult-contemporary source samples (the vaporwave-practice of taking commercial-easy-listening source material and pitching-down-and-time-stretching it into hypnotic-uncanny new arrangements), reverb-and-chorus processing producing dreamy-warped textures, song-form built on extended loops rather than verse-chorus structure, visual-aesthetic association with Roman-bust-statues, palm-trees, sunset-imagery, and 80s/90s commercial-aesthetic-graphics, and direct internet-distribution (Bandcamp, YouTube, SoundCloud) often free-of-cost. Distinguished from chillwave by sample-based-loop-construction over song-form; distinguished from synthwave by absence of new-composition and corporate-source palette; distinguished from straight ambient by source-material-foreground and uncanny-revival aesthetic stance.

items.name: Hypnagogic pop
items.lineage: Late-2000s onward American underground genre evocative of half-remembered 1980s pop-and-soundtrack production aesthetics, characterized by hazy lo-fi production, cassette-tape saturation, and nostalgia-as-subject-matter compositional posture — codified through Ariel Pink (Worn Copy 2003, House Arrest 2006), Ducktails, James Ferraro, Spencer Clark, with David Keenan's 2009 The Wire article naming the genre
items.description: Hypnagogic pop (2009-2012 internet-circulated American micro-genre, named in 2009 by critic David Keenan and crystallizing through Ariel Pink, James Ferraro, and Spencer Clark's bedroom-DAW productions), the 2010s lo-fi pop genre evoking false-memory-of-1980s commercial-music aesthetics. Defined by cassette-degraded production aesthetic (deliberate tape-saturation, pitch-warble, hiss preservation), reverb-and-chorus-drenched synth pads and electric piano evoking 1980s soft-rock and easy-listening sonic palette, uncanny-valley pop-song construction where familiar 80s pop signifiers recombine in ways that feel almost-but-not-quite right, lyrical content of childhood-suburban-memory and aestheticized-television-and-mall imagery, and DIY-cassette-and-vinyl-only release distribution. Distinguished from chillwave by greater commitment to deliberate-warpedness and 80s-specific reference; distinguished from vaporwave by song-form-rather-than-loop construction; distinguished from straight retro-revival by uncanny rather than nostalgic posture.

items.name: Bedroom pop
items.lineage: 2010s onward indie-pop subgenre originating in solo bedroom-DAW production — characterized by lo-fi or hi-fi DIY production, intimate vocal delivery, and adolescent thematic content — codified through Clairo (Pretty Girl 2017, Immunity 2019), Cuco, Boy Pablo, Mac DeMarco (Salad Days 2014, the genre's lineage-bearing predecessor), Beabadoobee, with the form serving as the late-2010s indie-pop mainstream
items.description: Bedroom pop (2010 onward, originating with first-wave SoundCloud and Bandcamp self-released DAW recordings before transitioning to streaming-platform breakout artists), the DIY indie-pop subgenre where home-laptop-DAW production is itself the genre signifier. Defined by intimate close-mic vocal recording without a tracking room (audible mouth sounds, room-tone, sometimes audible domestic background), deliberately-imperfect performance and mixing (off-pitch moments left in, low-fidelity drums or programmed sample-pad rhythms), a synth-and-drum-machine and electric-or-acoustic-guitar palette without traditional tracking-band instrumentation, lyrical content around bedroom-introspection subjects (heartbreak, isolation, internet-culture references), and lo-fi mastering aesthetic (noise floor preserved, bit-crushing accepted, no transparent commercial polish). Distinguished from singer-songwriter folk by synth-and-DAW palette and post-2010 timestamp; distinguished from chillwave by song-form-not-vamp construction; distinguished from hyperpop by gentleness rather than maximalist distortion.

items.name: Chillwave
items.lineage: 2009-2012 American online-distributed electronic-and-indie-pop genre characterized by lo-fi summer-nostalgic aesthetics, pitched-down vocal samples, and tape-saturated 1980s production references — codified through Washed Out (Life of Leisure 2009), Toro y Moi (Causers of This 2010), Neon Indian (Psychic Chasms 2009), Memory Tapes, with the David Carr Cole Hipster Runoff Wikipedia coinage providing the genre's name
items.description: Chillwave (2009-2012 American internet-circulated indie-electronic micro-genre, named in 2009 by Hipster Runoff blog and crystallizing through Memory Cassette, Washed Out, Toro y Moi, and Neon Indian early bedroom releases), the VHS-era summer-vacation nostalgic indie-electronic style. Defined by midtempo (90-110 BPM) synth-pop instrumental beds with hazy chorus-and-reverb-drenched processing evoking warped-tape or VHS-degraded fidelity, drum-machine and sample-based percussion under washed-out synth-pad textures, lo-fi vocal performance often pitched-shifted or chopped-and-screwed, lyrical and visual themes of summer beaches, suburban swimming pools, fading cassette tapes, and aestheticized memory-loss, and home-DAW production with deliberate fidelity-imperfection. Distinguished from synthwave by softer-and-hazier production and pre-darksynth-aesthetic warmth; distinguished from vaporwave by song-form-rather-than-loop-based construction and absence of corporate-Muzak source samples; distinguished from bedroom pop by instrumental-or-near-instrumental focus and synth-pad palette.

items.name: Pìobaireachd (Highland classical)
items.lineage: Highland Scottish solo bagpipe classical art-music — the highest formal genre of Great Highland Bagpipe music, distinct from light music (marches, strathspeys, reels); built around the urlar (ground), the slow-tempo composed melodic theme, and successive variations of increasing complexity through movements including siubhal (passing variation), taorluath (cumulative grace-note variation), and crunluath (the most complex variation). The 18th-century MacCrimmon family tradition (the hereditary pipers of Clan MacLeod of Skye, with the Boreraig piping college), preserved through the Piobaireachd Society codification from 1903 onward
items.description: Highland Scottish solo bagpipe classical art-music form; theme-and-elaborate-variation through urlar-siubhal-taorluath-crunluath structure, highly-codified ornamental gracing-passage system, slow-and-meditative tempo.

items.name: Uilleann pipe solo (Irish)
items.lineage: Irish bellows-blown indoor bagpipe (uilleann pipes, formerly called union pipes) solo virtuoso tradition codified through Leo Rowsome, Seamus Ennis, Willie Clancy, Liam OFlynn, Paddy Keenan, Davy Spillane — the most complex bagpipe instrument in the world with three drones, three regulators (chord-producing keys operated by the elbow), and a chanter capable of full chromatic range
items.description: Irish parlor-piping tradition on bellows-blown uilleann pipes; air-and-piece traditional repertoire, virtuoso ornamentation, regulator-chord punctuation, indoor-intimate volume against outdoor Highland piping.

items.name: Yidaki solo (Aboriginal Australian)
items.lineage: Northeast Arnhem Land Yolŋu ceremonial trumpet tradition — the yidaki (the Yolŋu Matha language name for the instrument that English speakers call didgeridoo) is the Aboriginal Australian ceremonial pipe, played through continuous circular breathing with vocalizations and tongue articulations producing complex polyrhythmic textures; deeply tied to Yolŋu manikay ceremonial song tradition and the broader Aboriginal Australian songline cosmology — 20th-century preservation through Djalu Gurruwiwi (the yidaki master and ceremonial-knowledge holder), Mark Atkins, the Yothu Yindi yidaki tradition extended into popular-music context
items.description: Northeast Arnhem Land Yolngu ceremonial drone-pipe tradition (yidaki specifically refers to the Yolngu instrument); circular-breathing-sustained-drone with overlaid vocalized animal-call timbral variations, ceremonial bunggul-dance accompaniment.

items.name: Gaita galega solo
items.lineage: Galician solo bagpipe tradition — the gaita galega is the Galician bellows-blown or mouth-blown pipe with three drones and chanter, distinct from the kindred Asturian gaita asturiana (single-drone) and the Scottish Highland bagpipe (three-drone but different chanter scale). 20th-century revival figures include Ricardo Portela, Ramón Casal Castro, Antón Corral, the contemporary master Carlos Núñez (whose 1996 A Irmandade das Estrelas album with collaborations from The Chieftains, Ry Cooder, and others brought Galician piping to global audiences), Cristina Pato (the female gaita virtuoso). The instrument is paired with tambor (snare drum) for outdoor festive contexts
items.description: Galician pipe / gaita gallega solo (codified pre-modern in northwest Iberian Peninsula across Galicia, with continuous tradition through to present and revival from 1970s onward), the Galician solo bagpipe tradition. Defined by the gaita gallega (a single-drone bagpipe with chanter producing two-octave range), repertoire organized by traditional dance-and-occasion category (alborada — dawn-piece, muiñeira — mill-dance in 6/8, marcha procesional — processional march, jota gallega — fast triple-meter dance), solo performance contexts spanning street procession, festival opening, religious procession (romería), and concert-stage solo presentation, and a regional pedagogy organized around gaita-school conservatory training. Distinguished from Asturian and Cantabrian regional pipe traditions by Galician-specific repertoire and ornamentation conventions; distinguished from Highland-Scottish piobaireachd by single-drone-not-three-drone configuration and Galician-not-Scottish repertoire; distinguished from Breton biniou koz by larger size and lower tonic pitch.

items.name: Cloud rap (experimental)
items.lineage: Early-2010s atmospheric-trap experimental hip-hop subgenre extending cloud-rap aesthetic through more ambient-arrangement, washed-out post-rock textures, and surreal lyrical content — codified through early Lil B (Rain in England 2010), Yung Lean (Unknown Death 2013), Sad Boys, Spaceghostpurrp, Awful Records, with the form serving as a key conduit for the late-2010s online-distributed rap scene
items.description: 2010s-onward ambient-leaning hip hop with hazy-pitched-vocal-sample backings, dreamy production aesthetic, melodic-rather-than-aggressive vocal delivery; descended from chopped-and-screwed and witch-house adjacencies.

items.name: Mumble rap
items.lineage: Mid-2010s Atlanta-and-Florida hip-hop subgenre characterized by sing-song melodic vocal delivery, slurred-and-melodic flow, autotune-saturated treatment, and emotional lyrical content — codified through Future (Dirty Sprite 2 2015, FUTURE 2017), Young Thug (Barter 6 2015), Migos (Culture 2017), Lil Uzi Vert (Luv Is Rage 2 2017), Playboi Carti, with the form serving as the late-2010s mainstream rap evolution
items.description: Mumble rap (codified 2014 onward through Future, Young Thug, Lil Yachty, and the Atlanta-Florida streaming-platform hip-hop scene, with the term itself a critical-pejorative that artists later embraced), the 2010s sub-style of trap-derived hip hop with deliberately-unclear-articulation vocal delivery. Defined by deliberately-unclear vocal articulation where words slur into one another and individual phonemes blur, melodic-leaning vocal lines that often function as quasi-sung melodic phrases over the trap-808 production foundation, auto-tune-saturated-vocal processing applied as vocal-aesthetic feature, ad-libs and vocal-interjections layered over the main verse providing percussive-and-textural elements, lyric content often addressing flexing, drug-references, and emotional-vulnerability subjects, and trap-genre production foundation (808 sub-bass, hi-hat triplets, halved-tempo perception). Distinguished from earlier hip-hop by deliberate articulation-as-feature; distinguished from cloud-rap by trap-808 foundation; distinguished from straight trap by greater commitment to vocal-melodic-foreground and auto-tune-saturation.

items.name: Hyperpop-rap (rage rap-adjacent)
items.lineage: Late-2010s onward maximalist hip-hop subgenre fusing hyperpop production techniques (over-the-top mixing, pitched-up vocal layers, glitchy sound design) with rap delivery and trap-derived rhythmic foundation — codified through Lil Uzi Vert (Eternal Atake 2020), Yeat, Bladee, ECCO2K (the Drain Gang lineage), 100 gecs (1000 gecs 2019), and continuing through the broader online-distributed digicore scene
items.description: Hyperpop rap (codified 2018 onward, descending from cloud-rap and hyperpop convergence through artists distributing on SoundCloud and TikTok), the late-2010s and 2020s rap-pop crossover with hyperpop-genre production-sensibility imports. Defined by pitched-up auto-tune-saturated vocal delivery (the cloud-rap melodic-vocal tradition extended through hyperpop-style pitch-and-formant manipulation), sound-design-forward production borrowing hyperpop synth-and-sample palette, abrupt section-edits and beat-switching mid-track, distortion and clipping embraced as production-feature, lyrical content alternating cloud-rap-tradition emotional-vulnerability with hyperpop-tradition irreverent-internet-culture references, and BPMs varying from 70 (cloud-rap-slow) to 150 (hyperpop-fast). Distinguished from straight cloud-rap by hyperpop-derived sound-design and beat-switching aesthetic; distinguished from straight hyperpop by retention of rap-MC verse-and-chorus vocal-form; distinguished from trap by absence of straight 808-based sub-bass foreground.

items.name: Rage (rap)
items.lineage: Late-2010s onward Atlanta-and-Memphis trap-derived hip-hop subgenre characterized by aggressive 808-bass-driven instrumentals, screamed-and-rasping vocal delivery, mosh-pit-targeted live-show energy, and explicit punk-and-metal cross-pollination — codified through Trippie Redd, Lil Uzi Vert, Playboi Carti (Whole Lotta Red 2020, the genre's definitive statement), Ken Carson, Destroy Lonely
items.description: Rage rap (codified 2020 onward through Playboi Carti's Whole Lotta Red and Yeat's underground breakout work establishing the genre, with continuous SoundCloud-and-streaming-platform diffusion through 2024), the 2020s aggressive-synth-driven trap sub-style. Defined by distorted-808 sub-bass foundation pushed past clipping into aggressive-distortion territory, screaming-saw synth leads (the rage-rap-specific high-pitched aggressive-saw-synth lead-line), hi-hat triplets and double-time hi-hat-rolls maintained from trap heritage, screamed-and-shouted MC vocal delivery (the rage in rage-rap referring to the vocal-performance aesthetic of high-aggression delivery), lyric content addressing flexing, hedonism, and personal-flex narratives, mosh-pit-functional dance-floor association at live shows, and tempos around 140-160 BPM. Distinguished from straight trap by distorted-808 and aggressive-synth foreground; distinguished from emo-rap by aggression rather than vulnerability register; distinguished from drill by absence of sliding-808 melodic foundation and rage-aesthetic vocal foreground.

items.name: 1960s Greenwich Village confessional folk
items.lineage: Early-1960s Greenwich Village (Cafe Wha, Gerdes Folk City, the Bitter End) folk-revival singer-songwriter circuit — Bob Dylan, Phil Ochs, Dave Van Ronk, Joan Baez early years, Tom Paxton, Eric Andersen
items.description: Greenwich Village confessional songwriting (1958-1965 New York Greenwich Village folk-revival scene, with second-wave 1965-1971 of the post-Dylan singer-songwriter generation), the personal-confessional folk-songwriter mode. Defined by protest-and-confessional original-text authorship (the songwriter writes both lyric and music, with personal-political-confessional first-person subject matter contrasting earlier folk-revival's traditional-text repertoire), fingerpicked acoustic-guitar accompaniment in standard or open tunings, performance contexts of Gerde's Folk City, the Gaslight Cafe, and other Bleecker-and-MacDougal Street folk venues, vocal delivery prioritizing intimate-spoken-clarity over operatic projection, and song-form combining traditional-folk-derived structural conventions (verse-chorus-verse, talking-blues structure) with extended literary-narrative ambition. Distinguished from earlier folk-revival by original-personal-text composition; distinguished from Brill-Building pop by craft-from-personal not craft-from-formula approach; distinguished from later confessional 60s singer-songwriter by Greenwich Village pre-1965 timestamp.

items.name: Late-60s interior confessional songwriter
items.lineage: Late-1960s confessional pop-folk songwriter tradition with intimate first-person lyrical subject matter — Leonard Cohen Songs of Leonard Cohen (1967), James Taylor James Taylor (1968, Apple Records), Joni Mitchell Song to a Seagull (1968) and Clouds (1969), Nick Drake Five Leaves Left (1969), Carole King Tapestry (1971)
items.description: Late-60s confessional songwriter mode emphasizing autobiographical interiority and sophisticated extended-harmony chord vocabulary; fingerpicked guitar or piano accompaniment, intimate vocal delivery.

items.name: 70s Laurel Canyon
items.lineage: Early-1970s Laurel Canyon (Los Angeles hill-neighborhood) singer-songwriter scene centered around Joni Mitchell, Crosby Stills Nash and Young, Jackson Browne, the Eagles, Linda Ronstadt, Carole King — codified through the A and M / Sunset Sound / Wally Heider studio canon
items.description: Laurel Canyon early-1970s singer-songwriter scene (1968-1974 Los Angeles, centered on the eponymous neighborhood and the social network around Joni Mitchell, Crosby Stills Nash & Young, Carole King, James Taylor, Jackson Browne, and the broader Asylum-Records-and-Geffen-management circle), the Los Angeles folk-rock-orchestral singer-songwriter circle. Defined by folk-rock-orchestral arrangements layering acoustic-and-electric guitar foundation with string-section overdubs, electric piano (Wurlitzer or Rhodes) accompaniment, harmony-vocal arrangements with multi-part stacked vocals (CSNY-style three-or-four-part harmony as reference), intimate-confessional first-person lyric content addressing personal-relationship subjects, and mid-tempo song-form built on extended verse-and-chorus with bridge-modulation pop-craft. Distinguished from Greenwich Village confessional songwriting by Los Angeles-not-New York centrality and post-1968 timestamp; distinguished from country-rock by retention of folk-acoustic-guitar foreground over country-electric-guitar; distinguished from soft-rock commercial mainstream by intimate-personal lyric register.

items.name: Britfolk revival
items.lineage: 1960s-70s UK folk-revival singer-songwriter movement codified through Bert Jansch and John Renbourn (the Pentangle nexus), Davey Graham (the DADGAD-tuning innovator), Anne Briggs, Shirley Collins, Nic Jones, June Tabor, the Watersons family ensemble, the Carthy family (Martin and Eliza), Fairport Convention, Steeleye Span — drawing heavily on the Cecil Sharp / Vaughan Williams field-collected canon and the Child ballad corpus
