items.name: Hardingfele slått (Hardanger-fiddle dance-tunes)
items.lineage: Norwegian Hardanger-fiddle slått dance-tune tradition of western-Norwegian mountain valleys (Hardanger, Voss, Telemark, Setesdal, Numedal regions). The hardingfele Hardanger-fiddle has four bowed melody strings plus four-or-five sympathetic resonant strings beneath the fingerboard, producing characteristic shimmering-overtone resonance. Slått (singular slått, plural slåttar) are solo virtuoso dance-tunes with strict regional-stylistic-conventions: springar three-beat asymmetric dance-tune, gangar two-beat walking-dance, halling acrobatic-male-display-dance, and rull rolling-tune. Performance: solo Hardanger-fiddle, with each regional sub-tradition (Setesdal, Hallingdal, Numedal, Valdres, Telemark) maintaining distinctive playing-conventions and ornamental-vocabulary.
items.description: Norwegian Hardanger-fiddle slått dance-tune tradition of western-Norwegian mountain valleys (Hardanger, Voss, Telemark, Setesdal, Numedal regions). The hardingfele Hardanger-fiddle has four bowed melody strings plus four-or-five sympathetic resonant strings beneath the fingerboard, producing characteristic shimmering-overtone resonance. Slått (singular slått, plural slåttar) are solo virtuoso dance-tunes with strict regional-stylistic-conventions: springar three-beat asymmetric dance-tune, gangar two-beat walking-dance, halling acrobatic-male-display-dance, and rull rolling-tune. Performance: solo Hardanger-fiddle, with each regional sub-tradition (Setesdal, Hallingdal, Numedal, Valdres, Telemark) maintaining distinctive playing-conventions and ornamental-vocabulary.

items.name: Swedish polska (traditional fiddle-dance)
items.lineage: Swedish polska traditional fiddle-dance tradition of Sweden, comprising several regional sub-types: åttondelspolska (eighth-note-pulse polska), sextondelspolska (sixteenth-note-pulse polska), Slängpolska (swing-polska), and several regional named variants. Performance configuration: solo fiddle, twin-fiddles (svenska låtspel), nyckelharpa (keyed fiddle), or small ensembles of these instruments. Distinguished by the canonical Swedish-fiddle ornamental conventions and the asymmetrical-triple-meter dance-pulse where the second beat is shortened. The post-1970s Swedish folk-music revival under the spelmanslag fiddler-group network consolidated institutional preservation; the annual Riksspelmansträff and Bingsjöstämman fiddle-festivals anchor performance circuit.

items.name: Asturian gaita (Iberian Celtic bagpipe)
items.lineage: Asturian gaita Iberian Celtic-bagpipe tradition of Asturias (northern Spain), the canonical Asturian regional-folk-music instrumental signature. The gaita asturiana is a mouth-blown single-drone bagpipe distinct from the larger Galician gaita gallega and the Scottish Highland pipes in tuning and ornament-vocabulary. Performance: solo gaita or gaita-and-tambor (drum-pair) accompanying voice, dance, or solo instrumental display. Repertoire spans foliada wedding-celebration repertoire, vaqueirada cattle-herder dance-music, and the canonical Asturian-Celtic revival-period compositions of the late-twentieth century. Distinguished from Galician gaita gallega by Asturian-specific tuning and ornamental conventions. The Asturian Cultural Council and the parallel Galician Real Academia de la Gaita anchor institutional preservation.

items.name: Basque bertsolaritza (improvised verse-dueling)
items.lineage: Basque bertsolaritza improvised-verse tradition of the Basque Country (Euskal Herria, northern Spain and southwestern France), in which bertsolari poet-singers improvise extempore verses in the Basque language on assigned topics, often in competitive-dueling exchange. Performance: solo unaccompanied voice in characteristic narrow-range Basque-folk melodic vocabulary, with strict Basque-poetic-meter conventions governing the improvisation. The annual Bertsolari Txapelketa Nagusia (Bertsolari Grand Championship, held every four years) constitutes the central institutional anchor; the Mintzola Foundation (founded 1996) and Xenpelar Dokumentazio Zentroa preserve the institutional archive. Distinguished from other Mediterranean improvised-poetic traditions by Basque-language base and Euskara-specific meter conventions.

items.name: Corsican paghjella modern revival
items.lineage: Corsican paghjella three-voice male polyphonic singing tradition of Corsica (France). Performance: three male singers in close-position polyphonic configuration: a bassu low-register foundational voice, a sicunda middle-register voice, and a terza high-register ornamental voice, all male-only, performing sacred (especially the canonical Mass-of-the-Dead repertoire) and secular repertoire. The genre nearly disappeared by the mid-twentieth century but was revived through the 1970s riacquistu Corsican-cultural-revival movement under the canonical group A Filetta. Distinguished from Sardinian cantu a tenore by Corsican paghjella's three-voice-male (vs four-voice-with-guttural-bass) configuration.

items.name: Banda sinaloense
items.lineage: Mexican brass-band tradition of Sinaloa state, derived from late-nineteenth-century German-immigrant military-band tradition adapted to Mexican-rural-popular celebration-music. Large ensemble of clarinets, trumpets, trombones, sousaphone, tambora, tarola, voice — entirely brass-and-percussion. Repertoire spans ranchera, corrido, cumbia. Banda El Recodo (founded 1938) anchors the canonical sound.

items.name: Norteño (northern Mexican)
items.lineage: Northern-Mexican popular-music of border states (Tamaulipas, Nuevo León, Coahuila, Chihuahua), accordion-and-bajo-sexto-led with bass-drum-kit. Origin in late-nineteenth-century German-Czech-Polish-immigrant accordion music synthesized with Mexican forms. Repertoire: corrido, ranchera, polka, cumbia. Falcon Records (McAllen, 1948 onward) anchored commercial circulation.

items.name: Sonidero (Mexican cumbia sound-system)
items.lineage: Mexican cumbia DJ-and-sound-system tradition of Mexico City and northern-Mexican border-cities, emerging 1960s-1970s. The sonidero plays cumbia records on large mobile sound-systems at outdoor street-parties, interspersed with extempore MC-shoutouts dedicated to attendees by name and Mexican-immigrant family members in the US. Slowed-down cumbia rebajada emerged through accidental incorrect-speed playback.

items.name: Cumbia rebajada (Monterrey slowed)
items.lineage: Slowed-down Mexican cumbia variant emerging accidentally in Monterrey 1980s-1990s when sonidero DJs played records at slower speed, producing characteristically lowered-pitch hypnotic-droning. Deliberate cultural practice followed, with sound-systems and bedroom-producers crafting deliberately slowed versions. Intersected with 2010s "tribal guarachero" Monterrey electronic-cumbia.

items.name: Son huasteco (Huasteca trio)
items.lineage: Regional Mexican son tradition of the Huasteca cultural region (Veracruz, Hidalgo, San Luis Potosí, Tamaulipas, Querétaro). Trio of huapanguero violin (with high-falsetto vocal ornament and improvisatory melodic-doubling), quinta huapanguera five-string acoustic-bass-guitar, and jarana huasteca five-string rhythm-guitar. Alternating violin-improvisation and falsetto-vocal-improvisation sections define the canonical huapango.

items.name: Son istmeño (Oaxaca Isthmus)
items.lineage: Regional Mexican son tradition of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec (southeastern Oaxaca), the Zapotec-cultural-region southern-Mexican-Pacific lowland. Zapotec-language vocal repertoire alongside Spanish, characteristic 6/8 alternating-with-3/4, and Tehuana-feminine cultural register. Marimba ensemble (parallel to but distinct from Guatemalan Maya marimba), acoustic-guitar, voice. La Sandunga (Andrés Gutiérrez 1853) is the unofficial Zapotec anthem.

items.name: Trío romántico (Mexican bolero trio)
items.lineage: Mexican trío romántico bolero-trio tradition emerging in 1930s-1940s Mexico City. Three-male-voice harmonized chorus with two acoustic guitars and one requinto (smaller higher-tuned lead guitar). Trio Los Panchos (founded 1944, New York) crystallized the form, established the requinto-lead-with-three-voice-harmony as canonical, and exported the genre internationally throughout Latin America.

items.name: Bolero mexicano
items.lineage: Mexican adaptation of the broader Latin-American bolero, developed in mid-twentieth-century Mexico City through Agustín Lara (born 1897) and the 1940s-1950s Mexican-cinema golden-age. Solo voice with piano-or-trio accompaniment, slow 2/4 meter with the canonical bolero rhythmic figure, intensely romantic-melancholic register. Distinguished from Cuban bolero by Mexican-Spanish lyrical register and elaborate harmonic-vocabulary.

items.name: Trova cubana
items.lineage: Cuban troubadour-song tradition emerging in late-nineteenth-century Santiago de Cuba and Havana from synthesis of Spanish romance ballad with Cuban son and bolero. Solo voice or duo with one or two acoustic guitars, intimate-confessional register. Trova tradicional (1890s-1920s, Sindo Garay, Manuel Corona) crystallized the genre; nueva trova (post-1968, Silvio Rodríguez, Pablo Milanés) integrated revolutionary-political content.

items.name: Filin (Cuban jazz-trova)
items.lineage: Cuban jazz-influenced song genre developed in late-1940s-early-1950s Havana. Young composer-performers (José Antonio Méndez, Cesar Portillo de la Luz, Frank Domínguez, Marta Valdés, Frank Emilio Flynn) integrated American-jazz extended-chord harmony, blue-note vocabulary, and intimate-confessional vocal-style with the older trova canon. Havana nightclub and bohemian-cafe contexts.

items.name: Descarga (Cuban jam session)
items.lineage: Cuban improvisational ensemble-form developed in 1950s Havana through after-hours jam sessions at Tropicana, Sans Souci, Habana Hilton hotel-clubs. Combines son montuno rhythmic framework with jazz-improvisational solos over canonical guajeo ostinato. Cachao y Su Ritmo Caliente sessions (1957, Israel "Cachao" López) are the foundational recorded document. Post-1960 exile to Miami and New York extended into broader Latin-jazz.

items.name: Songo (Cuban 1970s fusion)
items.lineage: Cuban dance-music developed in 1970s-1980s Havana by Los Van Van under Juan Formell, synthesizing son montuno, changüí, North American funk, and Cuban folkloric rumba. Introduced drum-kit alongside canonical timbales and congas, electric-bass with funk-derived ostinato, extended sectional structures. Directly informed subsequent 1990s timba emergence.

items.name: Salsa dura (hard 70s NY salsa)
items.lineage: Aggressive virtuoso style of New York salsa developed in 1970s through Fania All-Stars and broader Fania Records roster. Intense rhythmic-and-instrumental projection, virtuoso solo improvisations, extended compositional structures, politically-conscious socially-realist lyric content addressing immigration, poverty, Latin-American social-justice. Fania Records (1964, Johnny Pacheco, Jerry Masucci) constitutes the institutional anchor.

items.name: Salsa romántica (80s romantic)
items.lineage: Softer-romantic style of salsa developed in mid-1980s Miami and New York from older salsa dura. Reduced rhythmic-aggression, simpler arrangements, slower-mid-tempo, explicit romantic-love-and-relationship lyric content. Emerged through Latin-Caribbean commercial-radio-targeting and became dominant late-1980s-and-1990s salsa-mainstream. RMM Records and producer Sergio George consolidated canonical sound.

items.name: Salsa colombiana (Cali)
items.lineage: Colombian regional variant of salsa centered in Cali (Valle del Cauca, southwestern Colombia, "world capital of salsa"). Distinguished from New York and Puerto Rican salsa by faster-tempo, more aggressive-rhythmic-pulse, and the Cali dance-school choreographic culture emphasizing fast complex footwork. Grupo Niche (1980, Jairo Varela) and Orquesta Guayacán anchor canonical Cali sound.

items.name: Merengue urbano
items.lineage: Electronic-and-rap-influenced Dominican merengue variant emerging in 1990s-2000s. Synthesis of traditional merengue rhythmic pulse with hip-hop production and reggaeton harmonic-rhythmic vocabulary. Drum-machine-and-sampler production, faster 2/4 tempo than traditional merengue, simpler chord-progressions, explicit MC-rapped vocal sections alongside sung verse-and-chorus. Omega "El Fuerte" and El Cata anchored the 2000s commercial sound.

items.name: Merengue típico (Cibao traditional)
items.lineage: Traditional Dominican merengue variant of the Cibao region (Santiago, La Vega, Moca, San Francisco de Macorís). Button-accordion (German-immigrant introduction, adopted as canonical), tambora double-headed drum, güira metal-scraper, marímbula or electric-bass, voice. Tatico Henríquez (1944-1976) is the canonical tipico accordionist; Fefita La Grande (born 1943) is the canonical female lead.

items.name: Chutney (Indo-Caribbean)
items.lineage: Indo-Caribbean Trinidadian-and-Guyanese popular-music developed in late-twentieth-century Trinidad from synthesis of Bhojpuri-Hindi folk-song of the post-indenture Indian-laborer community with Trinidadian calypso-and-soca. Voice (often female), dholak, dhantal, tassa, electric-instruments. Sundar Popo's 1968 "Nana and Nani" is the canonical foundational chutney recording.

items.name: Twoubadou (Haitian troubadour)
items.lineage: Haitian rural-and-popular acoustic-song tradition emerging in early-twentieth-century Haiti from synthesis of Cuban son and bolero, Dominican merengue tipico, and Haitian rural folk-song. Acoustic-guitar, marímbula, mandolin, accordion, manouba scraper, voice. Working-class counterpart to elite-class urban kompa direct big-band tradition. Post-1980 acoustic-revival under Ti Coca, Manno Charlemagne, Beethova Obas.

items.name: Rasin (Haitian roots-Vodou rock)
items.lineage: Haitian rock-and-Vodou-fusion genre developed in late-1970s-1980s Haiti. Fusion of Haitian Vodou ceremonial-drumming-and-singing with rock-and-roots-music aesthetic. Emerged through Boukman Eksperyans (founded 1978 in Port-au-Prince by Theodore "Lolo" Beaubrun) and parallel groups Boukan Ginen, Sanba Yo, Rara Machine. Electric guitars-bass-drum-kit alongside Vodou-ceremonial percussion. The 1990 Vodou Adjae album consolidated international visibility.

items.name: Garifuna punta-rock (Belize/Honduras modern)
items.lineage: Modern-popular variant of older Garifuna punta dance-tradition, developed in 1970s-1980s Belize and Honduras. Pen Cayetano (born 1954, Dangriga) developed the punta-rock sound in mid-1970s; Andy Palacio (born 1960) extended internationally through his 2007 Wátina album (Stonetree Records). Electric instruments alongside Garifuna traditional drums (primero, segunda, tercero) and shaker.

items.name: Aguinaldo (Puerto Rican Christmas)
items.lineage: Puerto Rican Christmas-and-Three-Kings-Day song tradition performed during canonical Christmas season at parrandas door-to-door musical-visits. Cuatro puerto-rico (ten-string-paired Puerto Rican lute), acoustic-guitar, güiro scraper, percussion, voice. Repertoire spans religious-devotional Christmas content, picaresque parranda material, and patriotic-cultural Puerto-Rican content. Décima ten-line stanza characteristic of jíbaro music.

items.name: Chamamé
items.lineage: Folk-popular music of Argentine Mesopotamia region (Corrientes, Misiones, Entre Ríos, Formosa, Chaco) and adjacent eastern Paraguay. Synthesis of indigenous Guaraní vocal-melodic conventions, German-immigrant accordion-tradition, and Spanish-colonial folk-music inheritance. Voice with button-accordion, acoustic-guitar, contrabass. Lyrics draw on Guaraní and Castilian-Spanish, often bilingual.

items.name: Chacarera (Argentine northwest)
items.lineage: Argentine folk-dance-and-song tradition of northwestern provinces (Santiago del Estero, Tucumán, Salta, La Rioja). Characteristic 6/8 meter, fast-tempo paired-couple dance with handkerchiefs, lyrical content addressing rural-northwestern Argentine life. Voice with acoustic-guitar and bombo legüero large-frame-drum. Atahualpa Yupanqui and Los Hermanos Ábalos (founded 1932) consolidated canonical repertoire.

items.name: Zamba (Argentine slow-romantic)
items.lineage: Argentine slow-romantic folk-dance-and-song tradition of northwestern provinces, derived from Peruvian zamacueca (which also derived Chilean cueca and Andean tondero). Slow 6/8 meter, melancholic register addressing romance, loss, and northwestern-Argentine pampas-mountain landscape. Mid-twentieth-century commercial-folklore revival under Yupanqui, Cuchi Leguizamón, Mercedes Sosa consolidated canonical zamba repertoire.

items.name: Cueca (Chilean national)
items.lineage: Chilean national folk-dance-and-song tradition derived from broader Peruvian-Spanish zamacueca lineage, codified in mid-nineteenth-century Chile (formally declared national dance 1979). Characteristic 6/8 meter alternating with 3/4 polymeter, fast tempo with paired-couple handkerchief-and-stomping choreography. Post-1973 dictatorship period featured the dissident "cueca sola" performed solo by widows of disappeared persons.

items.name: Festejo (Afro-Peruvian celebration)
items.lineage: Afro-Peruvian folk-popular dance-and-song tradition of coastal Peru (Lima, Chincha, El Carmen, Ica regions), descended from West-African-enslaved-population cultural memory through colonial-Peruvian slavery period. Fast 6/8 meter, virtuoso cajón lead, quijada jawbone-rattle, acoustic-guitar. Nicomedes Santa Cruz (1925-1992) and Victoria Santa Cruz (1922-2014) consolidated twentieth-century cultural revival. Susana Baca, Eva Ayllón anchor contemporary scene.

items.name: Landó (Afro-Peruvian slow groove)
items.lineage: Afro-Peruvian slow-tempo groove-based form characterized by slow 12/8 with strong off-beat accent and characteristic syncopated cajón pattern. Distinguished from festejo by landó's slower-meditative-melancholic register. Addresses melancholy-romance, the experience of enslavement and its memory (canonical "María Landó" by Chabuca Granda with poetry of César Calvo, recorded by Susana Baca).

items.name: Currulao (Colombian Pacific)
items.lineage: Afro-Colombian marimba-and-percussion ensemble tradition of Pacific coastal region (Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Cauca, Nariño departments) and adjacent Ecuadorian Pacific coast. Marimba de chonta (wooden marimba with bamboo resonators), bombo and cununo drums, guasá tubular shakers, voice (often female-lead with chorus).

items.name: Champeta (Cartagena Afro-Colombian)
items.lineage: Afro-Colombian dance-music genre of Cartagena and the Colombian Caribbean coast, emerging in 1980s from synthesis of African soukous, juju, and highlife (transmitted through cassette-and-vinyl trade with Africa via maritime sailors) with local Colombian Caribbean costeño rhythmic-vocabulary. Performed at picós large mobile sound-systems in working-class barrios. Distinguished from cumbia by champeta's African-pop-derived (vs cumbia's indigenous-Afro-Spanish-syncretic) lineage.

items.name: Sertanejo universitário (Brazilian pop-country)
items.lineage: Brazilian sertanejo subgenre emerging in late-2000s as a urban-modern revival of the older sertanejo country-music tradition, targeted at younger university-student audiences. Characterized by pop-country-influenced harmonic vocabulary, slower mid-tempo love-ballad register, and twin-male-vocal-harmony presentation. Goiânia, Brasília, and São Paulo studios anchored the canonical sound. Michel Teló's 2011 "Ai Se Eu Te Pego" became the international-crossover hit.

items.name: Forró pé-de-serra (traditional forró)
items.lineage: Traditional Brazilian forró sub-form preserving the canonical Luiz Gonzaga-era 1940s-1960s northeastern Brazilian dance-music form. Trio configuration: sanfona button-accordion lead, zabumba double-headed bass-drum, triangle, plus voice. Distinguished from later forró eletrônico and forró universitário by pé-de-serra's acoustic-trio (vs full-band-electronic) instrumental signature. Repertoire centers on Luiz Gonzaga's canonical compositional corpus and parallel northeastern forró composers.

items.name: Brega and tecnobrega (Belém-Pará)
items.lineage: Brega and tecnobrega Brazilian popular-music genres of the northern Brazilian Amazonian Pará state (especially Belém). Brega ("kitsch") originated as a mid-late-twentieth-century commercial sentimental-popular music; tecnobrega is its 2000s-onward electronic-DIY remix-and-production reformulation, with characteristic synthesizer-and-808-drum-machine production, fast tempo, and an outdoor-aparelhagem sound-system street-party performance context. Distinguished from sertanejo by brega's northern-Amazonian-Brazilian regional base.

items.name: Pisadinha and arrocha (northeastern romantic)
items.lineage: Brazilian arrocha and pisadinha contemporary northeastern-Brazilian romantic-popular music genres. Arrocha (Bahian, 1990s-2000s) is a slow-tempo romantic ballad with Brazilian-pop-influenced harmonic-vocabulary. Pisadinha (Pernambuco/Bahia, 2010s-2020s) is the faster-tempo dance-derivative incorporating electronic-production. Both share the working-class northeastern-Brazilian cultural orientation distinct from sertanejo universitário's middle-class-university-targeting.

items.name: Repente and embolada (NE Brazilian improvised)
items.lineage: Brazilian repente and embolada improvised-poetic-dueling traditions of the northeastern Brazilian sertão (Pernambuco, Paraíba, Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte states). Repente is the canonical extended-improvised-verse form of cantadores (poet-singers) performing in pairs, often using rabeca (Northeastern fiddle) or viola (Brazilian ten-string lute) accompaniment. Embolada is the faster-tempo subform with characteristic mocking-and-humorous-couplet improvisation, typically over a pandeiro frame-drum beat.

items.name: Lambada and carimbó (Amazonian Pará)
items.lineage: Brazilian carimbó traditional Afro-Pará dance-music of the Amazonian Pará state, descended from West-African enslaved-population cultural memory. Lambada is the 1980s commercial-pop derivative of carimbó that achieved international fame through Kaoma's 1989 hit "Chorando se Foi" and the Brazilian Lambada dance-craze. Distinguished from broader Brazilian samba-and-forró by carimbó's Amazonian-Pará regional base and characteristic ass-jiggling tribal-rhythmic-pulse.

items.name: Coco brasileiro (NE Brazilian work-song)
items.lineage: Brazilian coco northeastern-Brazilian song-and-dance tradition of Pernambuco, Paraíba, and Alagoas, descended from the African-Brazilian colonial-period rural-work-song tradition (coco was originally a coconut-husking work-song with stamping-rhythm accompaniment). Performance: lead singer with chorus response, hand-clapping or ganzá-shaker rhythm, occasional pandeiro frame-drum. Repertoire spans rural-worker thematic content, coastal-fishing themes, and romantic-couplet improvisation. Genre revival under Nação Zumbi and Chico Science in 1990s integrated coco with rock-and-electronic-production.

items.name: Jongo (Afro-Brazilian Vale do Paraíba)
items.lineage: Afro-Brazilian jongo song-and-dance tradition of the Vale do Paraíba region (between São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro), descended from the Bantu-speaking enslaved population brought to the colonial-period coffee plantations. Performance: large frame-drum tambu and smaller candongueiro drum-pair, with male lead-singer-improvisor exchanging encoded ponto verses with the dancers in the surrounding circle. The encoded jongo language uses metaphorical references and indirection (originally as resistance-code under slavery).

items.name: Quechua wayno modern revival
items.lineage: Twentieth-and-twenty-first-century revival of the Quechua wayno Andean folk-music form, integrating electric-band-instruments and contemporary-pop production with the canonical Quechua-language vocal repertoire and Andean instrumental signature. Wayno chichero subgenre (1980s onward) introduced cumbia-influenced rhythmic vocabulary. The 1990s-2000s wayno-rock movement under Pelo Madueño, Tongo, and various Cusco-Lima fusion groups extended into rock-Andean-fusion contexts.

items.name: Maya marimba (Guatemalan Highlands)
items.lineage: Guatemalan Highlands Maya marimba tradition (Quetzaltenango, Sololá, Huehuetenango departments) and adjacent Chiapas, featuring large wooden-resonator marimba ensembles played by three-to-four marimberos simultaneously (marimba doble or marimba grande). Instrument arrived through West-African enslaved-population introduction and was adopted as Guatemalan-cultural-marker. Repertoire spans son chapín nineteenth-and-twentieth-century Guatemalan national-popular forms, religious cofradía music, and contemporary dance-band material.

items.name: Classical period (1750-1820)
items.lineage: European art-music period c.1750-1820 centered on Vienna, codifying balanced sonata-form, periodic-phrase symmetry, and the Classical orchestra (strings, paired woodwinds and brass, timpani). The Haydn-Mozart-Beethoven trinity established the canonical symphony, string quartet, sonata, and piano concerto repertoires. Distinguished from preceding Baroque by Classical period's homophonic textures, clear cadential punctuation, and dramatic-rhetorical phrase structure.

items.name: Early Romantic (1800-1850)
items.lineage: European art-music period c.1800-1850 emerging from late Beethoven through the first generation of explicitly Romantic composers. Characterized by expanded chromatic harmony, programmatic narrative content, virtuoso performer-composer figures, and the lieder cycle as song-form. Schubert's 600+ songs, Schumann's piano-cycles, Chopin's piano-études-and-nocturnes, and Mendelssohn's symphonies constitute the canonical core.

items.name: Late Romantic (1850-1910)
items.lineage: European art-music period c.1850-1910 expanding the Romantic vocabulary into extreme chromaticism (Wagner), massive orchestral forces (Mahler, Strauss, Bruckner), nationalist-folk integration (Dvořák, Smetana, Borodin), and the gradual approach to tonal dissolution. Wagner's Tristan chord (1859) is often cited as the precipitating moment of tonal crisis. The German-Austrian symphonic tradition reached its maximum extent with Mahler's 1000-performer Eighth Symphony (1910).

items.name: The Mighty Handful (Russian nationalist five)
items.lineage: Nineteenth-century Russian nationalist-composer collective in Saint Petersburg (Mily Balakirev, César Cui, Modest Mussorgsky, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov, Alexander Borodin), articulating a distinct Russian art-music identity through folk-melodic integration, modal-and-pentatonic vocabulary, programmatic-nationalist narrative content, and characteristic Russian-orchestration-color techniques. Mussorgsky's Boris Godunov (1869, revised 1872) and Pictures at an Exhibition (1874) constitute the canonical type-specimens. Direct precursor to Stravinsky's pre-1914 ballet trilogy.

items.name: Les Six (French interwar)
items.lineage: French interwar composer-collective (Georges Auric, Louis Durey, Arthur Honegger, Darius Milhaud, Francis Poulenc, Germaine Tailleferre) named in 1920 by critic Henri Collet by analogy with the Russian Mighty Five. Aesthetic of Cocteau-inspired anti-Romantic clarity, accessible-melodic neoclassicism, jazz-and-popular-music integration, and Parisian cafe-and-music-hall aesthetic. Erik Satie served as elder-mentor figure. The 1921 Les Mariés de la tour Eiffel ballet (collective composition) is the canonical group-document.

items.name: Second Viennese School (atonal serialism)
items.lineage: Twentieth-century Viennese composer-circle around Arnold Schoenberg and his students Anton Webern and Alban Berg, developing free-atonal compositional practice (c.1908-1923) followed by the twelve-tone-method serial-organization (1923 onward). Pierrot Lunaire (1912), Wozzeck (1925), and Webern's aphoristic late-period works constitute the canonical core. Distinguished from prior tonal-harmonic practice by complete suspension of triadic-tonal-hierarchy and systematic serial-row organization of pitch content.

items.name: Neoclassicism (interwar tonal-return movement)
items.lineage: Interwar compositional movement (c.1920-1950) characterized by return to clear textures, balanced forms, and reference to pre-Romantic models (Bach, Haydn, Stravinsky himself looking back to his Russian-folk past), combined with extended chromatic and rhythmic vocabulary. Stravinsky's Pulcinella (1920), Octet (1923), and Symphony of Psalms (1930) are the canonical type-specimens. Distinguished from Romantic by neoclassicism's anti-emotional-excess aesthetic and from Second Viennese serialism by retention of tonal-modal centers.

items.name: Darmstadt School (total serialism)
items.lineage: Post-war European avant-garde composer movement centered on the Internationale Ferienkurse für Neue Musik in Darmstadt (founded 1946), extending Webern's serial-row organization to all musical parameters (pitch, rhythm, dynamics, articulation, register) — "total serialism" or "integral serialism." Boulez's Structures Ia (1952), Stockhausen's Kreuzspiel (1951), and Nono's Il canto sospeso (1956) constitute the canonical type-specimens. The Darmstadt School defined the European-modernist mainstream of 1950s-1960s.

items.name: Polish avant-garde / sonorism
items.lineage: Polish post-war avant-garde compositional school of late-1950s through 1970s, distinct from Darmstadt total-serialism by emphasis on sound-texture, instrumental sonority, and dramatic-expressive content. Lutosławski's controlled-aleatoric texture, Penderecki's Threnody for the Victims of Hiroshima (1960) cluster-and-glissando textures, and Górecki's symphony-of-sorrowful-songs slow-spiritual register constitute three distinct stylistic strands within Polish sonorism.

items.name: Holy Minimalism (late 20th-century spiritual minimalism)
items.lineage: Late-twentieth-century compositional movement centered on Estonian Arvo Pärt, English John Tavener, and late-Polish Henryk Górecki, characterized by slow tempi, modal-and-triadic harmonic vocabulary, sacred-or-spiritual textual content (often Orthodox Christian liturgical), and minimal compositional means. Pärt's tintinnabuli style (developed 1976 onward in Spiegel im Spiegel, Cantus, and Tabula Rasa) and Tavener's The Protecting Veil (1989) constitute the canonical type-specimens.

items.name: American minimalism (1960s-1970s NYC and California)
items.lineage: American mid-twentieth-century compositional movement emerging in 1960s-1970s New York and California through La Monte Young, Terry Riley, Steve Reich, and Philip Glass. Characterized by repetitive-cellular structures, gradual-process-of-change compositional approach, modal-or-tonal harmonic vocabulary, and steady pulse. Riley's In C (1964), Reich's Drumming (1971), and Glass's Einstein on the Beach (1976) constitute the canonical type-specimens. Direct precursor to broader post-minimal compositional practice.

items.name: Spectralism (1970s-1980s French)
items.lineage: French compositional movement emerging in mid-1970s Paris through the Itinéraire ensemble (founded 1973 by Gérard Grisey, Tristan Murail, Michaël Levinas, and Roger Tessier), generating compositional material from the harmonic-spectrum analysis of acoustic sounds. Grisey's Les Espaces Acoustiques cycle (1974-1985) and Murail's Désintégrations (1982-83) constitute the canonical type-specimens. Distinguished from total serialism by spectralism's acoustic-physical (vs combinatorial-mathematical) compositional logic.

items.name: New Complexity (1970s-1980s British post-serial maximalism)
items.lineage: British-and-international compositional school emerging in 1970s-80s centered on Brian Ferneyhough's notational-and-technical maximalism, with extremely complex rhythmic-and-articulation specification often exceeding what performers can literally execute. Distinguished from Darmstadt total-serialism by New Complexity's expressionist-and-virtuoso (rather than rationally-structural) orientation. Ferneyhough's Time and Motion Studies (1973-77) and his Carceri d'Invenzione cycle (1981-86) constitute the canonical type-specimens.

items.name: Microtonal composition (twentieth-century non-12-TET)
items.lineage: American twentieth-century compositional movement systematically employing tunings outside twelve-tone-equal-temperament. Harry Partch (1901-1974) developed his 43-tone just-intonation system and built custom instruments (Cloud-Chamber Bowls, Marimba Eroica, Diamond Marimba) to realize it; Ben Johnston (1926-2019) extended just-intonation into traditional Western chamber-music; Pauline Oliveros, James Tenney, and La Monte Young extended into electronic-and-drone microtonality.

items.name: Acousmatic music (Schaeffer school post-musique-concrète)
items.lineage: French electroacoustic-composition tradition descended from Pierre Schaeffer's 1948-onward musique concrète at Studio d'Essai / GRM (Groupe de Recherches Musicales). Acousmatic refers to music heard from loudspeakers without seeing the source, organized through reduced-listening principles. The post-Schaeffer second generation (François Bayle, Bernard Parmegiani, Luc Ferrari, Beatriz Ferreyra) developed the form into a distinct compositional aesthetic.

items.name: Soundscape composition (Vancouver-school environmental)
items.lineage: Canadian-and-international compositional approach emerging in 1970s through R. Murray Schafer's World Soundscape Project at Simon Fraser University. Compositions integrate field-recorded environmental and ecological sounds with electroacoustic transformation, addressing acoustic-ecology and the listener's sonic-environmental awareness. Hildegard Westerkamp's Kits Beach Soundwalk (1989) and Schafer's Vancouver Soundscape (1973) constitute the canonical type-specimens.

items.name: Indeterminacy and aleatoric (mid-20th-century chance composition)
items.lineage: American twentieth-century compositional approach centered on John Cage (1912-1992) employing chance procedures (I Ching coin-tossing, star-charts, environmental noise) to determine compositional material, removing the composer's expressive intentionality. Music of Changes (1951), 4'33" (1952), Imaginary Landscape No. 4 (1951 for twelve radios), and the Number Pieces (1987-92) constitute the canonical types. Influenced subsequent Fluxus intermedia, conceptual composition, and improvisation traditions.

items.name: Fluxus intermedia composition
items.lineage: International intermedia-art movement (1962-1978 active period, lingering influences thereafter) founded by George Maciunas, including composer-artists George Brecht, La Monte Young, Yoko Ono, Nam June Paik, and Alison Knowles. Compositional output centered on event-scores (brief text-instructions for actions), conceptual-musical-performance, and the deliberate dissolution of boundaries between music, theatre, visual art, and life-art. Brecht's Drip Music (1959) and Young's Compositions 1960 series constitute the canonical type-specimens.

items.name: Ars antiqua and organum (medieval Paris)
items.lineage: Late-twelfth-and-thirteenth-century European art-music style centered on the Notre Dame Cathedral school of Paris under Léonin (Leoninus, fl. 1150s-1180s) and Pérotin (Perotinus, fl. 1190s-1220s). Codified rhythmic-modal notation, organum (two-, three-, and four-voice polyphony built on plainchant tenors), and clausula and motet forms. Compiled in the Magnus Liber Organi attributed to Léonin and revised by Pérotin. Distinguished from preceding plainchant by ars antiqua's systematic polyphonic-organization.

items.name: Ars Nova (fourteenth-century French)
items.lineage: Fourteenth-century French compositional style codified in Philippe de Vitry's 1322 treatise of the same name, introducing isorhythmic motet construction, mensural rhythmic notation, and increased rhythmic-and-harmonic complexity. Guillaume de Machaut (c.1300-1377) is the principal composer; his Messe de Nostre Dame (c.1365) is the first known complete polyphonic setting of the Mass Ordinary by a single composer. Distinguished from ars antiqua by ars nova's sophisticated rhythmic-isorhythmic and notational developments.

items.name: Burgundian School (early fifteenth century)
items.lineage: Mid-fifteenth-century compositional school centered on the courts of the Dukes of Burgundy (Philip the Good, Charles the Bold) at Dijon and Brussels. Guillaume Dufay (c.1397-1474) and Gilles Binchois (c.1400-1460) are the principal composers. Developed the Mass cycle (cyclic Mass based on a single cantus firmus), the rondeau and ballade chanson forms, and the smoother-consonant fauxbourdon harmonic style. Direct precursor of the Franco-Flemish polyphonic school.

items.name: Ambrosian chant (Milan rite)
items.lineage: Liturgical chant of the Ambrosian rite of Milan, attributed in legend to Saint Ambrose (Bishop of Milan 374-397), preserved in continuous use in the Archdiocese of Milan and adjacent dioceses of Lombardy (Italy) and Lugano (Switzerland). Distinguished from Gregorian chant by Ambrosian's distinct repertoire (with different proper-of-the-mass texts and melodic content), the eight Ambrosian modes (related to but distinct from Gregorian modes), and Milanese-specific liturgical structure. Survived medieval-and-Tridentine liturgical reforms as one of only two surviving Latin liturgical-music-traditions.

items.name: Mozarabic chant (Hispanic rite)
items.lineage: Iberian liturgical chant tradition of the pre-Roman-rite-imposition Hispanic Christian church, in continuous use in parts of Spain from late-antiquity through eleventh-century Roman-rite imposition. Survived after the eleventh-century replacement in restricted use at the Corpus Christi Chapel of Toledo Cathedral (where six Mozarabic chaplaincies were maintained) and the parish of Saints Justa and Rufina in Toledo. The post-Vatican-II 1988 Liber Antiphonarius Officii Mozarabici codified the modern recension. Distinguished from Gregorian by Mozarabic's distinct neume-notation system and Visigothic-Hispanic liturgical structure.

items.name: Sarum chant (English medieval rite)
items.lineage: Medieval English liturgical chant tradition of the Sarum rite (Use of Salisbury), the dominant English liturgical-use from the eleventh century through the 1549 Reformation imposition of the Book of Common Prayer. Distinguished from broader Roman-rite Gregorian repertoire by Sarum-specific propers, sequences (the canonical Salve mater misericordie Marian sequence), and the elaborate Procession-and-Station liturgical-choreography. Modern liturgical reconstruction by the Cambridge Sarum Group and Anglican-and-Anglo-Catholic communities in England.

items.name: Beneventan chant (southern Italian)
items.lineage: Pre-Gregorian liturgical chant tradition of Benevento and southern Italian Lombard-Beneventan duchies (sixth-thirteenth centuries), preserved fragmentarily in Beneventan-script manuscripts of the Benevento Cathedral Library and Montecassino Abbey. Replaced by Roman-rite Gregorian chant after eleventh-century imposition, but with significant Beneventan-melodic-material absorbed into the broader Italian Gregorian recension. Distinguished from Gregorian by Beneventan's distinct melodic style, narrower range, characteristic ornamental conventions, and Lombard-script notational tradition.

items.name: Lutheran chorale tradition
items.lineage: German Protestant vernacular hymn tradition emerging from Martin Luther's liturgical reforms (1520s-1540s), in which sturdy German-language hymn-tunes (chorales) became the canonical sung-prayer of the Lutheran congregation. The seventeenth-century four-voice harmonization tradition (codified by Hans Leo Hassler, Michael Praetorius, and later Johann Sebastian Bach in his approximately 400 chorale harmonizations) constitutes the canonical compositional layer. Direct precursor to broader Lutheran cantata-and-passion compositional tradition.

items.name: Methodist hymnody (18th-century English Protestant)
items.lineage: English Protestant hymn tradition codified through the 6,500+ hymn texts of Charles Wesley (1707-1788) and the canonical Methodist hymn-book A Collection of Hymns for the use of the People called Methodists (1780, John Wesley editor). The Methodist tradition emphasizes intensely personal-devotional content (the "warmed heart" theme), strong congregational singing as central liturgical practice, and the use of vernacular-popular-tune adaptations alongside specifically-composed Methodist hymn-tunes. Major influence on the broader English-speaking-world Protestant hymnody.

items.name: Shaker singing (Shaker hymnody)
items.lineage: American Shaker (United Society of Believers in Christ's Second Appearing) song tradition, comprising over 10,000 documented hymns composed by Shaker community members in the eighteenth-and-nineteenth-century Shaker communities of New England, New York, Ohio, and Kentucky. Performance: unison-and-octave congregational singing in characteristic strophic-narrative-or-praise form, often associated with the canonical Shaker "labor" of synchronized-rhythmic-walking-and-clapping worship-practice. The 1848 "Simple Gifts" composed by Joseph Brackett at Alfred, Maine became internationally famous after Aaron Copland's 1944 Appalachian Spring incorporation.

items.name: Mormon Tabernacle Choir tradition
items.lineage: Mormon Tabernacle Choir of the LDS Church (founded 1847 in Salt Lake City, Utah) liturgical-and-concert choral tradition, comprising approximately 360 unpaid volunteer LDS Church-member singers. The choir performs at LDS General Conference biannual sessions and weekly Music & the Spoken Word radio broadcasts (continuous since 1929). Repertoire spans Mormon-specific liturgical hymns from the LDS Hymnbook, broader Christian-Protestant hymn tradition, and twentieth-century American-Western art-music. Distinguished by its 360-voice scale and the Salt Lake Tabernacle Aeolian-Skinner pipe-organ.

items.name: Byzantine psaltic art (modern Greek Orthodox)
items.lineage: Modern Greek-Orthodox Byzantine chant tradition (post-1814 New Method notational reform by the Three Teachers Chrysanthos of Madytos, Gregorios the Protopsaltis, and Chourmouzios the Archivist). Performance: cantor (psaltis) and right-and-left choir (psaltries) alternating in the eight-mode oktoechos canonical liturgical-cycle. Distinguished from broader Byzantine-Orthodox chant by the New Method's simplified notational system and characteristic post-1814 vocal-style. The contemporary Mount Athos monastic tradition and the Athens-Constantinople patriarchal lineages constitute the institutional anchors.

items.name: Renaissance madrigal (Italian, English)
items.lineage: Renaissance secular polyphonic vocal genre developed in sixteenth-century Italy through Jacques Arcadelt, Adrian Willaert, and culminating in Carlo Gesualdo (1566-1613) and Claudio Monteverdi (1567-1643). Set Italian secular poetry in elaborate four-to-six-voice polyphonic textures with characteristic word-painting and increasingly chromatic harmonic vocabulary (especially in Gesualdo). The English madrigal school (Thomas Morley, John Wilbye, Thomas Weelkes) flourished briefly in 1580s-1610s as an Italian-derived English adaptation. Direct precursor to Baroque secular cantata and opera.

items.name: Opera seria (Baroque heroic opera)
items.lineage: Italian-language Baroque opera type focused on serious classical-mythological-and-historical subjects, codified by librettist Pietro Metastasio (1698-1782) whose libretti were set hundreds of times by Baroque composers. Performance configuration: three acts with strict da capo aria-and-recitative alternation, six characters (with castrato voices in the leading male hero roles), and minimal chorus. Handel's Giulio Cesare (1724) and Vivaldi's Orlando furioso (1727) are canonical type-specimens. Distinguished from later opera buffa by opera seria's elevated dramatic register.

items.name: Bel canto opera (early 19th-century Italian)
items.lineage: Early-nineteenth-century Italian operatic style characterized by virtuoso ornamental melodic-line writing, expanded coloratura vocal-technique, and dramatic emotional-vocal-projection. Gioachino Rossini, Vincenzo Bellini, and Gaetano Donizetti are the canonical bel canto composers (1810s-1840s active period). Bellini's Norma (1831), Donizetti's Lucia di Lammermoor (1835), and Rossini's Il barbiere di Siviglia (1816) are canonical type-specimens. Direct ancestor of mid-nineteenth-century Verdi-Wagner operatic maximalism.

items.name: Verismo opera (Italian realism)
items.lineage: Late-nineteenth-and-early-twentieth-century Italian operatic style emerging in 1890s as parallel to broader European-literary Naturalism. Characterized by contemporary working-class settings, violent passionate-realistic dramatic content, and direct-emotional vocal-projection (vs the more elaborate ornamental bel canto register). Pietro Mascagni's Cavalleria rusticana (1890), Ruggero Leoncavallo's Pagliacci (1892), and Giacomo Puccini's mature operas constitute the canonical type-specimens. Distinguished from broader Italian opera by verismo's working-class-realist (vs heroic-historical) dramatic orientation.

items.name: Grand opera (French nineteenth century)
items.lineage: Nineteenth-century French operatic style characterized by five-act structure, large historical-or-mythological subjects, elaborate ballet sequences, and massive choral and orchestral forces. Daniel Auber's La muette de Portici (1828), Giacomo Meyerbeer's Les Huguenots (1836) and Le Prophète (1849), and Hector Berlioz's Les Troyens (1858) are canonical type-specimens. The Paris Opéra and the Palais Garnier (opened 1875) constitute the institutional anchors. Distinguished from Italian opera by grand-opera's spectacular-scale and French-language declamatory recitative vocabulary.

items.name: Zarzuela (Spanish lyric theatre)
items.lineage: Spanish lyric-theatre tradition combining sung-operatic and spoken-dialogue sections, named after the Royal Palacio de la Zarzuela where the early seventeenth-century court entertainments were performed. The modern zarzuela emerged in mid-nineteenth-century Madrid through Francisco Asenjo Barbieri and Federico Chueca; the género chico shorter one-act form developed in 1880s-1900s and crystallized the canonical Madrid-urban-life subject matter. Distinguished from broader European operetta by zarzuela's Spanish-specific musical idioms (jota, habanera, fandango integration) and Madrid-and-regional Spanish settings.

items.name: Canzone napoletana (Neapolitan song)
items.lineage: Neapolitan-language art-popular song tradition, comprising the canonical Naples-and-Campania song-repertoire from the mid-nineteenth-century onward (the genre crystallized around the 1839 Piedigrotta Festival commissioned songs and continuing through the 1890s "golden age" with O sole mio, 1898 by Eduardo di Capua and Giovanni Capurro). The form combines elements of Italian operatic-melodic-vocabulary, Mediterranean folk-traditions, and Neapolitan-dialect literary poetry. Distinguished by canzone napoletana's strict use of the Neapolitan language (a distinct Romance language closely related to but distinct from standard Italian).

items.name: Dixieland (traditional/New Orleans-Chicago)
items.lineage: Earliest documented jazz style (c.1905-1928) emerging from New Orleans through cornet-led front-line (cornet/trumpet, clarinet, trombone) playing collective polyphonic improvisation over banjo/guitar-bass-drums rhythm section. Original Dixieland Jass Band's 1917 Livery Stable Blues was the first commercial jazz recording. Distinguished from later swing era by Dixieland's collective-improvisation (vs solo-feature) ensemble principle and 2/4 march-derived rhythmic pulse.

items.name: Chicago jazz (1920s)
items.lineage: Late-1920s jazz style developed in Chicago by young white musicians influenced by the New Orleans tradition transplanted to Chicago through the 1917 closure of Storyville. Characterized by greater solo-improvisation emphasis (vs Dixieland collective-improvisation), introduction of tenor saxophone, four-beat-to-the-bar rhythm (vs Dixieland's two-beat), and harder-edged "Chicago bite" articulation. The Austin High Gang (Bud Freeman, Frank Teschemacher, Jimmy McPartland) is the canonical Chicago school.

items.name: Swing big band (1930s-40s)
items.lineage: 1930s-1940s American jazz orchestra format with sectional brass-and-reed arrangement, 14-18 musicians, and dance-band repertoire emphasis. The Swing Era dominated American popular music c.1935-1945, with Benny Goodman, Count Basie, Duke Ellington, Glenn Miller, Tommy Dorsey, and Artie Shaw orchestras as canonical bandleaders. Distinguished from earlier hot-jazz by swing big band's formal-arranged composition (vs improvisational-collective) framework and dance-floor commercial-orientation.

items.name: Cool jazz / West Coast (1950s)
items.lineage: Late-1940s-1950s jazz substyle emerging in response to bebop's frenetic energy, characterized by lighter timbral palette, restrained dynamic register, and arrangement-heavy compositional approach. Miles Davis's Birth of the Cool sessions (1949-1950) established the canonical sound; the West Coast cool subgenre developed in 1950s Los Angeles through Gerry Mulligan, Chet Baker, Lennie Niehaus, Shorty Rogers, and Dave Brubeck. Distinguished from bebop by cool's slower-and-more-relaxed (vs frenetic) emotional register.

items.name: Smooth jazz (1980s commercial)
items.lineage: 1980s-onward commercial jazz format characterized by polished pop-production, mid-tempo grooves, melodic-rather-than-improvisational soloing, and radio-friendly song-form structures. Emerged from late-1970s jazz-fusion through Grover Washington Jr., George Benson, and Kenny G's consistent commercial success. Distinguished from broader jazz by smooth jazz's explicit commercial-radio-targeting and reduced improvisational-emphasis.

items.name: Acid jazz (UK 1990s)
items.lineage: UK-originated 1980s-1990s dance-club jazz fusion style integrating hard-bop and soul-jazz influences with dance-club rhythmic-foundation, hip-hop production-elements, and electronic-instrumentation. Acid Jazz Records (founded 1987 by Eddie Piller and Gilles Peterson) consolidated the canonical sound; Galliano, Brand New Heavies, Jamiroquai, Incognito, and James Taylor Quartet anchored the recording roster. Distinguished from broader 1980s-jazz-fusion by acid jazz's dance-club orientation and UK-cultural context.

items.name: Nu jazz / electro-jazz
items.lineage: 2000s jazz substyle integrating electronic-production techniques, sample-and-loop-based composition, and broader club-music-influenced rhythmic vocabulary with jazz harmonic-melodic content. Norwegian Jaga Jazzist, German Jazzanova, and Swedish Esbjörn Svensson Trio anchored the European canonical sound; American counterparts including The Bad Plus and Robert Glasper extended the style into American jazz mainstream.

items.name: M-Base collective (late-1980s Brooklyn-based jazz-avant-garde)
items.lineage: Late-1980s-and-onward jazz-avant-garde collective centered on alto saxophonist Steve Coleman (born 1956), pursuing a "Macro-Basic Array of Structured Extemporizations" compositional methodology integrating Yoruba metaphysical concepts, mathematical-rhythmic structures, and African diasporic musical-cultural inheritance. Cassandra Wilson's early-career M-Base recordings, Greg Osby's solo work, and Coleman's Five Elements and Council of Balance ensembles constitute the canonical core.

items.name: Third stream (jazz-classical fusion)
items.lineage: Mid-twentieth-century compositional movement (term coined 1957 by Gunther Schuller) explicitly synthesizing classical-art-music compositional procedures with jazz-improvisational practice. Schuller's own compositions, John Lewis's Modern Jazz Quartet recordings (especially with Gunther Schuller orchestrations), and the broader 1957-1972 Lenox School of Jazz workshop activity constitute the canonical core.

items.name: Klezmer-jazz fusion
items.lineage: 1980s-and-onward American-Jewish jazz-fusion style integrating klezmer modal-and-melodic vocabulary with jazz-improvisational practice. Don Byron's Plays the Music of Mickey Katz (1993) and the Klezmatics 1980s-onward recordings constitute the canonical type-specimens; the parallel Frank London-led ensembles and David Krakauer's solo work extended the genre. Distinguished from broader klezmer revival by jazz-fusion's explicit jazz-improvisation-and-harmonic emphasis.

items.name: Punk jazz / no-wave jazz
items.lineage: Late-1970s-1980s convergence of free-jazz improvisational practice with punk-rock-and-no-wave aesthetic, emerging from the New York Downtown scene. James Chance and the Contortions, James Blood Ulmer (with his harmolodic system), and the Lounge Lizards constituted the canonical core; the Knitting Factory NYC venue (founded 1987) anchored the institutional infrastructure for subsequent jazz-and-experimental development.

items.name: Mod (1960s British)
items.lineage: Early-1960s British youth-subculture and associated music style centered on sharp-suited working-class London-and-southern-English youth, characterized by integration of American R&B, soul, and Jamaican ska influences. The Who's My Generation (1965), Small Faces' Itchycoo Park (1967), and the broader Carnaby Street fashion-and-music nexus consolidated the canonical sound. The 1979 Mod revival under The Jam, Secret Affair, and The Chords renewed institutional visibility.

items.name: Merseybeat (Liverpool beat 1962-65)
items.lineage: Early-1960s Liverpool-and-Merseyside beat-music style emerging from the convergence of skiffle, American R&B, and rock-and-roll into the canonical guitar-bass-drums-and-vocal-harmony four-piece beat-group format. The Beatles, Gerry and the Pacemakers, the Searchers, the Merseybeats, and Cilla Black constituted the canonical roster; the Cavern Club Liverpool and the Star-Club Hamburg anchored the institutional performance circuit. Distinguished from broader British Invasion by Merseybeat's Liverpool-specific geographic-cultural identity.

items.name: Garage punk (60s American)
items.lineage: Mid-1960s American amateur-and-semi-professional rock style characterized by deliberately raw production, simple three-chord structure, fuzz-and-distortion guitar tone, and snarling vocal aggression. The Nuggets compilation (1972, edited by Lenny Kaye) canonized the canonical 1965-1968 American garage-punk recordings; The Sonics, ? and the Mysterians, the Standells, the Seeds, and Count Five constitute the canonical roster. Direct precursor of late-1970s punk rock.

items.name: Proto-punk (late 60s-early 70s)
items.lineage: Late-1960s-early-1970s American-and-European rock styles prefiguring punk's 1976-77 emergence. The Velvet Underground & Nico (1967), the Stooges (1969), the MC5 (1969), the New York Dolls (1973), and the Modern Lovers (recorded 1971-72) constitute the canonical American proto-punk core; the Detroit-MC5-Stooges nexus and the New York Velvet Underground-Dolls scene defined the principal geographic-cultural axes.

items.name: Anarcho-punk (Crass)
items.lineage: British post-1977 punk substyle centered on the Crass collective at Dial House (Essex commune, founded 1967, music project 1977-1984) and the parallel Poison Girls, Flux of Pink Indians, and Conflict scenes. Combines aggressive punk musical-aesthetic with explicit anarchist-pacifist-feminist-vegan political content, DIY-distribution-and-production self-organization, and rigorous anti-commercial cultural-stance. The 1980 Reality Asylum, 1981 Penis Envy, and 1982 Christ — The Album consolidated the canonical anarcho-punk register.

items.name: Crust punk (D-beat-derived UK 80s)
items.lineage: Mid-1980s British and European punk-and-extreme-metal hybrid genre developed from anarcho-punk through Discharge (Stoke-on-Trent, 1977-onward) and Amebix (Bristol, 1978-onward), integrating thicker distorted-guitar-and-bass production, slower-doom-influenced tempi alongside fast hardcore tempos, and bleak political content. The 1984 Amebix Arise! and the 1989 Doom Police Bastard albums anchored the canonical sound. Direct precursor of broader crustcore and grindcore.

items.name: D-beat (Swedish hardcore)
items.lineage: Punk subgenre named for the distinctive 1-and-3 kick / 2-and-4 snare beat-pattern codified by Discharge (UK 1977-onward). Swedish D-beat-revival scene centered on Anti-Cimex, Mob 47, and (in the 1990s D-beat wave) Driller Killer and Wolfpack drove international circulation. Characterized by Discharge-derived beat-pattern, distorted-bass-and-guitar tone, and bleak anti-war anti-government political content.

items.name: Powerviolence (US extreme hardcore)
items.lineage: Late-1980s-1990s American hardcore subgenre characterized by extreme tempo contrasts (alternating blast-beat-fast-sections with sludge-slow-sections), brief song durations (often under one minute), and explicit anti-musical aggression. Bay Area scene centered on Spazz, Crossed Out, Infest, and Man Is the Bastard. Distinguished from broader grindcore by powerviolence's slower-section-emphasis (vs grindcore's relentless-blast-beat) structural framework.

items.name: Screamo / skramz (90s-2000s)
items.lineage: 1990s emocore and 2000s screamo subgenre developed from hardcore-punk emotional-aggressive register, characterized by screamed-and-melodic vocal alternation, dynamic-contrasted song structure, and confessional-emotional lyrical content. Saetia, City of Caterpillar, Pg.99, Orchid, and Hot Cross constitute the canonical American skramz roster; the parallel European screamo scene (Funeral Diner, Envy from Japan) extended international reach.

items.name: Folk punk (American 80s-90s)
items.lineage: Punk subgenre synthesizing folk-instrumentation (acoustic guitar, banjo, fiddle, accordion) with punk lyrical-and-attitudinal aesthetic. The Pogues (1983-onward) inaugurated the British-Irish strain; American folk-punk wave through Andrew Jackson Jihad, Defiance Ohio, Pat the Bunny, Mischief Brew, and the broader Plan-It-X Records roster constitutes the 2000s-2010s American development.

items.name: Riot grrrl (early 90s feminist punk)
items.lineage: Early-1990s American feminist punk subgenre emerging in Olympia, Washington and Washington, D.C., addressing rape, domestic violence, female empowerment, and patriarchal critique through aggressive punk musical-aesthetic. Bikini Kill (1990 founded), Bratmobile, Heavens to Betsy, and Huggy Bear constitute the canonical roster; the Riot Grrrl manifesto and zine-distribution-network anchored the broader cultural movement. K Records and Kill Rock Stars provided institutional infrastructure.

items.name: Third-wave ska punk
items.lineage: 1990s American ska-punk hybrid synthesizing third-wave ska revival with American hardcore-and-pop-punk aesthetic. Operation Ivy (Berkeley 1987-1989), Rancid, NOFX (ska-tinged), Less Than Jake, Reel Big Fish, and the Mighty Mighty Bosstones constitute the canonical roster. Distinguished from earlier two-tone British ska revival by third-wave ska-punk's American-suburban (vs British-multicultural-protest) cultural orientation and faster-aggressive tempi.

items.name: Midwest emo (90s)
items.lineage: Mid-1990s American emo subgenre developed in the American Midwest (Champaign-Urbana, Kinsella-family-related Chicago, Milwaukee, and St. Louis) characterized by intricate twinkly-guitar arpeggios, math-rock-derived rhythmic complexity, and confessional-emotional vocal-delivery. Cap'n Jazz (1989-1995, Chicago) inaugurated the style; American Football (1997, Champaign-Urbana, Mike Kinsella), the Promise Ring, Mineral, and Sunny Day Real Estate (Pacific Northwest cognate) constitute the canonical roster.

items.name: Slowcore (early-1990s American indie-rock minimalism)
items.lineage: Early-1990s American indie-rock subgenre characterized by deliberately glacial tempo, minimalist instrumentation, sparse arrangements, and quiet emotional register. Codeine (NYC, 1989), Low (Duluth, 1993), Bedhead (Dallas, 1991), and Galaxie 500 (Boston, 1987) constitute the canonical roster. Distinguished from broader indie rock by slowcore's extreme-deceleration aesthetic and absence of dynamic-arc-resolution.

items.name: Sadcore (early-1990s American melancholic confessional indie)
items.lineage: Early-1990s American indie subgenre adjacent-to-slowcore, with greater compositional-and-melodic-development and confessional-personal lyrical content. Red House Painters (1989-2001, Mark Kozelek), American Music Club, and (later) Kozelek's Sun Kil Moon project constitute the canonical roster. Distinguished from slowcore by sadcore's emphasis on songwriter-confessional content (vs slowcore's sound-texture-and-mood focus).

items.name: Britpop (90s)
items.lineage: Mid-1990s British rock movement (peaking 1994-1997) characterized by deliberate British-cultural-identity assertion against American grunge dominance, melodic guitar-pop influences from the Kinks-and-Beatles British-Invasion era, and explicit working-and-middle-class British lyrical content. Blur, Oasis, Pulp, Suede, Elastica, and the Verve constitute the canonical roster; the 1995 Blur-vs-Oasis chart-rivalry constitutes the canonical cultural-event.

items.name: Madchester / baggy
items.lineage: Late-1980s-and-early-1990s Manchester-based British rock-and-dance subgenre synthesizing indie-rock with acid-house club rhythmic-influence. The Stone Roses, Happy Mondays, Inspiral Carpets, the Charlatans, and James constitute the canonical roster; the Hacienda nightclub (Manchester, opened 1982) provided the canonical performance venue. The 1989 Stone Roses self-titled debut and the parallel Happy Mondays Bummed (1988) consolidated the canonical sound.

items.name: Slacker rock (early-1990s American lo-fi indie)
items.lineage: Early-1990s American indie rock substyle characterized by deliberately-loose performance aesthetic, lo-fi production, deadpan vocal delivery, and oblique-fragmentary lyrical content. Pavement (Stockton, 1989-1999) is the canonical type-specimen; parallel acts include Sebadoh, Guided by Voices, Silver Jews, and Built to Spill. Distinguished from broader indie rock by slacker rock's explicit casual-attitudinal aesthetic and emphasis on rough-edged production.

The High Llamas (UK, 1992-onward, Sean O'Hagan), Belle and Sebastian, Lambchop, the Divine Comedy, and Sufjan Stevens constitute the canonical roster.

Procol Harum's A Whiter Shade of Pale (1967), the Beatles' Eleanor Rigby (1966) and broader Sgt. Pepper's (1967) deployments, the Left Banke's Walk Away Renée (1966), and the Zombies' Odessey and Oracle (1968) constitute the canonical type-specimens.

items.name: Speed metal
items.lineage: Mid-1980s heavy-metal subgenre emphasizing extreme tempo and virtuoso guitar-playing while retaining melodic-vocal lines and traditional heavy-metal song-structure (vs the simultaneously-emerging thrash metal's harsher vocal-and-rhythmic-aggression). Motörhead's 1979-onward catalog inaugurated the style; Helloween (Hamburg, 1984-onward), Iced Earth, and (especially in 1990s extension) the Italian power-metal scene continued the lineage. Distinguished from thrash metal by speed metal's retention of melodic-vocal lines and traditional metal harmonic-vocabulary.

Pantera (post-1990 reinvention from glam-metal origins) inaugurated the canonical groove-metal sound through Cowboys from Hell (1990) and Vulgar Display of Power (1992); Sepultura (post-1991 Arise reinvention), Machine Head, and Lamb of God (2000s extension) constitute the broader canonical roster.

Ministry's The Land of Rape and Honey (1988), Nine Inch Nails' The Downward Spiral (1994), and Rammstein's 1995-onward German-language work constitute canonical type-specimens. Distinguished from broader industrial by integration of guitar-band rock framework.

items.name: Gothic metal

Paradise Lost's Gothic (1991), My Dying Bride, Anathema, the Theatre of Tragedy (Norway, 1993-onward), and the Type O Negative (NYC, 1989-2010) anchored the canonical roster.

items.name: Stoner rock
items.lineage: Late-1980s-and-1990s heavy-metal-and-rock subgenre developed primarily in California (Palm Desert "desert rock" scene) and northern Europe, characterized by down-tuned-distorted guitar tone, slow-to-mid-tempo grooves, vintage-1970s-Sabbath-Hendrix sonic reference, and improvisational-jam-oriented composition. Kyuss (Palm Desert, 1987-1995) and Sleep (San Jose, 1990-1998) inaugurated the canonical American sound; Queens of the Stone Age (1996-onward, Kyuss successor) extended the genre commercially.

items.name: Desert rock (Palm Desert scene)
items.lineage: Late-1980s-and-1990s Palm Desert California scene that birthed stoner rock through generator-party performances in the high desert outside Palm Springs and Joshua Tree. The "generator parties" allowed local bands (Kyuss, Yawning Man, Across the River, Fatso Jetson) to perform with the band powered by gasoline generators in remote desert locations free of police interference. The 1988-1992 generator-party period mythologized the geographic-cultural specificity of the desert-rock scene.

items.name: Space rock (late-1960s through 1970s psychedelic cosmic rock)
items.lineage: Late-1960s-and-1970s rock subgenre integrating extended psychedelic instrumental passages with science-fiction-cosmic thematic content. Hawkwind (UK 1969-onward) inaugurated the canonical style with Space Ritual (1973); Pink Floyd's pre-Dark-Side material, Gong's Radio Gnome Invisible trilogy, and (in the 1980s revival) Spacemen 3 and Loop continued the lineage. Distinguished from broader progressive rock by space rock's specific psychedelic-cosmic thematic focus and extended-instrumental-passage emphasis.

items.name: Zeuhl (French progressive Magma)
items.lineage: 1970s French progressive-rock subgenre invented by drummer-composer Christian Vander's Magma (founded 1969), characterized by Kobaïan invented-language vocals, complex polyrhythmic compositional structures, dark-symphonic orchestration, and explicit science-fiction mythological-narrative content. Magma's Mëkanïk Dëstruktïẁ Kömmandöh (1973), Köhntarkösz (1974), and Üdü Ẁüdü (1976) constitute the canonical core. The genre influenced subsequent French-progressive Univers Zéro, Art Zoyd, and Magma-affiliated solo projects.

items.name: Canterbury scene (UK progressive)
items.lineage: Late-1960s-and-1970s British progressive-rock subgenre centered on the city of Canterbury and the interconnected musicians of the Wilde Flowers (1964-1969), from which Soft Machine and Caravan emerged. Characterized by jazz-influenced harmonic vocabulary, dry-witty English-language lyrical content, and complex extended-form composition. Soft Machine, Caravan, Hatfield and the North, Gong (early), National Health, and Egg constitute the canonical roster.

items.name: Nu metal
items.lineage: Late-1990s-and-early-2000s American heavy-rock subgenre integrating hip-hop rhythmic-vocal influence, down-tuned-seven-string-guitar metal aesthetic, and confessional-aggressive-personal-trauma lyrical content. Korn (Bakersfield, 1993-onward), Deftones, Limp Bizkit, Slipknot, and Linkin Park constitute the canonical roster. The 1998 Family Values Tour consolidated the genre's commercial peak.

items.lineage: Early-1990s-and-onward American heavy-rock subgenre integrating hip-hop vocal-delivery and rhythmic-foundation with heavy-metal guitar-bass-drum aesthetic. Rage Against the Machine (Los Angeles, 1991-2000, 2007-onward) is the canonical type-specimen, with explicit revolutionary-political lyric content; the parallel Body Count (Ice-T project) and (later) the 2000s wave of Hed PE and Sevendust extended the genre.

items.name: Funk metal (mid-1980s funk-slap-bass heavy rock)
items.lineage: Mid-1980s-and-onward American rock subgenre integrating funk slap-bass and rhythmic-syncopation with heavy-rock guitar-bass-drum aesthetic. Red Hot Chili Peppers (Los Angeles, 1983-onward) inaugurated the canonical sound; Faith No More, Primus, Mr. Bungle, and Fishbone constitute the canonical roster. Distinguished from broader rock by funk metal's explicit syncopated-funk-bass emphasis.

items.name: Latin rock (late-1960s Afro-Cuban-percussion rock)
items.lineage: Late-1960s-and-onward rock subgenre integrating Afro-Cuban percussion (congas, timbales, bongos) and Latin-American rhythmic-harmonic-vocabulary with rock guitar-bass-drum aesthetic. Santana (San Francisco, 1966-onward) inaugurated the canonical Latin rock sound through the 1969 Woodstock performance and the first three Santana albums (1969-1971); Malo, El Chicano, War, and (later) Café Tacuba and Maná in Spanish-language Latin-rock extended the genre.

items.name: Greek rock
items.lineage: Greek-language rock music developed from 1960s onward, integrating Greek-laiko and rebetiko folk-music influences with broader Western rock vocabulary. The 1960s Pavlos Sidiropoulos and Stamatis Spanoudakis era inaugurated the form; the 1980s-90s "Greek rock" wave through Magic de Spell, Trypes, Tripes, Pyx Lax, and the broader post-1981 Athens scene consolidated commercial visibility. Distinguished by Greek-language lyrics and frequent integration of bouzouki/baglamas folk-instruments into rock contexts.

items.name: Aussie pub rock (70s-80s)
items.lineage: 1970s-and-1980s Australian rock subgenre developed through the working-class pub-circuit performance economy of Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide, and Perth. Cold Chisel, the Angels, Rose Tattoo, Midnight Oil, and AC/DC (Sydney-formed) constitute the canonical roster; the Australian-Crawl and (later) INXS extended the genre into international circulation. Distinguished by tight-rhythm-section-and-melodic-vocal pub-band aesthetic and Australian-cultural-identity lyrical content.

items.name: East Coast hip-hop (classic NY)
items.lineage: New York City classic hip-hop tradition encompassing Bronx-origin 1970s-era breakbeat-DJ-and-MC culture through 1990s "golden age" of Native Tongues, Boom Bap, and Wu-Tang Clan-led hardcore-NY sound. Characterized by sample-based production drawing on jazz, soul, and funk record collections, virtuoso lyrical-technique emphasis, and dense urban-NY cultural-narrative content. The Premier-Pete-Rock-RZA production lineage and the canonical Rakim-Nas-Biggie-Jay-Z MC tradition define the canonical East Coast aesthetic.

items.name: West Coast hip-hop (classic LA)
items.lineage: Los Angeles classic hip-hop tradition emerging in late-1980s through Ice-T, N.W.A, and the broader Compton-and-South-Central LA gangsta-rap movement. Characterized by funk-and-P-funk-derived synthesizer-heavy production (especially in 1990s G-funk era), confrontational street-life narrative content, and slower mid-tempo grooves than East Coast. Dr. Dre's The Chronic (1992) and Snoop Doggy Dogg's Doggystyle (1993) consolidated the canonical G-funk sound.

items.name: Southern hip-hop (classic South)
items.lineage: Late-1980s-and-onward Southern US hip-hop tradition spanning Houston (Geto Boys, Rap-A-Lot Records), Atlanta (Outkast, Dungeon Family), Miami (2 Live Crew, Miami Bass), and Memphis (Three 6 Mafia). Characterized by drawled vocal-delivery, Roland 808-prominent production, and explicit Southern-cultural-identity assertion against the East Coast / West Coast geographic dichotomy. Outkast's Aquemini (1998) and Geto Boys' We Can't Be Stopped (1991) consolidated regional visibility.

items.name: Bay Area hyphy
items.lineage: Mid-2000s San Francisco Bay Area hip-hop subgenre characterized by hyperactive vocal-delivery, distinctive synth-heavy production with Roland 808 emphasis, and explicit Bay Area dance-culture-and-sideshow-cruising thematic content. E-40's My Ghetto Report Card (2006), Mac Dre's post-mortem catalog (Dre died 2004), and the broader Mistah F.A.B.-Federation-Keak da Sneak scene defined the canonical hyphy roster.

items.name: Memphis rap (mid-1990s through 2000s Tennessee horrorcore)
items.lineage: Mid-1990s-and-2000s Memphis Tennessee hip-hop subgenre characterized by dark-ominous-horror-influenced production (drawing on horror-film soundtrack samples), ultra-slow tempo with chopped vocal-delivery, and graphic violence-and-drug lyrical content. Three 6 Mafia (Memphis 1991-onward, founded by DJ Paul and Juicy J) is the canonical type-specimen with their 1995 Mystic Stylez and 2005 Academy-Award win for Hustle & Flow. Direct ancestor of phonk subgenre.

items.name: Atlanta trap (classic 2000s)
items.lineage: Atlanta hip-hop subgenre crystallizing in mid-2000s through T.I.'s 2003 Trap Muzik album, characterized by hi-hat-rapid-roll percussion, Roland 808 bass emphasis, dark-keyboard-orchestral production, and explicit drug-dealing trap-house narrative content. Young Jeezy, Gucci Mane, Shawty Lo, and Rick Ross constitute the canonical 2000s trap roster; the genre subsequently spread to become the dominant 2010s American hip-hop production aesthetic.

items.name: Atlanta trap modern (2010s-20s)
items.lineage: Modern Atlanta trap subgenre developed in 2010s as evolution of classic Atlanta trap, characterized by melodic-singing-rapping hybrid vocal delivery, more elaborate keyboard-and-string production, and Auto-Tune integration. Future's 2014-onward catalog inaugurated the canonical modern trap sound; Migos, Young Thug, 21 Savage, Lil Baby, and Gunna anchor the canonical contemporary roster. Producer Metro Boomin defines the dominant late-2010s production aesthetic.

items.name: Houston chopped and screwed
items.lineage: Houston Texas hip-hop production-style invented by DJ Screw (born 1971) in early 1990s, in which existing hip-hop tracks are slowed dramatically (typically to 60-70% of original tempo) and chopped (rearranged in cut-and-paste sequence with repeats and skips). DJ Screw's Screwed Up Click crew (including Lil' Keke, Big Moe, Z-Ro, Lil' Flip) defined the canonical roster. Distinguished by the chopped-and-screwed technique's production-method-as-genre identity.

items.name: DC go-go (1970s-onward)
items.lineage: Washington D.C.-specific funk subgenre developed in mid-1970s by Chuck Brown (1936-2012), characterized by continuous percussion-and-bass-and-vocal groove without breaks between songs (the "go-go" of perpetual-motion), call-and-response between bandleader and audience, and Latin-percussion (congas, timbales, cowbell) integration with funk-band horn-section. Trouble Funk, Rare Essence, Experience Unlimited, and Backyard Band extended the canonical roster.

items.name: New jack swing (late 80s)
items.lineage: Late-1980s-and-early-1990s R&B-and-hip-hop hybrid genre invented by producer Teddy Riley (born 1967), characterized by syncopated-swing-eighth-note hip-hop drum-programming, R&B vocal-delivery, and explicit hip-hop production-aesthetic-and-fashion integration. Bobby Brown's Don't Be Cruel (1988), Guy's self-titled debut (1988), Bell Biv DeVoe's Poison (1990), and the early Mary J. Blige and Jodeci catalogs constitute the canonical core. Direct precursor of broader 1990s R&B and hip-hop-soul.

items.name: Crunk (early 2000s Memphis-Atlanta)
items.lineage: Early-2000s Memphis-and-Atlanta hip-hop subgenre characterized by simple-aggressive shouted-call-and-response vocal-delivery, hyperactive drum-machine production with 808 bass emphasis, and explicit club-anthem function. Lil Jon and the East Side Boyz (Atlanta 1997-onward) inaugurated the canonical sound; Three 6 Mafia, Ying Yang Twins, and the broader BME Recordings roster constitute the canonical roster. The 2003 "Get Low" hit consolidated commercial peak.

items.name: Snap music (mid-2000s Atlanta)
items.lineage: Mid-2000s Atlanta hip-hop subgenre developed from crunk through stripped-back minimal production replacing crunk's aggressive synth-and-808 with finger-snap-percussion-led beats. D4L's "Laffy Taffy" (2005) and Dem Franchize Boyz' "Lean Wit It, Rock Wit It" (2005) inaugurated the genre; Yung Joc, Soulja Boy (whose 2007 "Crank That" extended snap into broader commercial mainstream), and the Mojoe-and-Drumma-Boy production lineage constitute the canonical roster.

items.name: Phonk (lo-fi Memphis sample-based)
items.lineage: Late-2010s and 2020s electronic-hip-hop subgenre characterized by lo-fi production sampling 1990s Memphis-rap acapellas and beats (especially Three 6 Mafia, Tommy Wright III, DJ Paul), cassette-tape distortion, and slowed-down-pitched-vocal aesthetic. Originated through SoundCloud-Bandcamp distributed-production scene; the parallel drift phonk subgenre (faster-tempo, dancier, often associated with TikTok car-drifting videos) extended phonk into mainstream-internet popularity from 2019-onward.

items.name: Drift phonk (2020s TikTok)
items.lineage: 2019-onward extension of phonk into faster-tempo (140-160 BPM) dance-oriented variant, often heavily associated with TikTok car-drifting video content. Characterized by 4/4 dance-beat-derived structure with chopped-vocal phonk-sampling aesthetic, aggressive cowbell-percussion, and explicit Russian-and-Eastern-European-producer geographic-cultural orientation (the Russian phonk scene through Kordhell, MoonDeity, and Pharmacist became the dominant 2021-2023 international scene).

items.name: Plugg (cloud-bass plugg)
items.lineage: Late-2010s and 2020s hip-hop subgenre characterized by dreamlike-floating ambient-keyboard production with sparse Roland 808 percussion, slow-to-mid tempo, and melodic-or-deadpan vocal-delivery. Originated through Atlanta-and-Memphis SoundCloud production scene; producer MexikoDro is credited with inventing the canonical plugg-sound. Future-and-Lil-Uzi-Vert circle of producers extended the style into broader trap mainstream.

items.name: Pluggnb (R&B-plugg hybrid)

Producer Sxlxmxn defined much of the early pluggnb sound; Summrs, Autumn!, kankan, and TaTa constitute canonical artists. Distinguished from plugg by pluggnb's explicit R&B-melodic emphasis and romantic-relationship lyrical content.

items.name: Sad rap / emo trap
items.lineage: Late-2010s hip-hop subgenre integrating emo-rock melancholic-emotional register with trap production. Characterized by Auto-Tune sung-rapping, depression-and-relationship-loss lyrical content, electric-guitar samples integrated with 808 drums, and high-emotional-intensity vocal performance. Lil Peep (1996-2017) and Juice WRLD (1998-2019) — both deceased of overdoses — constitute the canonical type-specimens; XXXTentacion (1998-2018), Trippie Redd, and Iann Dior anchor the broader roster.

items.name: SoundCloud rap
items.lineage: 2015-2018 hip-hop wave defined less by sonic-stylistic conventions than by distribution-platform — the SoundCloud upload-and-share infrastructure that allowed bedroom-producers and amateur rappers to bypass traditional A&R gatekeeping. The wave produced Lil Pump, Smokepurpp, 6ix9ine, Ski Mask the Slump God, and the broader Florida-NYC-Chicago younger-generation rapper roster. Aesthetically marked by deliberately-amateurish vocal delivery, mumble-rap convention, face-tattoos, and explicit drug-and-violence lyrical content.

items.name: Chicago drill (early 2010s)
items.lineage: Early-2010s Chicago hip-hop subgenre emerging from the South Side of Chicago, characterized by ominous-keyboard-and-strings production, slower mid-tempo drilling-hi-hat patterns, and explicit street-violence-and-gang-life lyrical content addressing the Chicago South Side gang-violence epidemic. Chief Keef (born 1995) and producer Young Chop inaugurated the canonical sound through "I Don't Like" (2012); Lil Durk, Lil Reese, King Louie, and (later) Polo G, Lil Bibby, and G Herbo constitute the canonical roster.
