items.description: The Bengali kanna gaan (literally "weeping-song", also "vilāp gan" elegy-song) women's mourning-song tradition continuous from medieval-Bengal rural practice through colonial-period documented performance into modern Bangla-language domestic mourning practice across West Bengal and Bangladesh; less codified as a professional-role tradition than Tamil oppāri but documented in folk-ethnographic literature; Defined by free-meter melismatic Bangla-vocal phrasing, Bengali-folk-modal vocabulary related to but distinct from formal Hindustani-classical practice (Bhairavi and Bhupali frequent), sob-glottalization vocal technique, Bangla-language text register with frequent praise-of-the-deceased and grief-narrative lyric content, women's-voice primary tradition particularly performed by elder women of the family at the time of death.
exemplars: Rabindranath Tagore — "Mritunjaya" art-song treatment of Bengali mourning

items.name: Korean kok (곡, funeral wailing)
items.lineage: Korean Confucian-and-shamanic funeral mourning tradition codified from the Joseon-dynasty period through Confucian ritual-mourning specification (the codified mourning-stages including kok wailing-cycles); continuous through 20th-century practice particularly in rural Korean Confucian funeral context
items.description: The Korean kok (곡, "wailing" — also goksori 곡소리, "wailing-sound") funeral-mourning tradition codified from the Joseon-dynasty period forward through Confucian ritual-mourning specification; the codified mourning-stages of Confucian-Korean funeral practice include kok wailing-cycles at specific procession-points (the iʻyŏn or "hand-banner-procession," the chŏnʻyŏn or "approach to the grave," etc.) with prescribed ritual-frequency and gendered-role conventions. Continuous through 20th-century practice particularly in rural Korean Confucian-funeral context. Defined by free-meter intense weeping-into-pitch Korean-vocal phrasing, characteristic gradual buildup of vocal-intensity within each kok-cycle, Korean-pansori-adjacent vocal-ornament technique applied to ritual-mourning, the Korean syllabic-vocable "aigo aigo" (아이고 아이고) functioning as the canonical wailing-refrain, both male-and-female participation with women's lead, performed within structured Confucian-mourning-stage framework.

items.name: Yoruba ìrèmọjẹ (hunters' and widows' funeral dirge)
items.lineage: Yoruba mourning-song tradition continuous from pre-colonial Yoruba ritual-practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance by Yoruba hunters'-guild and hunters'-widows; particularly preserved in Ọ̀yọ́, Òṣun, Ọ̀ǹdó, Èkìtì Yoruba cultural zones
items.description: The Yoruba ìrèmọjẹ (hunters' and widows' funeral dirge) tradition continuous from pre-colonial Yoruba ritual-practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance by Yoruba hunters'-guild (egbé ọdẹ) and hunters'-widows; particularly preserved in Ọ̀yọ́, Òṣun, Ọ̀ǹdó, Èkìtì Yoruba cultural zones in southwestern Nigeria. Defined by free-meter recitative Yoruba-vocal phrasing, Yoruba tonal-language constrained-melodic-vocabulary (the Yoruba three-tone system constrains the lament's melodic contour to follow speech-tone patterns), call-and-response group-participation with lead-singer and chorus, occasional dùndún talking-drum support, Yoruba-language text register with extensive ọrọ-ìrèmọjẹ (hunters'-lament word) specialized vocabulary, performed during the dúró-ìrèmọjẹ vigil at the deceased hunter's compound. Distinguished from Yoruba praise-poetry oríkì by funeral-function and specialized ìrèmọjẹ-text-tradition.
exemplars: Akin Euba — Yoruba ritual-music documentation including ìrèmọjẹ
Ọ̀ǹdó ìrèmọjẹ widow's-lament tradition (Olusegun Stephens documentation)
Yoruba egbé ọdẹ hunters'-guild ritual-songs cycle

items.name: Hawaiian kanikau (mele kanikau, mourning-chant)
items.lineage: Hawaiian mourning-chant tradition continuous from pre-contact Hawaiian ritual-practice through 19th-century Hawaiian-Kingdom-era continuous performance and publication (kanikau were published in Hawaiian-language newspapers from the 1830s-onward) into 20th-century Hawaiian-cultural-revival
items.description: The Hawaiian kanikau (mele kanikau, "mourning-chant") tradition continuous from pre-contact Hawaiian ritual-practice through 19th-century Hawaiian-Kingdom-era continuous performance and publication (kanikau-texts were published in Hawaiian-language newspapers such as Ka Nupepa Kuokoa from the 1830s onward, constituting one of the largest documented corpus of any Polynesian poetic tradition) into 20th-century Hawaiian-cultural-revival. Defined by oli (chant) free-meter recitation in characteristic Hawaiian voice-production (the kāmākau voice-production with specific glottal-onset on 'okina), Hawaiian-language text register with extensive praise-of-the-deceased and place-naming (the kanikau text typically names the genealogy and the places associated with the deceased), unaccompanied solo-vocal performance, ritual-bounded performance context particularly at the deceased's family compound or ancestral place. Distinguished from broader Hawaiian mele performance by funeral-function and kanikau-specific poetic-tradition.
exemplars: Queen Lili'uokalani — "He Mele Lahui Hawai'i" and personal kanikau compositions
Mary Kawena Pukui — kanikau ethnographic-and-creative documentation
Pualani Kanaka'ole Kanahele — contemporary kanikau performance

items.name: Māori waiata tangi (mourning-song)
items.lineage: Māori mourning-song tradition continuous from pre-contact Māori ritual-practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance at tangihanga (Māori funeral rites) into modern Māori-cultural-revival; the waiata tangi is one of the codified Māori waiata categories alongside waiata aroha (love-song) and waiata oriori (lullaby)
items.description: The Māori waiata tangi (mourning-song) tradition continuous from pre-contact Māori ritual-practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance at tangihanga (Māori funeral rites) into modern Māori-cultural-revival; the waiata tangi is one of the codified Māori waiata categories alongside waiata aroha (love-song) and waiata oriori (lullaby) within the broader Māori sung-poetic tradition. Defined by narrow-range pentatonic-leaning melodic-vocabulary characteristic of Māori traditional waiata practice (te reo Māori voice-production), free-meter recitation with rhythmic-text-pulse, Māori-language te reo text register with extensive whakapapa (genealogy) naming and deceased-praise content, unaccompanied solo-or-group vocal performance, ritual-bounded performance context at the marae during tangihanga. The waiata tangi is integral to the structure of tangihanga and is performed by family-and-tribal members at specific stages of the funeral process.
exemplars: Hirini Melbourne — traditional waiata tangi recordings 1980s-1990s
Documented Te Awa Kairangi waiata tangi tradition
Tūhoe tribal waiata tangi corpus (Best 1925 ethnography)

items.name: Yiddish wedding bulgar and freylekhs
items.lineage: Ashkenazi-Jewish wedding-dance-music tradition continuous from 19th-century Eastern-European-shtetl klezmer practice through New-York Yiddish-American post-1880s immigration era through the 1970s klezmer-revival; the bulgar (Bulgarian-origin double-line dance) and freylekhs (joyful-dance) are the canonical Ashkenazi wedding-dance forms
items.description: The Ashkenazi-Jewish wedding-dance-music tradition centered on bulgar (Bulgarian-origin double-line dance form, ⁴⁄₄ moderately-fast tempo) and freylekhs ("joyful-dance," ⁴⁄₄ moderate-tempo line-dance); continuous from 19th-century Eastern-European-shtetl klezmer practice through post-1880s New-York Yiddish-American immigration era through the 1970s klezmer-revival. Defined by characteristic Freygish (Ahava Raba) modal vocabulary with augmented-second color, klezmer-clarinet-and-fiddle foreground virtuosic ornament (krekhts cry, dreydl turn, kneytsh wail), accordion-and-doibass-and-frame-drum dance-rhythm-section foundation, instrumental-dance-foreground with occasional call-and-response vocal interjection, characteristic mode-modulation across the dance-set, Yiddish wedding-functional context with badkhn (wedding-jester) verse-improvisation interludes. The Naftule Brandwein and Dave Tarras 1920s-1940s 78rpm recordings constitute the canonical pre-revival corpus.
exemplars: Dave Tarras — Yiddish wedding bulgar canonical recordings 1930s-1960s
The Klezmatics — modern Yiddish wedding repertoire

items.name: Roma Balkan svatba (wedding music)
items.lineage: Roma-Balkan wedding-music tradition continuous from 19th-20th century Roma musical-professionalization across Bulgaria, Macedonia, Serbia, Romania, Turkey, and broader Balkan zones; particularly codified in the 1980s-2000s Goran-Bregović-era and the broader Balkan brass-band wedding tradition documented by Bartók and later ethnomusicologists
items.description: The Roma-Balkan svatba wedding-music tradition continuous from 19th-20th century Roma musical-professionalization across Bulgaria, Macedonia, Serbia, Romania, Turkey, and broader Balkan zones; defined by Balkan-aksak odd-meter rhythmic vocabulary (7/8, 9/8, 11/8 wedding-dance meters including ručenica and lesno), Eastern-modal vocabulary with maqam-style microtonal inflection, virtuosic accordion-and-clarinet-and-fiddle ensemble foreground with brass-band (trumpet-and-saxophone-led) festive arrangement, characteristic Roma cocek dance-form, ululation-and-shouted-vocal celebratory practice, dense ensemble-texture with sustained-energy dance-foreground spanning multiple-hour wedding-feast performance. The Goran Bregović 1989-onward film-and-soundtrack work canonized the form for international audiences; the Slavic Soul Party and Boban Marković Orkestar are the modern-codified-Balkan-brass-wedding reference.
exemplars: Boban Marković Orkestar — Serbian Roma wedding-brass canonical
Goran Bregović — wedding-music film-scores (Time of the Gypsies 1988, Underground 1995)
Fanfare Ciocărlia — Romanian Roma brass-band wedding repertoire
Esma Redžepova — Macedonian Roma wedding-vocal queen

items.name: Sardinian wedding cantu and launeddas music
items.lineage: Sardinian wedding-music tradition continuous from pre-Christian Sardinian rural practice through medieval-and-early-modern continuous performance; the launeddas (triple-clarinet) is the canonical Sardinian wedding-music instrument and the cantu a tenore polyphonic male-quartet vocal also features at weddings
items.description: The Sardinian wedding-music tradition continuous from pre-Christian Sardinian rural practice through medieval-and-early-modern continuous performance; the launeddas (triple-clarinet, the canonical Sardinian wedding-music instrument with documented continuity from Nuragic-era 8th-century-BCE bronze figurine evidence) provides the dance-music foundation and the cantu a tenore polyphonic male-quartet vocal also features at weddings particularly in Nuorese-Sardinian zones. Defined by characteristic Sardinian-modal vocabulary, drone-foundation polyphonic-vocal texture, the launeddas' continuous-circular-breathing performance practice (the player sustains an unbroken drone-line for hours), Sardinian-language text register, Logudorese-and-Campidanese-and-Nuorese regional variants.
exemplars: Luigi Lai — canonical Sardinian launeddas master
Tenores di Bitti Mialinu Pira — cantu a tenore wedding repertoire

items.name: Greek gamílio glendí (γαμήλιο γλέντι, wedding feast music)
items.lineage: Greek wedding-music tradition continuous from Byzantine-era through Ottoman-period through 19th-20th-century modern-Greek continuous practice; regionally distributed with strongest preservation in Crete, Mani, Epirus, and Pontic-Greek diaspora
items.description: The Greek gamílio glendí (γαμήλιο γλέντι, wedding-feast music) tradition continuous from Byzantine-era through Ottoman-period through 19th-20th-century modern-Greek continuous practice; regionally distributed with strongest preservation in Crete (where the Cretan-lyra-and-laouto wedding ensemble is canonical), Mani peninsula, Epirus (clarinet-and-violin-led Epirotic wedding ensemble), and Pontic-Greek diaspora. Defined by characteristic Greek-Eastern modal vocabulary (dromos system shared with rebetiko), regional-instrument-led ensembles, syrtos-and-kalamatianos-and-hasapikos canonical wedding-dance forms, ornamented melodic vocabulary, demotic-Greek-and-regional-dialect text register, festive uptempo dance-foreground arrangement spanning multi-hour wedding-feast performance.
exemplars: Nikos Xylouris — Cretan wedding-music canonical recordings
Ross Daly — Cretan lyra wedding-repertoire revival recordings
Petros Loukas Chalkias — Epirotic clarinet wedding-music master
Domna Samiou — Greek wedding-traditional documentary collections
Cretan rizitiko wedding-songs (Sfakia and Lasithi regions)

items.name: Albanian dasma (wedding music)
items.lineage: Albanian wedding-music tradition continuous from medieval Albanian rural practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance; particularly preserved in Northern Albanian highland zones, Southern Albanian iso-polyphonic zones, Kosovo, and Arbëresh-Italian diaspora
items.description: The Albanian dasma (wedding) music tradition continuous from medieval Albanian rural practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance; particularly preserved in Northern Albanian highland zones (Gegërisht-speaking, with çifteli-led wedding ensemble — though çifteli is not in catalog so cifteli-substitute clarinet-led ensemble represents here), Southern Albanian iso-polyphonic zones (Toskërisht-speaking, with iso-drone polyphonic vocal practice in the wedding context), Kosovo, and Arbëresh-Italian Southern-Italian diaspora. Defined by Albanian-Balkan modal vocabulary with Eastern-modal inflection, ⁵⁄₈ ⁷⁄₈ ⁹⁄₈ aksak rhythmic-meter wedding dances, valle-and-vallja line-dance arrangement, characteristic ululated-and-shouted celebratory vocal, dense ensemble texture, Albanian-language text register coexisting with regional dialect.
exemplars: Saban Bajramović — Albanian Roma wedding-music canonical recordings
Bajram Kërpi — traditional Albanian dasma repertoire
Vaçe Zela — modern Albanian wedding-vocal recordings

items.name: Persian aroosi (عروسی, wedding music)
items.lineage: Persian wedding-music tradition continuous from medieval Persian-domestic-music practice through Qajar-and-Pahlavi-era documented performance into modern Iranian and Iranian-diaspora practice; defined by daf-and-tar-and-vocal ensemble
items.description: The Persian aroosi (عروسی, wedding) music tradition continuous from medieval Persian-domestic-music practice through Qajar-and-Pahlavi-era documented performance into modern Iranian and Iranian-diaspora practice; defined by daf (Persian frame-drum) and tar/setar (Persian long-necked lutes) and tonbak (goblet-drum) ensemble accompaniment to vocal-foreground celebratory songs, Persian dastgāh-modal vocabulary inflected toward the lighter Shur and Bayāt-e Tork gushehs appropriate to wedding-affect (avoiding the gravitas of Mahur or the lament-leaning Dashti), 6/8 reng-dance and 4/4 tasnif-song forms canonical for wedding repertoire, Farsi-Persian celebratory text register, henna-night and bandari-coastal-tradition variants. The Mohammad Reza Lotfi and Hossein Alizadeh classical-context recordings provide the canonical art-music elevation; the broader Tehrani pre-revolutionary popular-vocalist wedding-repertoire is the more-domestic continuous tradition.
exemplars: Mohammad Reza Lotfi — Persian wedding-music classical recordings
Bandari-Persian wedding-music (Bushehri and Hormozgani coastal traditions)

items.name: Lebanese-Arab wedding takht (تخت العرس)
items.lineage: Lebanese-and-pan-Arab wedding-music tradition centered on the takht (small classical Arabic ensemble of oud, qanun, riq or tabla, violin or rebab, and vocalist); continuous from 19th-century Levantine-Arab classical-and-domestic-music practice through 20th-century Beirut-Cairo-Damascus golden-age wedding-music recording
items.description: The Lebanese-and-pan-Arab wedding-music tradition centered on the takht (small classical Arabic ensemble of oud, qanun, riq or tabla-darbuka, violin or rebab, and vocalist); continuous from 19th-century Levantine-Arab classical-and-domestic-music practice through 20th-century Beirut-Cairo-Damascus golden-age wedding-music recording (the Fairuz, Wadih el Safi, and broader Rahbani-era Lebanese wedding repertoire). Defined by Arabic-maqam modal vocabulary (Bayāti, Hijaz, Nahawand, Saba especially), microtonal quarter-tone pitch inflection, characteristic dabke line-dance rhythmic-meter (4/4 or 6/8 dabke-specific feel), zaghareet ululation as canonical celebratory vocalization, ornamented melismatic vocal, classical-Arabic-or-Levantine-dialect text register, mawwāl improvised-prelude into festive dabke-song form arrangement.
exemplars: Wadih el Safi — Lebanese wedding-mawwāl master
Najwa Karam — modern Lebanese wedding-popular crossover

items.name: Berber Amazigh ahidus (wedding dance)
items.lineage: Berber-Amazigh wedding-music tradition continuous from pre-Islamic North African Berber rural practice through Islamic-period continuous performance into modern Tamazight-speaking Moroccan and Algerian Berber-zone domestic practice; particularly preserved in the Atlas Mountains (Middle and High Atlas Tamazight zones) and the Kabyle Algeria
items.description: The Berber-Amazigh ahidus (wedding-dance music) tradition continuous from pre-Islamic North African Berber rural practice through Islamic-period continuous performance into modern Tamazight-speaking Moroccan and Algerian Berber-zone domestic practice; particularly preserved in the Middle Atlas (Tamazight-speaking ahidus tradition with synchronized circle-dance), High Atlas (Tashelhit-speaking ahwash variant), and Kabyle Algeria. Defined by frame-drum-foundation (bendir, tar) percussive accompaniment, group-vocal call-and-response with antiphonal men-and-women alternation, characteristic Berber-pentatonic melodic vocabulary, ululated zaghareet celebratory vocalization, Tamazight-and-Tashelhit-language text register, synchronized-circle-dance choreographic arrangement spanning multi-hour wedding-feast performance.
exemplars: Middle Atlas ahidus circle-dance traditional recordings

items.name: Indian sangeet (women's pre-wedding music night)
items.lineage: Pan-Indian (Hindi-Urdu, Punjabi, Bengali, and broader North-Indian) pre-wedding sangeet ceremony music continuous from medieval Mughal-era domestic-music practice through 20th-century filmi-Bollywood appropriation into modern South-Asian-and-diaspora wedding practice
items.description: The pan-Indian (Hindi-Urdu, Punjabi, Bengali, and broader North-Indian) pre-wedding sangeet ceremony-music tradition continuous from medieval Mughal-era domestic-music practice through 20th-century filmi-Bollywood appropriation into modern South-Asian-and-diaspora wedding practice; the sangeet is the women's-music night before the wedding featuring extended-family women performing traditional and Bollywood-derived wedding-songs with dholak-and-harmonium accompaniment. Defined by Hindustani raga-derived melodic vocabulary (Yaman, Bhairavi, Pilu, Khamaj frequent in sangeet rep), characteristic Punjabi-and-Hindi wedding-song forms (the suhag, geet, ghori repertoires), dholak-foundation rhythmic accompaniment, ornamented women's-vocal foreground with chorus-response, Hindi-Urdu-Punjabi-Bengali language register, filmi-Bollywood song integration alongside traditional repertoire.
exemplars: Traditional Punjabi suhag and ghori wedding-song repertoire
Sangeet-cinema repertoire ("Mehndi laga ke rakhna" Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge 1995)

items.name: Indian baraat (groom's wedding procession)
items.lineage: Pan-Indian groom's wedding-procession music tradition continuous from medieval-era Indian royal-and-domestic processional-music practice through 19th-20th century commercial-baraat-band evolution into modern South-Asian-and-diaspora wedding practice; defined by the band-baaja-baaraat ensemble with shehnai, dhol, trumpet, and brass-and-percussion arrangement
items.description: The pan-Indian baraat (groom's wedding-procession) music tradition continuous from medieval-era Indian royal-and-domestic processional-music practice through 19th-20th century commercial-baraat-band evolution (the "band-baaja-baaraat" ensemble code-name) into modern South-Asian-and-diaspora wedding practice; defined by shehnai-and-dhol-and-trumpet-led brass-and-percussion ensemble providing the outdoor-procession music as the groom's party approaches the bride's home, characteristic shehnai-melody-foreground over dhol-and-tabla rhythmic foundation, raga-derived melodic vocabulary, festive uptempo dance-music arrangement with characteristic baraat repertoire including the canonical "Aaj Mere Yaar Ki Shaadi Hai" Bollywood-baraat song, dancing-friend-and-relative group-vocal participation, North-Indian-and-Punjabi linguistic register predominant.
exemplars: Bismillah Khan — canonical shehnai wedding-baraat master
"Aaj Mere Yaar Ki Shaadi Hai" (Aadmi Sadak Ka 1977 film-baraat canonical)

items.name: Chinese xǐqìng (喜慶) wedding music
items.lineage: Chinese wedding-music tradition continuous from imperial-era Chinese ceremonial-music practice through Republican-period and post-1949 evolution into modern Chinese-Mandarin-speaking domestic practice across mainland China, Taiwan, and Chinese-diaspora communities; the suona (Chinese shawm) is the canonical wedding-music instrument though here represented by sheng-and-dizi-and-erhu substitute ensemble
items.description: The Chinese xǐqìng (喜慶, "wedding-celebration") music tradition continuous from imperial-era Chinese ceremonial-music practice through Republican-period and post-1949 evolution into modern Chinese-Mandarin-speaking domestic practice across mainland China, Taiwan, and Chinese-diaspora communities; the suona (Chinese shawm — though absent from this catalog so substituted with sheng-and-dizi-and-erhu ensemble) is the canonical wedding-music instrument providing the loud-outdoor-celebratory melodic foreground. Defined by Chinese pentatonic (gong-shang-jue-zhi-yu) melodic vocabulary, characteristic xǐqìng repertoire including "Bǎi Niǎo Cháo Fèng" (百鸟朝凤, "Hundred Birds Worship the Phoenix") suona-canonical, percussion-and-gong-and-cymbal accompaniment ensemble providing rhythmic foundation, ceremonial-and-festive dual-function repertoire arrangement, Mandarin-Putonghua text register.
exemplars: "Bǎi Niǎo Cháo Fèng" (百鸟朝凤, suona wedding-music canonical)
"Hǎo Rì Zi" (好日子, modern Chinese wedding-pop)
Cantonese wedding-music yueju repertoire (Guangdong regional variant)

items.name: Javanese wedding gamelan music
items.lineage: Javanese wedding-music tradition continuous from medieval Javanese court-and-village gamelan practice through Islamic-period (post-15th-century) continuous performance into modern Indonesian-and-Javanese-diaspora practice; defined by gamelan-ensemble accompaniment to ceremonial-and-celebratory wedding-music repertoire
items.description: The Javanese wedding-music tradition continuous from medieval Javanese court-and-village gamelan practice through Islamic-period (post-15th-century) continuous performance into modern Indonesian-and-Javanese-diaspora practice; defined by gamelan-ensemble (the full Central-Javanese gamelan with bonang, saron, gender, gong, kendang, and pesinden vocal soloist) accompaniment to ceremonial-and-celebratory wedding-music repertoire, characteristic gendhing-form compositional vocabulary spanning the ceremonial-stages of the Javanese wedding (panggih bride-and-groom-meeting, sungkeman parent-reverence, kacar-kucur grain-pouring, dahar-klimah shared-meal). Pelog-and-slendro tuning systems, restrained court-vocal practice (legato, syllabic, in contrast to more melismatic East-Javanese-or-Sundanese practice), Javanese-language text register.

items.name: Yoruba aso ebi wedding music
items.lineage: Yoruba wedding-music tradition continuous from pre-colonial Yoruba ritual-practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Yoruba-and-Yoruba-diaspora domestic practice across southwestern Nigeria, Benin, Togo, and the Atlantic Afro-diaspora; the aso ebi (unified-dress) wedding tradition emphasizes group-celebration vocal-and-drumming participation
items.description: The Yoruba wedding-music tradition continuous from pre-colonial Yoruba ritual-practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Yoruba-and-Yoruba-diaspora domestic practice across southwestern Nigeria, Benin, Togo, and the Atlantic Afro-diaspora; the aso ebi (unified-dress) wedding tradition emphasizes group-celebration vocal-and-drumming participation where extended-family-and-friends-of-the-couple wear matching cloth and participate in the celebration as unified social-group. Defined by talking-drum (dùndún) and dunun-and-bata percussion-foreground ensemble, Yoruba tonal-language vocal-melody constrained by speech-tone patterns, call-and-response group-vocal foreground, ìjò Yoruba dance-rhythmic-vocabulary, Yoruba-language ojúfò (wedding-praise) and oríkì (praise-poetry) text-tradition. Modern Yoruba wedding integrates juju and fuji popular-music traditions alongside traditional aso ebi practice.
exemplars: Sunny Adé — Yoruba juju wedding-music canonical
King Wasiu Ayinde Marshal — fuji wedding-music
Traditional Yoruba aso ebi wedding-procession songs

items.name: Ethiopian eskista (እስክስታ) wedding music
items.lineage: Ethiopian wedding-music tradition continuous from medieval Ethiopian Orthodox-Christian-and-Amhara cultural practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Ethiopian-and-Ethiopian-diaspora domestic practice; the eskista is the canonical Ethiopian shoulder-dance music
items.description: The Ethiopian wedding-music tradition continuous from medieval Ethiopian Orthodox-Christian-and-Amhara cultural practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Ethiopian-and-Ethiopian-diaspora domestic practice; the eskista (እስክስታ, the canonical Ethiopian shoulder-dance characterized by rapid shoulder-shaking motion) is the central wedding-celebration dance-form. Defined by masenqo (single-string bowed-lute) and kebero (Ethiopian drum) and washint (flute) and krar (lyre) traditional-instrument ensemble (with accordion as common modern addition), Ethiopian qenet pentatonic-modal vocabulary (tezeta, ambassel, bati, anchihoye modes), characteristic shoulder-dance rhythmic-foundation, Amharic-and-Oromo-and-Tigrinya language text register, festive uptempo arrangement with virtuosic vocal-and-instrumental foreground.
exemplars: Mulatu Astatke — Ethio-jazz wedding-music modern integration

items.name: Andean matrimonio huayno (wedding huayno)
items.lineage: Andean Quechua-and-Aymara wedding-music tradition continuous from pre-Columbian Andean ritual-practice through colonial-period syncretic continuous performance into modern Quechua-and-Aymara-speaking domestic practice across Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, and the Andean diaspora; the huayno is the canonical Andean dance-form across multiple ceremonial contexts including weddings
items.description: The Andean Quechua-and-Aymara wedding-music tradition continuous from pre-Columbian Andean ritual-practice through colonial-period syncretic continuous performance into modern Quechua-and-Aymara-speaking domestic practice across Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, and the Andean diaspora; the huayno (Quechua wayñu, Aymara waynu) is the canonical Andean dance-form across multiple ceremonial contexts including weddings. Defined by charango (small ten-string lute) and quena (Andean notched-flute) and zampoña (panpipes) and accordion (post-colonial addition) instrumental ensemble accompanying voice, Andean pentatonic-modal vocabulary, characteristic 2/4 huayno rhythmic-foundation with the canonical "tan-takataka" foot-pattern, Quechua-and-Aymara-and-Spanish text register, call-and-response group-vocal participation, festive dance-foreground spanning multi-hour wedding-feast performance.
exemplars: Picaflor de los Andes — Peruvian wedding-huayno canonical

items.name: American folk-revival protest song
items.lineage: American protest-song tradition continuous from Industrial-Workers-of-the-World early-20th-century labor anthems (Joe Hill, "Solidarity Forever") through the 1930s Almanac Singers and Popular Front lineage through 1960s civil-rights-and-anti-war folk-revival continuous into the modern indie-protest singer-songwriter scene
items.description: The American folk-revival protest-song tradition continuous from IWW early-20th-century labor anthems (Joe Hill's "Solidarity Forever," "There Is Power in a Union," "The Preacher and the Slave") through the 1930s Almanac Singers and Popular Front lineage (Woody Guthrie, Pete Seeger, Lee Hays) through the 1960s civil-rights-and-anti-war folk-revival (Joan Baez, early Bob Dylan, Phil Ochs, Tom Paxton, Buffy Sainte-Marie, Odetta) continuous into the modern indie-protest singer-songwriter scene. Defined by acoustic-guitar-and-voice (and frequently banjo and harmonica) foreground arrangement, narrative verse-chorus song-form built to be sung by crowds, melodic-vocabulary intentionally accessible (limited range, simple chord progressions), strophic structure permitting infinite topical-verse extension, frequent adoption of pre-existing folk-and-hymn tunes ("We Shall Overcome" from "I'll Overcome Someday" 1900s gospel), English-language plainspoken-text register, traditional songbook-and-songsheet transmission supplemented by recordings.
exemplars: Woody Guthrie — "This Land Is Your Land" 1940 / "Tom Joad" / "Pretty Boy Floyd"
Pete Seeger — "Where Have All the Flowers Gone?" "If I Had a Hammer" "We Shall Overcome"
Phil Ochs — "I Ain't Marching Anymore" 1965 anti-war canonical
Joe Hill — "The Preacher and the Slave" 1911 IWW canonical
Bob Dylan — "Blowin' in the Wind" 1962 / "The Times They Are a-Changin'" 1964

items.name: Chilean nueva canción
items.lineage: Chilean nueva canción ("new song") tradition emerging late-1960s through the Allende-era 1970-1973 to mid-1970s Pinochet-coup-era political folk-revival; centered on Víctor Jara, Violeta Parra, Quilapayún, and Inti-Illimani with Indigenous-Andean-instrument integration alongside Western-folk songwriter format
items.description: The Chilean nueva canción ("new song") tradition emerging late-1960s through the Allende-era 1970-1973 to mid-1970s Pinochet-coup-era political folk-revival; centered on Víctor Jara (assassinated September 1973 in the Estadio Chile days after the Pinochet coup), Violeta Parra (foundational figure documenting Chilean folk-tradition who took her own life in 1967), Quilapayún, Inti-Illimani, and the Discoteca del Cantar Popular DICAP-label scene. Defined by integration of Indigenous-Andean instruments (charango, quena, zampoña, bombo) with Western-folk acoustic-guitar songwriter-format, Andean-pentatonic melodic vocabulary alongside Spanish-language verse-chorus song-form, narrative-and-anthemic political-grievance lyric content, characteristic acoustic-warm timbre, frequently censorship-faced and post-coup exile-context performance (Inti-Illimani spent 14 years exiled in Italy).
exemplars: Víctor Jara — "Te Recuerdo Amanda" 1968 / "El Derecho de Vivir en Paz" 1971 / "Manifiesto" 1973
Violeta Parra — "Gracias a la Vida" 1966 / "La Carta" 1962 / Canciones Funcionales DICAP
Quilapayún — "El Pueblo Unido Jamás Será Vencido" 1973 canonical anthem
Isabel Parra and Ángel Parra — DICAP-label Parra-family rep

items.name: Argentine canto nuevo / canto popular
items.lineage: Argentine canto nuevo / canto popular protest-song tradition continuous from 1960s-1980s Argentine military-dictatorship-era political folk-and-songwriter scene; centered on Mercedes Sosa, Atahualpa Yupanqui (foundational figure), León Gieco, and the Movimiento del Nuevo Cancionero
items.description: The Argentine canto nuevo (also canto popular) protest-song tradition continuous from 1960s-1980s Argentine military-dictatorship-era (1976-1983 Dirty War period) political folk-and-songwriter scene; centered on Mercedes Sosa (the voice of Latin America, censored and exiled 1979-1982), Atahualpa Yupanqui (foundational figure documenting Argentine folk-tradition from Communist-Party-affiliated political position), León Gieco ("Solo le Pido a Dios" 1978 canonical), and the 1963 Movimiento del Nuevo Cancionero founded by Mercedes Sosa, Tito Francia, Armando Tejada Gómez, and Oscar Matus. Defined by acoustic-guitar-and-bombo-legüero (Argentine bass-drum) accompaniment to voice-foreground arrangement, integration of Argentine folk-forms (zamba, chacarera, carnavalito), Spanish-Argentine-Quechua text register, narrative-and-anthemic political-grievance lyric content frequently disguised through metaphor to evade censorship.
exemplars: Mercedes Sosa — "Solo le Pido a Dios" / "Gracias a la Vida" / "Cuando Tenga la Tierra" canonical exile-era
Atahualpa Yupanqui — "El Arriero" / "Los Hermanos" / foundational Argentine folk-protest
León Gieco — "Solo le Pido a Dios" 1978 (recorded with Mercedes Sosa)
Movimiento del Nuevo Cancionero 1963 manifesto by Tejada Gómez and Matus

items.name: Italian canti partigiani (Resistance songs)
items.lineage: Italian Resistance-and-Partisan-songbook protest-song tradition continuous from 1943-1945 anti-fascist Resistance era ("Bella Ciao" as the Resistance anthem in its post-1948 mythologized form, though the song's actual partisan-era usage is disputed by scholars) through post-war Italian Communist Party and Italian left-wing political-songwriter tradition continuous into modern Italian protest-song repertoire
items.description: The Italian canti partigiani (Resistance-and-Partisan songbook) protest-song tradition continuous from 1943-1945 anti-fascist Resistance era ("Bella Ciao" as the Resistance anthem in its post-1948 mythologized form, though the song's actual partisan-era usage is disputed by scholars and Tom Behan and Cesare Bermani research traces its WWII partisan-era propagation primarily to the Maiella and Garibaldi brigades) through post-war Italian Communist Party and Italian left-wing political-songwriter tradition (Ivan Della Mea, Giovanna Marini, Cantacronache collective, the Nuovo Canzoniere Italiano scene) continuous into modern Italian protest-song repertoire. Defined by acoustic-guitar-and-voice songwriter-format or unaccompanied-group-vocal arrangement, Italian-folk-modal melodic vocabulary, strophic verse-chorus song-form for crowd-singability, Italian-language plainspoken political-grievance text register, anti-fascist-and-labor-and-anti-war lyric content, transmission via partisan-period oral tradition through 1960s-70s political-songbook publication.
exemplars: "Bella Ciao" canonical Resistance anthem (post-1948 mythologized form)
"Siamo i ribelli della montagna" partisan-era documented
Giovanna Marini — Nuovo Canzoniere Italiano canonical post-war singer-archivist
Ivan Della Mea — Italian post-war political-songwriter

items.name: Portuguese música de intervenção
items.lineage: Portuguese música de intervenção ("intervention music") protest-song tradition continuous from 1960s-1974 Estado Novo dictatorship-era political folk-and-songwriter scene; centered on José Afonso, Adriano Correia de Oliveira, Sérgio Godinho, José Mário Branco; José Afonso's "Grândola Vila Morena" was the radio-signal that triggered the April 25 1974 Carnation Revolution
items.description: The Portuguese música de intervenção ("intervention music") protest-song tradition continuous from 1960s-1974 Estado Novo dictatorship-era political folk-and-songwriter scene through post-1974 Carnation-Revolution era continuous performance; centered on José Afonso (the foundational figure whose "Grândola Vila Morena" 1971 was broadcast on Rádio Renascença at 00:25 on April 25 1974 as the radio-signal triggering the Carnation Revolution that overthrew the Estado Novo), Adriano Correia de Oliveira, Sérgio Godinho, José Mário Branco, Fausto Bordalo Dias, and the Movimento das Forças Armadas-aligned songwriter scene. Defined by acoustic-guitar-and-voice songwriter-format with frequent guitarra-portuguesa fado-instrumental integration, fado-and-folk-modal melodic vocabulary inflecting the Western-songwriter frame, Portuguese-language literary-political text register, anti-Estado-Novo-and-anti-colonial-war (anti-Angola-Mozambique-Guinea-Bissau-colonial-war) lyric content, frequently censorship-faced and exile-context performance.
exemplars: José Afonso — "Grândola Vila Morena" 1971 Carnation Revolution canonical
José Afonso — "Os Vampiros" / "Eu Vou Ser Como a Toupeira" canonical-era catalog
Adriano Correia de Oliveira — "Trova do Vento que Passa" 1963
José Mário Branco — "FMI" 1982 / "Mudam-se os Tempos, Mudam-se as Vontades"

items.name: South African freedom song (anti-apartheid)
items.lineage: South African anti-apartheid freedom-song tradition continuous from late-1940s post-apartheid-codification group-vocal protest practice through the 1976 Soweto Uprising and 1980s-1990s liberation-and-transition era; defined by group-vocal harmony-singing, toyi-toyi marching-chant, and canonical anthems integrated into both the African National Congress and broader liberation movements
items.description: The South African anti-apartheid freedom-song tradition continuous from late-1940s post-apartheid-codification group-vocal protest practice through the 1976 Soweto Uprising and 1980s-1990s liberation-and-transition era; defined by group-vocal harmony-singing in the South-African isicathamiya-derived close-harmony arrangement, toyi-toyi (foot-stamping marching-chant of liberation-movement origin), and canonical anthems integrated into both African National Congress mass-mobilization and broader liberation movements. Defined by unaccompanied group-vocal close-harmony arrangement, call-and-response architecture with lead-and-chorus alternation, characteristic anti-apartheid lyric content in isiZulu, isiXhosa, Sesotho, Afrikaans, and English, characteristic Zulu-and-Xhosa modal vocabulary in the harmonic underpinning, toyi-toyi rhythmic-foot-pattern integrated into vocal arrangement during liberation-era marching contexts.
exemplars: "Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika" 1897 Enoch Sontonga canonical (now part of the South African national anthem)
Hugh Masekela — "Bring Him Back Home" 1987 / "Soweto Blues" 1976

items.name: Korean minjung gayo (민중가요, people's song)
items.lineage: Korean minjung gayo ("people's song") democracy-movement protest-song tradition continuous from late-1970s anti-Park-Chung-hee resistance through the May 1980 Gwangju Uprising through 1980s anti-Chun-Doo-hwan student-and-labor-movement era; canonical anthems include "Imjin River" and "Marching for our beloved" ("님을 위한 행진곡")
items.description: The Korean minjung gayo (민중가요, "people's song") democracy-movement protest-song tradition continuous from late-1970s anti-Park-Chung-hee Yushin-regime resistance through the May 18 1980 Gwangju Uprising (the foundational event of Korean democratic-movement memory) through 1980s anti-Chun-Doo-hwan student-and-labor-movement era continuing into the 1987 June Democratic Movement and broader Korean democratization-era political culture. Defined by acoustic-guitar-and-voice songwriter-format or unaccompanied-group-vocal mass-singing arrangement, Korean-Hangul plainspoken political-grievance text register, characteristic anthemic-march tempo and Western-folk-modal melodic vocabulary, group-singing crowd-anthem function. The canonical anthem "Marching for our beloved" ("님을 위한 행진곡") composed 1981 in commemoration of Gwangju Uprising martyrs Yoon Sang-won and Park Ki-soon has become a pan-Asian democracy-movement song (also adopted in Hong Kong, Thailand, Myanmar pro-democracy protests).
exemplars: "님을 위한 행진곡" (Marching for our beloved) 1981 canonical Gwangju anthem

items.description: The Catalan Nova Cançó ("new song") minority-language protest-song tradition continuous from 1959 founding by Els Setze Jutges collective (the "Sixteen Judges" — sixteen Catalan-language-singer-songwriters who united against Franco-regime Catalan-language suppression) through the Franco-era 1959-1975 Catalan-cultural-resistance period continuous into post-Franco 1975-onward Catalan-cultural-revival; centered on Lluís Llach (whose "L'Estaca" 1968 became a transnational anti-authoritarian anthem covered in Polish, Russian, French, and dozens of other languages), Raimon, Joan Manuel Serrat (who sang in both Catalan and Spanish), Maria del Mar Bonet (Mallorcan-Catalan), Pi de la Serra, and the broader Els Setze Jutges-aligned scene. Defined by acoustic-guitar-and-voice songwriter-format with chanson-française stylistic inheritance (the Catalan scene was deeply influenced by Georges Brassens and Jacques Brel), Catalan-language commitment as central political-cultural statement, melodic-folk vocabulary inflected by Catalan-folk-modal traditions, intimate-acoustic timbre.

items.description: The Algerian raï tradition from its 1920s-1930s Oran-region origin as Bedouin-Andalusian women's-tradition (the cheikha women-singers performing in cafe-and-cabaret contexts the political-and-erotic-and-anti-clerical raï repertoire considered scandalous by both colonial-French and Islamic-conservative-Algerian authorities) through 1970s-1980s pre-commercial cheikha-and-cheb politicization era through 1990s commercial-pop-raï crossover. The political-and-anti-clerical content of pre-commercial raï made it a target of both Algerian-state censorship and Islamist-fundamentalist violence — Cheb Hasni was assassinated September 1994.

items.description: The Egyptian political-vocal tradition founded by Sayyed Darwish (1892-1923, the early-20th-century musical pioneer who composed in support of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British occupation including the song "Bilady, Bilady, Bilady" that became the Egyptian national anthem) continuous through Sheikh Imam Eissa (1918-1995, the blind oud-and-voice political-protest singer whose collaborations with the colloquial-Arabic poet Ahmed Fouad Negm produced the canonical 1960s-1990s anti-Nasser-and-anti-Sadat political-protest songbook that circulated underground throughout the Arab world). items.description: The Polish poezja śpiewana ("sung poetry") and piosenka literacka ("literary song") protest-song tradition continuous from 1960s-1980s Communist-era Polish political-songwriter scene through the 1980-1989 Solidarność-and-martial-law era continuous into post-1989 democratization-era continuous performance; centered on Jacek Kaczmarski (the Solidarność-aligned songwriter-bard whose "Mury" 1978 — adapted from Lluís Llach's "L'Estaca" with new Polish lyrics — became the Solidarność anthem), Przemysław Gintrowski, Zbigniew Łapiński, Wojciech Bellon, and the broader student-cabaret-and-political-songwriter scene. items.description: The Vietnamese nhạc phản chiến ("anti-war music") protest-song tradition continuous from 1960s-1975 Vietnam-War-era South-Vietnam political-songwriter scene continuous through post-1975 reunification-era continuous performance (though heavily restricted under unified-Vietnam government for songs critical of either side of the conflict); centered on Trịnh Công Sơn (1939-2001, the most-iconic Vietnamese songwriter whose "Nối Vòng Tay Lớn" 1969 anti-war anthem and broader anti-war catalog made him simultaneously banned by both the South-Vietnam-republic and post-1975-North-Vietnam-government for periods), Phạm Duy, Khánh Ly (Trịnh Công Sơn's canonical vocalist). items.name: Brazilian MPB-era protest (música popular brasileira during dictatorship)

items.description: The Brazilian Música Popular Brasileira (MPB) protest-song tradition continuous from 1964-1985 Brazilian-military-dictatorship-era political-songwriter scene; centered on Chico Buarque (the foundational figure whose subtle-allegorical anti-dictatorship songs evaded censorship most consistently — "Cálice" 1973 punned on "shut up" pun in Portuguese, "Apesar de Você" 1970 disguised as a love-song), Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil (the Tropicália foundational figures arrested and exiled 1969-1972), Geraldo Vandré ("Pra Não Dizer que Não Falei das Flores" 1968 became the canonical Brazilian protest-anthem after its Festival Internacional da Canção performance), Milton Nascimento (the Clube da Esquina collective), Edu Lobo. Defined by nylon-string-guitar-and-voice songwriter-format with samba-and-bossa-nova harmonic-and-rhythmic vocabulary inflecting the protest-song frame, Brazilian-Portuguese literary-text register with extensive allegorical-disguise (necessary under censorship), sophisticated-extended-chord harmonic vocabulary descended from bossa-nova, intimate-acoustic-orchestral timbre.
exemplars: Geraldo Vandré — "Pra Não Dizer que Não Falei das Flores" 1968 canonical

items.description: The Greek politicized éntechno ("artistic music") protest-song tradition centered on Mikis Theodorakis (1925-2021, the foundational figure whose Communist-Party-aligned political-songwriter career spanned the 1944-1945 Civil-War partisan era through the 1967-1974 Greek Junta exile-and-imprisonment era and continuous through post-Metapolitefsi democratic-era continuous performance — Theodorakis was arrested-imprisoned-and-internally-exiled during the Junta years 1967-1970 and his music was banned during that period); the canonical Theodorakis songbooks include the Mauthausen Trilogy 1965 (texts by Holocaust survivor Iakovos Kambanellis), Romiosini settings of Yannis Ritsos texts, and Epitaphios setting of Yannis Ritsos's 1936 elegy. Defined by bouzouki-and-guitar-and-voice songwriter-format with Greek-Eastern-modal melodic vocabulary, rebetiko-instrumental-lineage integration, classical-Greek-poetic-text register (Ritsos, Elytis, Seferis, Kambanellis poetic-text settings), political-anti-Junta-and-anti-fascist lyric content frequently encoded through poetic-allegory.

items.description: The Irish rebel-song tradition continuous from 18th-century 1798-United-Irishmen rebellion songs ("The Wearing of the Green" 1798 / "Bold Robert Emmet" 1803) through 19th-century Young Ireland and Fenian songbook (Thomas Davis "A Nation Once Again" 1844 canonical) through 1916 Easter Rising era ("The Foggy Dew" canonical 1916-era) through Northern-Irish Troubles 1968-1998 era (the late-20th-century rebel-songbook of The Wolfe Tones, Christy Moore, and others) continuous into modern Irish-traditional-music repertoire. Defined by acoustic-guitar-and-fiddle-and-tin-whistle-and-voice arrangement, Irish-modal melodic vocabulary (Dorian and Mixolydian predominantly), English-language and occasional Irish-Gaelic-language text register, anti-British-and-anti-colonial-and-Republican-Movement lyric content, group-singing pub-and-session context, frequent adoption of pre-existing folk-tunes for new political-text settings.

items.description: The Yoruba oríkì praise-poetry tradition continuous from pre-colonial Yoruba ritual-practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Yoruba-and-Yoruba-diaspora practice across southwestern Nigeria, Benin, Togo, and the Atlantic Afro-diaspora; the oríkì is the canonical Yoruba praise-poetry-song-form naming the praise-receiver through accumulated epithet-and-ancestral-name lineage. Defined by talking-drum (dùndún) and dunun foundation supporting recitative vocal declamation, Yoruba tonal-language vocal-melody constrained by speech-tone patterns, free-meter declamatory phrasing permitting extensive name-and-epithet interpolation, accumulated-epithet structural form where each line builds on the previous through ancestral-name-and-praise-epithet sequence, Yoruba-language text register with specialized oríkì vocabulary, performed at weddings, funerals, ritual-installations, and family-gatherings.

items.description: The Zulu izibongo praise-poetry tradition continuous from pre-colonial Zulu royal-court praise-singer (imbongi) practice through 19th-century Shaka-kaSenzangakhona-era continuous performance into modern South-African Zulu cultural-practice; the imbongi is the hereditary praise-poetry-and-political-orator role with specialized voice-projection-and-recitation training. Defined by unaccompanied heightened-speech declamation (the imbongi practice is closer to oratorical-declaimed-speech than to song proper), free-meter rapid-paced recitation, Zulu tonal-language vocal-melody constrained by speech-tone patterns, characteristic vocal-projection-and-overtone-rich timbre, isiZulu-language text register with specialized izibongo metaphorical-and-praise vocabulary, accumulated-epithet structural form (each Zulu king is praised through a documented sequence of epithets across generations). The izibongo tradition extended into modern South-African political-oratory — Nelson Mandela was eulogized through imbongi praise-poetry at his funeral.

Linda Mkhize — Zulu izibongo modern continuous-tradition

items.description: The Akan-Asante royal court-music kete tradition continuous from pre-colonial Asantehene court-music practice (17th-19th century Asante Empire era) through colonial-period continuous performance into modern Ghanaian Asante cultural-practice; the kete ensemble (the royal-court praise-music ensemble featuring talking-drum-and-percussion-and-vocal-foreground ensemble) is one of the most documented Akan court-music traditions. Defined by talking-drum (atumpan) and dunun-and-supporting-drum ensemble providing rhythmic-foundation, atumpan-talking-drum encoding praise-text through Twi-tonal-language tone-matching (the atumpan player "speaks" the praise-text through drumming), call-and-response group-vocal foreground with hereditary-court-praise-singer leading, Akan-Twi text register with specialized royal-praise vocabulary, performance at Asantehene court-ceremonies, royal-funerals, and Akwasidae festival.

Modern Manhyia Palace kete continuous performance

items.description: The Shona mbira-and-vocal praise-music tradition continuous from pre-colonial Zimbabwe Karanga-Shona ritual-practice through colonial-period continuous performance into modern Zimbabwean Shona-cultural practice; the mbira dzavadzimu ("mbira of the ancestors") is the canonical Shona ritual-and-praise instrument used at bira ceremonies for ancestor-praise-and-spirit-possession-induction. Defined by interlocking-mbira-pattern foundation (the kushaura "leading" and kutsinhira "interweaving" parts woven by two mbira players), seven-tone Shona modal vocabulary (the mbira tuning system is distinct from twelve-tet Western), call-and-response vocal-foreground with kudeketera-poetic-vocal-improvisation over the cycling mbira pattern, ChiShona text register with specialized ancestor-praise vocabulary, cyclical-form structure permitting hours-long bira ceremony performance.

Thomas Mapfumo — Shona mbira-derived chimurenga political-praise

items.description: The pan-Indian Hindu devotional praise-song tradition continuous from medieval Bhakti-movement era (12th-18th century North-and-South-Indian bhakti-saints including Kabir, Mirabai, Tulsidas, Surdas, Tyagaraja, Annamacharya) through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Hindu-and-Hindu-diaspora practice; stuti (formal praise-hymn of a specific deity) and bhajan (devotional-praise song-form, more popular-accessible than stuti) constitute the canonical praise-vocabulary. Defined by harmonium-and-tabla-and-tanpura accompaniment to vocal-foreground, raga-derived melodic vocabulary (Yaman, Bhairavi, Bhupali, Kafi, Bilawal frequent), Hindi-Urdu-Sanskrit text register with deity-praise lyric content, ornamented melismatic vocal practice, group-singing accessibility (bhajan-mandali community-singing context), strophic structure permitting infinite verse-and-name interpolation.

Anup Jalota — modern bhajan canonical vocalist

items.name: Sikh shabad kirtan (Gurbani praise)

items.description: The Sikh devotional kirtan tradition continuous from 15th-16th century Guru-Nanak-era Sikh-spiritual-music foundation through codification under Guru Arjan (the fifth Guru who compiled the Adi Granth scripture with specific raga-assignments for each shabad) and continuous performance through 17th-19th century historical-Punjab-region into modern Sikh-and-Sikh-diaspora practice; the kirtan ensemble accompanies shabad (Gurbani-scriptural) text-recitation in gurdwara (Sikh-temple) context. Defined by harmonium-and-tabla-and-tanpura accompaniment with hereditary raagi-jatha (Sikh-traditional-kirtan ensemble) vocal foreground, raga-derived melodic vocabulary specifically prescribed for each shabad in the Adi Granth (the scriptural codification of raga-text-pairings is one of the most-elaborated in any tradition), Punjabi-Gurmukhi text register with Gurbani-scriptural-text foreground, devotional-praise lyric content, congregational-listening performance context.

items.name: Sufi munajat and naat (praise of God and Prophet)

items.description: The Sufi devotional praise-song tradition continuous from medieval Sufi-poetic era (13th-15th century Rumi, Hafez, Saadi era when the Sufi-poetic-praise corpus was codified) through Indo-Persian-Mughal-era continuous performance into modern Sufi-and-Muslim-diaspora practice; munajat (intimate-supplication praise of God) and naat (praise of the Prophet Muhammad) are the canonical Sufi praise-forms, distinct from the broader qawwali ecstatic-praise form (which is more elaborate and ensemble-driven). Defined by Arabic-maqam-or-Persian-dastgāh-or-Hindustani-raga modal vocabulary depending on cultural-regional variant, harmonium-and-tabla accompaniment to vocal-foreground (in Indo-Persian-Mughal variants), classical-Persian-or-Arabic-or-Urdu poetic-text register with Sufi-mystical-poetic vocabulary, ornamented melismatic vocal practice, devotional-praise-of-God-and-Prophet lyric content.

items.description: The Tibetan-Buddhist praise-recitation tradition continuous from 8th-9th century Indo-Tibetan-Buddhist-foundation era through 11th-14th century Sarma-school monastery-formalization era into modern Tibetan-Buddhist-monastic and Tibetan-Buddhist-diaspora practice; thödröl ("liberation through hearing," the Tibetan-Buddhist Bardo-Thödröl praise-recitation traditions including the famous Book-of-the-Dead recitation) and broader lama-praise repertoires constitute the praise-vocabulary distinct from the multiphonic Gyuto-Gyume monastic chant practice which is more liturgical. Defined by unaccompanied or sparse-bell-and-cymbal-accented vocal recitation, free-meter ametrical chant practice, low-fundamental drone-overtone voice production characteristic of Tibetan-monastic vocal-training, Tibetan-classical text register with Sanskrit-derived Buddhist-philosophical vocabulary, devotional-praise-of-bodhisattvas-and-lineage-lamas lyric content.

Dzogchen Ponlop Rinpoche — modern Tibetan-Buddhist praise
Modern Sera-Gaden-Drepung monastic praise continuous tradition

items.name: Welsh moliannu and cerdd dant (Welsh praise-poetry)
items.lineage: Welsh medieval praise-poetry tradition continuous from 6th-7th-century Taliesin-and-Aneirin foundational era (the Cynfeirdd "early-poets") through 12th-13th century Gogynfeirdd "poets-of-the-princes" era of court-praise-poetry through continuous-Welsh-bardic transmission into modern penillion-singing and cerdd dant ("string-craft") harp-and-voice tradition
items.description: The Welsh medieval praise-poetry tradition continuous from 6th-7th-century Taliesin-and-Aneirin foundational era (the Cynfeirdd "early-poets" preserved in the 13th-14th century manuscript Book of Taliesin) through 12th-13th century Gogynfeirdd "poets-of-the-princes" era of court-praise-poetry (the Welsh princes Gruffydd ap Cynan, Owain Gwynedd, Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, Llywelyn ap Gruffydd received elaborate moliannu praise-poetry from court-bards) through continuous-Welsh-bardic transmission via the 17th-19th century cyff arwest poetry tradition into modern cerdd dant ("string-craft") harp-and-voice and penillion-singing-tradition. Defined by Celtic-harp accompaniment to vocal-foreground (the cerdd dant pattern features harp playing a hymn-tune while voice declaims a different metrical poem-text), Welsh-strict-meter (cynghanedd) text register, intricate-internal-consonant-and-vowel pattern, Welsh-historical-and-religious-praise lyric content, hereditary-bardic professional role.
exemplars: Taliesin — 6th-century foundational Welsh praise-poet (Book of Taliesin manuscript)
Bryn Terfel — modern Welsh praise-vocal cerdd dant performance

items.name: Hawaiian mele inoa (name-song / praise-chant)
items.lineage: Hawaiian praise-and-name-chant tradition continuous from pre-contact Hawaiian ritual-practice through 19th-century Hawaiian-Kingdom-era continuous performance and publication into 20th-century Hawaiian-cultural-revival; the mele inoa is the canonical Hawaiian praise-chant-form naming the praise-receiver through genealogical-and-place-name lineage
items.description: The Hawaiian praise-and-name-chant tradition continuous from pre-contact Hawaiian ritual-practice through 19th-century Hawaiian-Kingdom-era continuous performance and publication (mele inoa, like kanikau funeral-chants, were published in Hawaiian-language newspapers from the 1830s onward) into 20th-century Hawaiian-cultural-revival; the mele inoa ("name-song") is the canonical Hawaiian praise-chant-form naming the praise-receiver (typically a chief, ali'i royal-figure, or beloved person) through genealogical-and-place-name lineage. Defined by oli (chant) free-meter recitation in characteristic Hawaiian voice-production (the kāmākau voice-production with specific glottal-onset on 'okina), Hawaiian-language text register with extensive praise-of-the-recipient and place-naming, unaccompanied solo-vocal performance, ritual-bounded performance context. Distinguished from kanikau (funeral-chant) by praise-of-living-person function rather than mourning-of-the-deceased.
exemplars: Queen Lili'uokalani — mele inoa compositions including Aloha 'Oe
Mele inoa for Kamehameha I, II, III, IV, V (canonical Hawaiian-royal-praise corpus)
Mary Kawena Pukui — mele inoa ethnographic-and-creative documentation
Edith Kanaka'ole — modern mele inoa-revival chant
Modern mele inoa for new-born babies (continuous-living tradition)

items.name: Māori waiata mōteatea / patere (Maori praise-chant)
items.lineage: Māori praise-chant tradition continuous from pre-contact Māori ritual-practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance at marae context into modern Māori-cultural-revival; patere (women's rapid-recitation praise-and-genealogy-chant) and pao (impromptu praise-song) are the canonical Māori praise-chant forms
items.description: The Māori praise-chant tradition continuous from pre-contact Māori ritual-practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance at marae context into modern Māori-cultural-revival; patere (women's rapid-recitation praise-and-genealogy-chant typically performed in response to slights or insults requiring whakapapa-defense) and pao (impromptu praise-song often two-line couplet praise-improvisations) are the canonical Māori praise-chant forms within the broader waiata mōteatea (chant-song) category. Defined by narrow-range pentatonic-leaning melodic-vocabulary characteristic of Māori-traditional vocal practice, free-meter rapid-paced recitation, te-reo-Māori text register with extensive whakapapa (genealogy) and praise-and-historical-narrative content, unaccompanied solo-or-group vocal performance, ritual-bounded performance context at marae.
exemplars: Hirini Melbourne — traditional waiata mōteatea recordings 1980s-1990s
Patere repertoire documented by Apirana Ngata (Ngā Mōteatea Vol I-IV collection)
Whirimako Black — modern Māori praise-chant revival
Tūhoe tribal waiata mōteatea corpus (Best 1925 ethnography)

items.name: Arabic madh and qasida (Arabic praise-poetry)
items.lineage: Arabic classical praise-poetry tradition continuous from pre-Islamic jāhiliyya-era qasida ode-form (the canonical pre-Islamic Mu'allaqat seven-poem collection) through medieval-Islamic-era continuous performance into modern Arabic-classical-poetry recitation practice; madh (praise) and qasida (extended-ode) are the canonical Arabic praise-poetry-and-song forms
items.description: The Arabic classical praise-poetry tradition continuous from pre-Islamic jāhiliyya-era qasida ode-form (the canonical pre-Islamic Mu'allaqat seven-poem collection from 6th-7th century Arabian-peninsula) through medieval-Islamic-era continuous performance into modern Arabic-classical-poetry recitation practice; madh (praise) and qasida (extended-ode following the classical Arabic-poetry monorhyme-and-monometer form) are the canonical Arabic praise-poetry-and-song forms. Defined by oud-and-voice arrangement when sung (the qasida is foundationally a recited-poetic form rather than a sung-musical form, but sung-qasida traditions continue particularly in Andalusi-Maghreb and Levantine traditions), classical-Arabic text register with elaborate-rhetorical embellishment, melismatic vocal practice in sung-variants, praise of the patron-or-tribal-figure or in Islamic-era praise-of-the-Prophet (the latter overlapping with the naat tradition).
exemplars: Mu'allaqat seven-poem pre-Islamic praise-and-ode collection canonical
Imru' al-Qais — pre-Islamic Mu'allaqat poet canonical
Lebanese-Egyptian sung-qasida continuous tradition (Umm Kulthum-era settings)

items.name: Mande jeli / griot praise-song
items.lineage: Mande-and-Wolof West-African praise-song tradition continuous from medieval Mali Empire era (13th-15th century Sundiata Keita era when the jeli/griot caste-tradition was codified) through colonial-period continuous performance into modern Mande-and-Wolof and Mande-diaspora practice; the jeli is the hereditary praise-singer-and-historian role with documented professional-genealogical lineage
items.description: The Mande-and-Wolof West-African praise-song tradition continuous from medieval Mali Empire era (13th-15th century Sundiata Keita era when the jeli/griot caste-tradition was codified) through colonial-period continuous performance into modern Mande-and-Wolof and Mande-diaspora practice across Mali, Senegal, Guinea, Gambia, Burkina Faso, and the broader Sahel; the jeli (Mande) / géwél (Wolof) / griot (French-colonial-loanword) is the hereditary praise-singer-and-historian role with documented professional-genealogical lineage (the Kouyaté and Diabaté and Tounkara families being among the most-documented jeli lineages). Defined by kora (21-string harp-lute) and ngoni and balafon and voice arrangement, Mande-pentatonic modal vocabulary, characteristic praise-narrative-form structure (the canonical Sundiata epic is the foundational jeli-praise-narrative), Manding-Maninka-Bambara-Wolof-Mandinka text register with specialized praise-and-genealogical vocabulary, accumulated-name-and-epithet declamatory style. Distinguished from the broader West-African pop traditions descended from jeli practice (Salif Keita and Toumani Diabaté's Symmetric Orchestra crossing into popular form).
exemplars: Kasse Mady Diabaté — Mande jeli-vocal canonical
Ali Farka Touré — Songhai-influenced Mande blues-praise
Sundiata Keita epic-praise-narrative (foundational jeli text canonical 13th-century)

items.name: English nursery rhyme
items.lineage: English-language nursery-rhyme tradition continuous from medieval and early-modern English play-song origins through 18th-century chapbook publication (Tommy Thumb's Pretty Song Book 1744 the earliest documented English nursery-rhyme collection) through Iona and Peter Opie's 20th-century Lore and Language of Schoolchildren ethnographic documentation
items.description: The English-language nursery-rhyme tradition continuous from medieval and early-modern English play-song origins through 18th-century chapbook publication (Tommy Thumb's Pretty Song Book 1744 the earliest documented English nursery-rhyme collection; Mother Goose's Melody 1765 codifying many canonical rhymes) through Iona and Peter Opie's 20th-century Lore and Language of Schoolchildren ethnographic documentation establishing the durability of oral-transmission across British-and-American-childhood generations. Defined by narrow-range pentatonic-or-hexatonic melodic vocabulary, repeating short melodic cells durable across centuries (the "Mary Had a Little Lamb" tune is the documented first sound-recorded human voice on Edison's 1877 tinfoil cylinder), action-coordination structure for hand-game and circle-game and counting-out applications, English-language plain-text register, unaccompanied voice as primary performance medium.
exemplars: "Mary Had a Little Lamb" 1830 Sarah Josepha Hale text
"Ring Around the Rosie" (Iona and Peter Opie documentation)
"Twinkle Twinkle Little Star" 1806 Jane Taylor text (on French "Ah! vous dirai-je, maman" tune)
"London Bridge Is Falling Down" medieval-origin English ring-game

items.name: French comptines (counting-out and play-song rhymes)
items.lineage: French-language children's play-song and counting-out-rhyme tradition continuous from medieval-and-early-modern French folk-play-song origins through 19th-century French-Republic school-curriculum codification into modern continuous French-and-French-Canadian-and-Francophone-African childhood-practice
items.description: The French-language children's play-song and counting-out-rhyme (comptine) tradition continuous from medieval-and-early-modern French folk-play-song origins through 19th-century French-Republic school-curriculum codification into modern continuous French-and-French-Canadian-and-Francophone-African childhood-practice. Defined by narrow-range melodic vocabulary, characteristic French-language text register with the syllabic-stress pattern of French (final-syllable stress) shaping musical-phrase delivery, action-coordination structure for circle-game and finger-game and counting-out applications, characteristic French-folk-modal pentatonic-leaning vocabulary, durable oral transmission. The canonical French nursery-rhyme corpus includes Frère Jacques (Brother John), Sur le pont d'Avignon (On the Avignon Bridge), Au clair de la lune (By the Light of the Moon), Alouette (Lark, with French-Canadian skinning-the-lark text-tradition).
exemplars: "Sur le pont d'Avignon" medieval-origin French ring-game
"Au clair de la lune" 18th-century French folk-song

items.description: The German-language children's play-song (Kinderlieder) and counting-out-rhyme (Abzählreime) tradition continuous from medieval-and-early-modern German folk-play-song origins through Brothers Grimm 19th-century Kinder- und Hausmärchen documentation context (the Grimm collection includes children's-rhyme apparatus) and Des Knaben Wunderhorn 1805-1808 Brentano-Arnim folk-poetry collection through 19th-20th century German school-curriculum codification into modern continuous Austrian-and-Swiss-and-German childhood-practice. Defined by characteristic German-language stress-pattern (initial-syllable-stress) shaping musical-phrase delivery, narrow-range pentatonic-or-hexatonic melodic vocabulary, action-coordination structure for finger-game (Hoppe hoppe Reiter knee-bouncing rhyme), counting-out (Abzählreim), and circle-game applications, durable oral transmission across centuries.
exemplars: "Ein Männlein steht im Walde" forest-walking rhyme

items.name: Italian filastrocche (nursery rhymes)
items.lineage: Italian-language children's play-song (filastrocche) tradition continuous from medieval-and-early-modern Italian folk-play-song origins through 19th-century Italian-unification-era folklore-collection context into modern continuous Italian-and-Italian-diaspora childhood-practice
items.description: The Italian-language children's play-song (filastrocche) tradition continuous from medieval-and-early-modern Italian folk-play-song origins through 19th-century Italian-unification-era folklore-collection context into modern continuous Italian-and-Italian-diaspora childhood-practice. Defined by characteristic Italian-language stress-pattern (penultimate-syllable-stress in most words) shaping musical-phrase delivery, narrow-range melodic vocabulary, action-coordination structure for circle-game (Giro giro tondo, the Italian counterpart to Ring Around the Rosie) and clapping-game applications, regional dialect-variation across Northern-Italian, Tuscan, Roman, Neapolitan, and Sicilian filastrocche corpora.

items.name: Spanish and Latin American rondas (children's circle-songs)
items.lineage: Spanish-language children's circle-song (ronda) tradition continuous from medieval-and-early-modern Spanish folk-play-song origins through colonial-period transmission to Latin America and continuous practice across the Spanish-speaking Americas into modern Mexican-and-Latin-American childhood-practice
items.description: The Spanish-language children's circle-song (ronda) tradition continuous from medieval-and-early-modern Spanish folk-play-song origins through colonial-period transmission to Latin America and continuous practice across the Spanish-speaking Americas (Mexico, Colombia, Argentina, Chile, Peru, and broader Latin American childhood-practice) into modern Mexican-and-Latin-American childhood-practice. Defined by call-and-response group-vocal structure characteristic of circle-game performance, Spanish-language text register, action-coordination structure for circle-game and clapping-game applications, regional-variation across Iberian-Spanish, Mexican, Andean, Argentine, and Caribbean ronda corpora.
exemplars: "La víbora de la mar" Mexican circle-game canonical
"El patio de mi casa" Spanish circle-game ronda

items.name: Russian poteshki and pestushki (children's rhymes)
items.lineage: Russian-language children's play-song tradition continuous from medieval-and-early-modern Russian folk-play-song origins through 19th-century Russian-folklorist documentation (Vladimir Dahl and others) into modern continuous Russian childhood-practice; poteshki (entertaining-rhymes for older children) and pestushki (caretaking-rhymes for infants) constitute the core repertoire
items.description: The Russian-language children's play-song tradition continuous from medieval-and-early-modern Russian folk-play-song origins through 19th-century Russian-folklorist documentation (Vladimir Dahl's mid-19th-century folklore collection canonical) into modern continuous Russian childhood-practice; poteshki (потешки, "entertaining-rhymes" for older children) and pestushki (пестушки, "caretaking-rhymes" for infants, typically performed by adults during infant-bathing, infant-dressing, and infant-feeding routines) constitute the core repertoire. Defined by characteristic Russian-language stress-pattern shaping musical-phrase delivery, narrow-range melodic vocabulary, infant-caretaking action-coordination structure in pestushki and circle-game-and-counting-out structure in poteshki, durable oral transmission within family-household setting.
exemplars: "Идёт коза рогатая" (Idyot koza rogataya) goat-chase infant-rhyme
"От топота копыт пыль по полю летит" tongue-twister rhyme

items.description: The Romanian-language children's play-song tradition continuous from medieval-and-early-modern Romanian folk-play-song origins through 19th-century Romanian-folklorist documentation (Vasile Alecsandri and the broader Romanian-folklore-collection movement) into modern continuous Romanian childhood-practice. Defined by characteristic Romanian-language stress-pattern shaping musical-phrase delivery, narrow-range melodic vocabulary, action-coordination structure for circle-game and counting-out applications, integration with the broader Romanian colinde Christmas-caroling and seasonal-festivity children's-song traditions.
exemplars: "Bate vântul frunzele" Romanian children's song canonical
"A ruginit frunza din vii" autumn-leaves children's song

items.name: Korean dongyo (동요, children's songs)
items.lineage: Korean children's song (dongyo) tradition continuous from premodern Korean folk-play-song origins through early-20th-century Korean-modernization codification (the 1920s-1940s Korean dongyo movement specifically created modern children's-song repertoire for school-curriculum-and-radio-broadcast use) into modern continuous South-and-North-Korean childhood-practice
items.description: The Korean children's song (동요, dongyo) tradition continuous from premodern Korean folk-play-song origins (the traditional warabe-uta-equivalent Korean children's repertoire including ganggangsullae circle-game) through early-20th-century Korean-modernization codification (the 1920s-1940s Korean dongyo movement specifically created modern children's-song repertoire for school-curriculum-and-radio-broadcast use during the Japanese-colonial era as a vehicle for Korean-language cultural-preservation) into modern continuous South-and-North-Korean childhood-practice. Defined by characteristic Korean-language Hangul-syllabic vocal-melody mapping, narrow-range pentatonic-or-Western-folk-modal melodic vocabulary, action-coordination structure, school-curriculum-integration codifying Korean-cultural-identity through children's repertoire.
exemplars: "엄마야 누나야" (Eomma-ya Nuna-ya) Yoon Geuk-yeong-text 1922 dongyo canonical

items.name: Japanese warabe-uta (童歌, children's play-songs)
items.lineage: Japanese children's play-song (warabe-uta) tradition continuous from premodern Japanese folk-play-song origins (Heian-era and earlier) through Edo-period continuous performance into modern continuous Japanese childhood-practice; distinct from the modern dōyō (童謡) school-curriculum-created children's-song movement of the 1920s-onward
items.description: The Japanese children's play-song (童歌, warabe-uta) tradition continuous from premodern Japanese folk-play-song origins (Heian-era and earlier documented sources reference warabe-uta) through Edo-period continuous performance into modern continuous Japanese childhood-practice; distinct from the modern dōyō (童謡) school-curriculum-created children's-song movement of the 1920s-onward (Kitahara Hakushū and Saijō Yaso text-tradition). Defined by Japanese yonanuki-pentatonic (no-fourth-no-seventh pentatonic) or in-scale (semitone-containing pentatonic) melodic vocabulary, characteristic Japanese-language mora-based syllabic mapping, action-coordination structure for circle-game (the famous Kagome-kagome game), hand-clapping-game (Sen-no Sen, Sen-no Sen), and finger-game applications, durable oral transmission within family-and-school settings.
exemplars: "ずいずいずっころばし" (Zui zui zukkorobashi) finger-game rhyme
"あんたがたどこさ" (Anta-gata doko sa) Kyushu-region ball-bouncing rhyme
"いっぽんでもニンジン" (Ippon demo ninjin) counting-rhyme

items.name: Mandarin tóngyáo (童謠, children's rhymes)
items.lineage: Mandarin-Chinese children's rhyme (童謠, tóngyáo) tradition continuous from premodern Chinese folk-play-song origins (the Shijing Book of Songs includes children's-rhyme apparatus from the 11th-7th-century-BCE Zhou-era) through imperial-Chinese continuous performance into modern continuous Mainland-Chinese-and-Taiwanese-and-Chinese-diaspora childhood-practice
items.description: The Mandarin-Chinese children's rhyme (童謠, tóngyáo) tradition continuous from premodern Chinese folk-play-song origins (the Shijing Book of Songs includes children's-rhyme apparatus from the 11th-7th-century-BCE Zhou-era) through imperial-Chinese continuous performance into modern continuous Mainland-Chinese-and-Taiwanese-and-Chinese-diaspora childhood-practice. Defined by Chinese pentatonic (gōng-shāng-jué-zhǐ-yǔ) melodic vocabulary, characteristic Mandarin-tonal-language vocal-melody constrained by speech-tone patterns (tone-shape-and-pitch-contour shaping musical-phrase delivery), narrow-range hexatonic-or-pentatonic melodic vocabulary, action-coordination structure for circle-game and hand-game applications, regional Mandarin-and-Cantonese-and-other-Sinitic-variant corpora.
exemplars: "两只老虎" (Liǎng zhī lǎohǔ) Two Tigers canonical (on Frère Jacques tune)
"小燕子" (Xiǎo yànzi) Little Swallow children's-song canonical
"小白兔" (Xiǎo báitù) Little White Rabbit rhyme

items.name: Hindi nursery rhyme (Indian school-curriculum children's songs)

items.description: The pan-Indian Hindi-medium children's school-song tradition continuous from late-19th-century Indian-Republican-modernization-era school-curriculum codification through post-independence 1947-onward Hindi-medium school-curriculum continuous practice; the tradition is intentionally constructed school-curriculum-music rather than continuous-folk-tradition (the "Lakdi ki kathi" and "Chubby Cheeks" rep are mid-late-20th-century compositions designed for school-curriculum use). Defined by Hindi-language text register with simple Devanagari-script-aligned syllabic mapping, raga-derived melodic vocabulary (predominantly Bhupali, Yaman, Bilawal) inflecting the school-curriculum frame, narrow-range hexatonic-or-Western-folk melodic vocabulary, action-coordination structure for school-classroom-and-home applications.
exemplars: "Lakdi ki kathi" (लकड़ी की काठी) Masoom 1983 film-canonical
"Chanda Mama" (चंदा मामा) Uncle Moon canonical bedtime-rhyme
"Hum Honge Kamyab" Hindi-translation of "We Shall Overcome" (school-curriculum)

items.description: The Tamil-language children's play-song tradition continuous from premodern Tamil folk-play-song origins through 20th-century Tamil-Nadu-and-Sri-Lankan-Tamil school-curriculum codification into modern continuous Tamil childhood-practice. items.description: The Bengali-language children's play-song tradition continuous from premodern Bengali folk-play-song origins through 19th-20th century Bengali-Renaissance literary-elevation (Rabindranath Tagore's Sahaj Path 1930 children's-curriculum rhyme-and-text reader canonical) and Sukumar Ray's nonsense-verse Abol Tabol 1923 (the foundational Bengali-children's-nonsense-poetry collection) into modern continuous Bengali-and-Bangladeshi childhood-practice. Defined by Bengali-language text register with characteristic Bangla-script syllabic mapping, raga-derived melodic vocabulary inflecting the children's-song frame, narrow-range hexatonic vocabulary, action-coordination structure, Tagore-inflected literary register in the school-curriculum-rep distinct from folk-tradition rhymes.

items.description: The Yoruba children's play-song tradition continuous from pre-colonial Yoruba family-and-community-rearing practice through 19th-20th century continuous performance into modern Yoruba-and-Yoruba-diaspora childhood-practice across southwestern Nigeria, Benin, Togo, and the Atlantic Afro-diaspora. Defined by Yoruba tonal-language vocal-melody constrained by speech-tone patterns (the tonal-Yoruba constraint produces characteristic falling-and-rising melodic-contour patterns specific to the language), call-and-response group-vocal structure for circle-game and clapping-game applications, hand-clapping-and-foot-stamping rhythmic accompaniment, Yoruba-language ọmọ-iya (child-of-mother / sibling) play-song repertoire integrating moral-instruction and animal-story content.
